Our results show that long‐term studies can be used to inform and interpret participatory science data to provide a framework that strengthens our understanding of how individual behaviours underlie differential responses to environmental variation across geographic scales.
ncf872ca8caa4: Our work examines how thermal stress and exposure duration jointly influence the foraging dynamics of incipient Lasius niger colonies, a rarely studied stage in which limited workforce may heighten vulnerability. Abstract Global warming affects organismal performance across biological levels, from molecular processes to complex behaviours. Ectotherms are particularly vulnerable to thermal stress, as their body temperature critically depends on ambient environmental conditions. Warming may affect their foraging behaviour and/or their activity patterns. Here, we experimentally investigated the effects of acute and chronic thermal stresses on foraging by an ectotherm species. Social insects are important ecosystem engineers. Colony survival and growth depend on successful foraging, and colonies are more susceptible to warming when they are young and have fewer workers. We investigate how heat intensity and exposure duration influence foraging dynamics and survivorship in young colonies of the Lasius niger ant. Using laboratory assays, we studied the effects of acute heat stress by exposing foragers to short (10 min) and intermediate (1 h) heat pulses of 25°C (control), 30°C, 35°C and 40°C. Furthermore, we investigated the effects of chronic heat stress by rearing colonies at 25°C:20°C (day:night, control conditions) or 35°C:30°C (heat stress) for 2 weeks. After heat exposure, we recorded the latency to initiate foraging, the number of foraging visits and individual and colony survival between treatments. We hypothesized that ants could cope with relatively low and relatively short heat shocks, but not with high or long heat exposures. We found that prolonged and high heat exposure indeed increased the mortality of foragers and colonies, increased the delay before foraging, and decreased the number of foraging trips. Reduced foraging capacity in young colonies is likely to have strong fitness consequences. The establishment of colonies is dependent on the rapid acquisition of resources to sustain exponential growth. Any slowdown in resource intake can limit colony development and prolong the duration of the incipient (newly founded) and vulnerable stage, ultimately reducing the likelihood of successful establishment. Résumé Le réchauffement climatique affecte les performances des organismes à tous les niveaux d'organisation biologique, des processus moléculaires aux comportements complexes. Les ectothermes sont particulièrement vulnérables au stress thermique, car leur température corporelle dépend étroitement des conditions environnementales. L'augmentation des températures peut ainsi modifier leurs comportements de recherche de nourriture et leurs rythmes d'activité. Nous avons étudié expérimentalement les effets de stress thermiques aigus et chroniques sur le comportement de fourragement d'une espèce ectotherme. Les insectes sociaux ont un rôle majeur d'ingénieurs des écosystèmes. La survie et la croissance des colonies dépendent du succès du fourragement, et les jeunes colonies, qui ont un peu d'ouvrières, sont particulièrement sensibles au réchauffement climatique. Nous avons examiné comment l'intensité et la durée d'exposition à la chaleur influencent la dynamique du fourragement et la survie de jeunes colonies de la fourmi Lasius niger. À l'aide d'expériences en laboratoire, nous avons évalué les effets d'un stress thermique aigu en exposant des ouvrières fourrageuses à des épisodes de chaleur de courte durée (10 min) ou de durée intermédiaire (1 h) à 25°C (contrôle), 30°C, 35°C et 40°C. Nous avons également étudié les effets d'un stress thermique chronique en maintenant des colonies pendant deux semaines sous un régime thermique de 25°C:20°C (jour:nuit; condition contrôle) ou de 35°C:30°C (stress thermique). Après exposition à la chaleur, nous avons mesuré le délai avant l'initiation du fourragement, le nombre de sorties de fourragement, ainsi que la survie des individus et des colonies.…
n7c0760d661f3: Behavioural variation can contribute to reproductive isolation and can be an important driver of speciation. Here, we show that a previously undescribed mechanism, parental care, can function as a postzygotic reproductive isolating barrier when dysregulated in hybrids. Abstract Variation in behaviour can contribute to reproductive isolation by preventing gene flow among populations. Here, we tested the novel hypothesis that parental care, when dysregulated, can function as a reproductive isolating mechanism in three‐spined stickleback fish (Gasterosteus aculeatus). In the typical ‘common’ stickleback ecotype, males provide care to their offspring by fanning with their pectoral fins and defending their nest. By contrast, a divergent ‘white’ stickleback ecotype has evolutionarily lost care and disperses embryos into the surrounding environment. We examined how paternal care from common, white and F1 hybrid fathers influenced offspring survival. We detected no intrinsic incompatibilities in embryos, but F1 hybrid fathers exhibited dysregulated parental care that coincided with decreased survival of parented offspring. The increased offspring mortality may be explained by further dysregulation of feeding and parenting circuitry, as F2 hybrids exhibited significantly higher rates of post‐fertilization filial cannibalism than common or white fathers. Additionally, despite strong divergence in nesting–building and courtship behaviour, F1 hybrids achieved mating success at a similar rate as male commons and whites, suggesting that prezygotic barriers against hybrids may be weak. The observed postzygotic isolation, and potentially weak prezygotic isolation in lab‐based studies, suggest that hybridization is likely occurring at low rates in the wild. Population genetic analysis supported this, as low proportions of putative hybrids were detected in sympatric sites. Together, these results may help explain why genetic divergence between these phenotypically distinct ecotypes is low and provide evidence that dysregulated parental behaviour can act as a newly discovered postzygotic reproductive isolating barrier.
nd671b2021907: Research Highlight: Lattanzio, M. S. (2026). Beyond thermoregulation: Active behavioural regulation of ultraviolet light exposure by a free‐ranging lizard. Journal of Animal Ecology, https://doi.org/10.1111/1365‐2656.70321. Exposure to ultraviolet radiation (UV) is both inevitable to any diurnal organism and a biological necessity for many animals. In many vertebrates, including lizards, UV exposure prompts important biological processes such as the endogenous production of vitamin D3. Overexposure, however, can damage DNA, cells and tissues. Despite an extensive literature on how heliothermic lizards regulate body temperatures in heterogeneous environments by moving between areas with different levels of sun exposure, very little attention has been given to how these organisms might also regulate UV exposure. In a study combining laboratory experiments to assess preferred body temperatures and levels of UV exposure and field observations of lizards in contrasting environments, Lattanzio (2026) demonstrates that ornate tree lizards (Urosaurus ornatus) are capable of effectively maintaining preferred body temperatures in environments with and without plentiful shade access. At the same time, lizards could effectively regulate their levels of UV exposure in environments with shade, but were poor at doing so on tree snags without sufficient cover. This suggests that lizards may suffer consequences, either due to the physiological impacts of overexposure to UV or due to behavioural trade‐offs, in these environments. Establishing the ecological relevance of UV exposure to lizard physiology, behaviours and life‐histories provides direction to exciting new research avenues, expanding the field of lizard thermoregulation to additional axes of environmental variation.
nf49e32d65281: Graphical summary of the main findings in Potts et al. (2026). Using GPS‐collar data from 586 individuals spanning 23 mammal species (10 carnivores, 13 herbivores) across five continents, comprising over 1,100,000 location fixes, the study tested how COVID‐19 lockdown restrictions on human movement affected mammal avoidance behaviour. Overall, avoidance of human presence weakened by 36% during lockdown; carnivores showed roughly twice the reduction observed in herbivores, though this difference was not statistically confirmed. The relaxation in avoidance was context‐dependent on the Human Footprint Index (HFI): in high‐HFI landscapes (left), animals ranged measurably closer to infrastructure once human movement declined, while in low‐HFI landscapes (right), avoidance distances held steady. Together, these results indicate that ongoing human activity, rather than infrastructure itself, is the primary driver of mammal avoidance behaviour. Abstract Urban and rural infrastructures with their human inhabitants are usually difficult to distinguish as separate entities, as they almost always coexist. Consequently, it remains unclear whether wildlife avoids buildings due to the physical barriers themselves or because of the people who live and move around them. To address this question, the authors utilised GPS‐tracking data from 586 individuals of 23 terrestrial mammal species at 35 sites across the globe. The featured study treats the COVID‐19 lockdowns of 2020 as a natural experiment that temporarily restricted human movement without changing the built‐up environment. The authors show that avoidance of buildings weakened during lockdowns, but only in landscapes with a high Human Footprint Index; in more remote, natural areas, avoidance barely changed at all. This context‐dependent response suggests that it is the presence and movement of people, not infrastructure on its own, that shapes how mammals use human‐modified landscapes, a finding with direct relevance for forecasting wildlife responses to future changes in human activity.
n7f9e39168a71: Across six European cities, great tits in more impervious territories had paler carotenoid‐based plumage, but not lower brightness or UV chroma. This suggests that urban habitat imperviousness is associated specifically with lower carotenoid pigment deposition, rather than broad changes in feather reflectance or structural quality. Abstract Urbanisation alters resource availability and exposes wildlife to novel environmental stressors, potentially driving phenotypic divergence. Carotenoid‐based plumage colouration is a condition‐dependent trait linked to dietary carotenoid acquisition and physiological allocation trade‐offs. Although urban populations are often reported to exhibit paler carotenoid colouration than rural populations, these patterns have rarely been tested along continuous fine‐scale urbanisation gradients at a continental scale. We investigated how reflectance parameters of the yellow breast plumage of adult Great Tit (Parus major) covary with territory‐scale local imperviousness, used here as a broad descriptor of urban habitat structure, across six European cities. Using 838 adult observations spanning 2005–2024 and sub‐meter‐resolution satellite imagery, we quantified the proportion of impervious surface within 100 m of nest boxes and related this metric to feather carotenoid chroma, brightness and UV chroma. Carotenoid chroma declined significantly with increasing impervious surface cover within breeding territories across Europe, corresponding to an expected decrease of 0.053 chroma units across the observed 0%–88% imperviousness gradient. This relationship remained robust across bootstrap resampling, leave‐one‐city‐out analyses and models controlling for among‐city variation in mean carotenoid chroma. Older individuals exhibited higher carotenoid chroma than yearlings, while males tended to be more chromatic and brighter than females. Impervious surface cover was not associated with feather brightness or UV chroma, indicating that urban habitat structure is linked specifically to carotenoid pigment deposition rather than feather structural properties and overall quality. Because carotenoid‐based colouration depends on dietary intake, higher levels of impervious cover and reduced vegetation may reflect lower availability of carotenoid‐rich resources in urban territories, although imperviousness should be interpreted as a multifactorial habitat descriptor rather than a direct mechanistic proxy. Our study provides the first continent‐scale evidence that carotenoid‐based colouration declines along a continuous urbanisation gradient. These findings identify plumage carotenoid chroma as a phenotypic correlate of local imperviousness within European cities and highlight the importance of fine‐scale habitat characterisation for understanding phenotypic responses to urbanisation. Future studies should test the mechanistic links between territory‐scale imperviousness, diet composition, pollutant exposure, physiological condition and fitness.
nc3834ceb83a6: Using Structure‐from‐Motion photogrammetry in a longitudinal study, we show that although coral reef habitat complexity had declined significantly by the end of the most prolonged tropical marine heatwave on record, no further losses were detected and 3 years later the reef had begun to recover this critical ecosystem function. Abstract Globally, climate change‐driven marine heatwaves are causing increased coral bleaching and mortality events with cascading effects, including reef habitat complexity. Given that habitat complexity positively influences biodiversity and organismal abundance, such losses have negative ramifications for these ecosystems. Past studies have documented habitat complexity changes following heatwaves, yet the timing and persistence of habitat structural complexity losses arising from these events, and subsequent recovery rates, remain largely unknown. Here, we used Structure‐from‐Motion (SfM) photogrammetry to survey permanent shallow forereef quadrats (4 m × 4 m; n = 30) in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean at the epicentre of the third global coral bleaching event, the 2015–2016 El Niño, prior to, during and after the event. Reef three‐dimensional habitat complexity metrics calculated from the SfM images were then used to examine the immediate and long‐term impacts of the mass coral mortality. Coral reef structural habitat complexity, quantified as surface complexity (1.18‐fold decline), vector ruggedness measure (VRM; 1.52‐fold decline) and fractal dimension (1.03‐fold decline), declined significantly during the heatwave. However, contrary to expectation, no subsequent loss (i.e. due to erosion of dead coral colonies) was detected. We found that exposure to underlying local anthropogenic disturbance had already reduced reef complexity before the heatwave, such that the least disturbed sites showed the largest habitat complexity losses from it. All three complexity metrics increased significantly between 2017 and 2019, but not to pre‐heatwave levels. Furthermore, through fine‐scale morphological classification of the substrate, we show that all coral structure (regardless of whether dead or alive) contributed to habitat complexity, and that live submassive coral had the strongest correlation to the complexity metrics despite it seldom being mentioned in the literature as a morphology providing structural complexity. Morphologies contributing to habitat complexity also shifted over time, as more thermally sensitive corals (e.g. branching, foliose and tabulate) experienced much greater losses than thermally tolerant ones (e.g. submassive and massive). Our results illustrate how rapidly habitat complexity can be lost during climate change induced mass mortality events and imply complexity will be comprised of distinct coral morphologies on future coral reefs and that recovery will take many years.
n042ae11270d7: Male and female waxbills (Estrilda astrild) have similar social dominance as young adults but, in breeding seasons, most ageing females become subordinate. While sex differences in animals are often considered fixed, our findings reveal a plastic nature of sex differences, emerging when females face the challenges of old age and breeding. Abstract Social dominance shapes group structure and the collective behaviour of gregarious animals. Senescence, the progressive physiological deterioration associated with ageing, may influence behaviour, including social dominance, while reproductive roles may lead to different onset times or rates of senescence between the sexes. However, how ageing shapes sex differences in sociality remains poorly understood, largely due to the scarcity of long‐term studies comparing male and female social behaviour. To address this gap of knowledge, we monitored dominance hierarchies during foraging in an ageing, semi‐natural population of adult common waxbills (Estrilda astrild). Our study lasted 5 years, which is more than most adult waxbills would live in the wild, to facilitate detecting effects of senescence. At the onset of the study, sex differences in dominance were negligible but became pronounced with ageing during breeding seasons. In contrast, sex differences remained weak during non‐breeding seasons. Females showed stronger longitudinal and seasonal changes in dominance than males, whose dominance patterns remained more consistent across breeding and non‐breeding periods. Nonetheless, social dominance also increased, on average, as the number of years until death decreased. Although sex differences in animal sociality are often thought of as largely fixed, our findings reveal a dynamic pattern in which sex differences in dominance emerge with ageing and are context‐dependent, varying across breeding seasons. Overall, our results suggest that senescence and seasonal context shape sociality later in life.
nc7acd0845cdc: The study finds that climate warming reshapes sex‐specific life‐history trajectories without necessarily shortening telomeres, challenging the widely held assumption that thermal stress‐induced faster growth inevitably causes telomere erosion. It also demonstrates that time‐dependent telomerase maintains telomere length under warming conditions, particularly in fast‐growing males. Abstract Understanding how climate warming reshapes animal life histories is crucial for assessing population persistence and evolutionary trajectories. This is particularly important in ectotherms, whose physiology, performance and, ultimately, fitness are strongly influenced by environmental temperature. Because climate warming can alter key life‐history traits such as growth and survival, its effects may differ between sexes, potentially generating divergent organismal responses and long‐term consequences. Identifying the mechanisms underlying these sex‐specific patterns is therefore essential for explaining how ectotherms cope with warming environments. To determine whether climate warming induces sex‐specific life‐history responses and to elucidate physiological mechanisms underlying these responses, we conducted a longitudinal experiment in which toad‐headed agamas (Phrynocephalus przewalskii) were exposed to simulated higher temperatures under seminatural conditions. We specifically monitored growth, survival, telomere dynamics, telomerase expression and oxidative status throughout development. Males exposed to elevated temperatures showed accelerated growth and a slight reduction in survival, whereas females showed no detectable changes in growth or survival. This suggests divergent sex‐specific responses in life history to warming. At the physiological level, warming did not lead to telomere shortening; instead, the telomere length increased over time in both sexes. This was accompanied by a transient up‐regulation of telomerase expression in rapidly growing males, which could contribute to the maintenance of the telomere during accelerated growth. However, telomerase expression declined at the end of the experiment in both sexes exposed to warming. Finally, warming increased lipid oxidative damage in both sexes despite activation of antioxidant responses at elevated temperatures. Our results show that climate warming can reshape sex‐specific life‐history trajectories without necessarily inducing telomere shortening, challenging the expectation that faster growth under thermal stress is inevitably associated with telomere erosion. However, warming can still impose physiological costs with potential long‐term consequences for organismal health, as indicated by elevated oxidative damage. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating sex‐specific life‐history responses with physiological mechanisms to improve predictions of species responses to climate change.
n7bddf81ce496: Using 18 years of data on eastern grey kangaroos, we show that drivers of individual reproductive success often do not scale up to population recruitment. Birth asynchrony could buffer population recruitment against environmental variability, such that variables affecting individual reproduction have little impact at the population level. Abstract Population growth depends upon individual survival and reproduction, but do drivers of individual reproductive success scale up to population recruitment? Factors affecting individuals may have little effect on population dynamics if individuals within a population experience different conditions. When seasonal resource availability is unpredictable and breeding season long, average conditions over a breeding cycle may poorly reflect the environment experienced by many individuals. We compared the drivers of individual reproductive success and population recruitment in an asynchronously breeding large herbivore, the eastern grey kangaroo (Macropus giganteus). We analysed 18 years of individual‐based data using multivariate hierarchical Bayesian models to first identify the causal mechanisms relating population density, environmental conditions and maternal traits to individual success. We then assessed whether the drivers of individual reproductive success scaled up to determine population recruitment. Most maternal and environmental covariates strongly influenced individual reproductive success, with distinct effects on juvenile survival before and after pouch exit. Maternal traits had a greater influence in the pouch, whereas environmental conditions became increasingly important once young exited the pouch. Most drivers of individual reproductive success did not affect population recruitment. Recruitment decreased with population density and increased with mean body condition of adult females. Weather harshness had a weak positive effect on recruitment, which appeared independent of female age structure, previous recruitment or forage. Most drivers of individual reproductive success did not scale up to population recruitment. Birth asynchrony could buffer population recruitment against environmental variation such that variables affecting individual reproduction have little impact at the population level. Large herbivores that reproduce asynchronously may therefore be more resilient to environmental variability than synchronous breeders.
n1574882a7996: Preparing to sample fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium) in a recently burned forest patch in northern Idaho, USA. Abstract The forage maturation hypothesis predicts that herbivores should select plants at intermediate growth stages because they strike a balance between biomass and nutritional quality. Methods for identifying this key stage of plant phenology commonly rely on satellite-based greenness indices and their derivatives. By combining such indices with fine-scale movement data, ecologists have uncovered many novel behaviours and life-history strategies, including ‘green-wave surfing’ by herbivores. Yet, few studies have evaluated the degree to which greenness indices accurately reflect variation in forage characteristics or their selection by herbivores in forested habitats. We studied relationships among remotely sensed greenness indices, on-the-ground measures of forage biomass and quality and resource selection by white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), elk (Cervus canadensis) and moose (Alces alces) in the coniferous forests of northern Idaho, USA. We hypothesized that remote-sensing methods for measuring the green wave (i.e. the phenological progression of understory food plants) are not useful in coniferous forests because variation in greenness is driven mainly by conifers. We also hypothesized that patterns of forage selection by large herbivores are not detectable in the forest using greenness indices. We tested predictions derived from these hypotheses using on-the-ground measures of forage biomass and quality and more than 10 years of movement data from GPS collars. Remotely sensed greenness indices explained <2.5% of variation in forage biomass (adjusted R 2 < 0.024), which was more readily predicted by variation in tree canopy cover, topography and climate (total biomass: adjusted R 2 = 0.313; high-quality biomass: adjusted R 2 = 0.174). Moreover, with only one exception (elk selected pixels where the instantaneous rate of green-up was near its peak), greenness indices were among the least useful predictors of selection by large herbivores. Indeed, although all three species selected forage biomass, elk and moose simultaneously avoided greener pixels. Our results indicate that greenness indices are of limited value for predicting variation in forage resources or their selection by large herbivores in forested environments. Despite their intuitive appeal and ease of accessibility, such indices cannot always be substituted for on-the-ground measurements of plant traits that directly influence nutrient intake by herbivores.
n73eddb6a3958: Among plant diversity metrics, phylogenetic diversity was the strongest predictor of root exudate chemodiversity. Root exudate carbon content promoted denitrification and DNRA, whereas greater chemodiversity was negatively associated with these pathways but positively associated with anammox. Carbohydrates and organic acids contributed more to explaining variation in N transformations than amino acids. These findings provide insights into the metabolite‐level mechanisms linking plant diversity to soil N transformations. Abstract Plants can regulate soil biogeochemical processes via root exudates, yet how exudate quantity and composition influence soil nitrogen (N) transformations remains unclear. We conducted complementary pot and microcosm experiments across gradients of plant species, phylogenetic and functional group diversity to examine effects of root exudates on anaerobic N transformation processes in soils, including dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), denitrification and anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox). Results showed that both rhizosphere metabolite and root exudate chemodiversity increased with multidimensional plant diversity, with phylogenetic diversity explaining more variance than species or functional group diversity. Carbohydrates and organic acids had stronger effects on N transformation processes than amino acids, with shikimic acid and sucrose identified as key components influencing DNRA and denitrification rates. Notably, higher exudate carbon (C) content significantly enhanced DNRA and denitrification, whereas exudate chemodiversity negatively correlated with these two processes but positively associated with anammox. Additionally, both exudate C content and chemodiversity directly or indirectly affected soil N transformations through changes in soil N availability, rather than microbial communities. Synthesis. These findings advance the mechanistic understanding of how plant diversity–mediated variation in root exudate quantity and composition regulates soil N cycling, highlighting its pivotal role in shaping ecosystem nutrient dynamics.
n97be4dcb5227: Ecology has undergone a profound methodological transformation through the rapid growth in new technologies, data volume, statistical innovation and analytical sophistication. These developments create unprecedented opportunities for novel ecological insights, but have also magnified longstanding concerns about quantitative training, which persist despite more than a century of debate and repeated calls for reform. Here, we posit why, despite enduring and widespread agreement on educational goals, progress in quantitative ecology education has remained limited. We argue that limited progress reflects a mismatch between widely supported reforms and the conditions needed to implement them at scale. While discussions of quantitative education have often focused on curricular content—what ecologists should learn—progress is also shaped by pedagogical, interpersonal, institutional and disciplinary factors. We discuss these interconnected components and argue that their combined influence helps explain the inertia that continues to characterise quantitative ecology education. Building on this diagnosis, we offer an integrated vision for quantitative ecology education. We argue that durable quantitative literacy is best developed through inclusive, context‐rich and people‐centred pedagogies that address barriers to learning, support diverse learners and ensure that procedural competence is grounded in strong conceptual understanding. We further advocate for coordinated action from disciplinary leaders, stronger institutional support for educators and learners, recognition of heterogeneous cohorts as a pedagogical strength, greater interdisciplinary collaboration between ecologists and quantitative specialists, and a shift from expectations of universal fluency towards a model of distributed expertise underpinned by foundational quantitative literacy. As ecology evolves, the need for quantitative literacy is greater than ever. Progress will depend not simply on identifying what should be taught and how, but on addressing the broader conditions that constrain the pace and scale of implementation of widely supported educational aspirations. We argue that reframing persistent challenges as interconnected problems of implementation, rather than aspiration, will help in overcoming a century of inertia in quantitative ecology education.
