Com base neste diagnóstico, oferecemos uma visão integrada para o ensino quantitativo em ecologia.…
n6071ef4cc8bf: Functional redundancy is a key biological concept that offers critical insights into microbial ecosystem stability and responses to environmental perturbations. Existing methods to quantify redundancy typically rely on gene annotations as functional units, limiting their ability to capture complex or partially characterised traits and making analyses from metagenomic data—often fragmented or incomplete—challenging. Here, we present miFRED (microbial Functional REDundancy), an accessible computational approach to quantify functional redundancy of microbial phenotypes and communities based on phenotypic rather than genetic annotations. Leveraging 86 machine‐learning‐predicted phenotypes as functional units, miFRED bridges the genotype–phenotype gap and enables interpretable and accurate assessment of redundancy at both community and single phenotype levels, as demonstrated on simulated communities. As case studies, miFRED was applied to over 300 metagenomic samples from anaerobic systems, to a longitudinal dataset of a gut microbiome subject to antibiotic treatment and 100 marine and soil metagenomes. Across these applications, miFRED elucidated relationships between redundancy, community structure and functional organisation. Comparison to gene annotation‐based analyses highlighted the improved interpretability of phenotype‐based redundancy estimates, which allowed clearer resolution of functional changes associated with microbiome perturbation and recovery in the human gut dataset. In anaerobic digestion communities, analyses considering environmental conditions uncovered changes in redundancy, complexity and functional profiles with rising temperatures, with more extreme conditions favouring simpler, more redundant communities and shifts in redundant functions. Using phenotype‐based functional units, miFRED provides a practical and general framework for consistent functional redundancy analyses across environments and metagenomic datasets. By interpreting redundancy patterns in the context of community organisation and environmental factors, it enables exploration of microbial functional landscapes across environmental conditions in both natural and engineered ecosystems.
n8171fbc521d1: Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAIV) increasingly threatens wild birds, poultry, non‐human mammals and humans, yet gaps and opportunities in avian influenza virus (AIV) transmission modelling have not been comprehensively synthesized. We reviewed 182 articles published through 2025, categorized dimensions, including modelling approaches, data, host types, biological levels, spatial scales, temporal scales and model objectives, examined associations among these dimensions, and synthesized author‐stated limitations and recommendations. Statistical and mechanistic models dominated. Model data centred on population dynamics and demography, disease surveillance, host epidemiology and competence, meteorology and land use and land cover. Most studies focused on poultry or wild birds at regional spatial scales, seasonal/annual and multi‐year temporal scales, population or multi‐population levels, and were retrospective. Machine learning and decision‐making models were less common. Immunity, behaviour and life history, community composition, morphology, viral genetics and viral persistence received less attention. Non‐human mammals, individual and community biological levels, local and broader spatial scales, daily temporal scales and prospective modelling were also less frequently modelled. The authors frequently reported limitations related to data availability, surveillance sampling and reporting bias, and model simplification, while commonly recommending improved data quality and greater model complexity and realism. Future studies can align and integrate modelling approaches, data and structures around clearly defined transmission processes, while accounting for uncertainty and keeping model complexity commensurate with empirical evidence. Priorities include model‐guided surveillance that accounts for imperfect detection, broader integration of understudied hosts and transmission processes, more prospective modelling and expanded applications of machine learning and decision‐making where appropriate. Questions spanning spatiotemporal scales and biological levels may require multi‐scale and multi‐level integration through agent‐based or individual‐based models, complemented with hierarchical Bayesian inference, or linked modules designed around shared objectives. 摘要 高致病性禽流感病毒(HPAIV)对野生鸟类、家禽、非人类哺乳动物和人类的威胁日益加剧，但禽流感病毒(AIV)传播建模中的研究空白与发展机会尚缺乏全面总结。 我们系统回顾了截至2025年发表的182篇文献，从建模方法、数据、宿主类型、生物组织层次、空间尺度、时间尺度和模型目标等维度进行分类，分析了这些维度之间的关联，并总结了文献作者提出的研究局限与建议。 统计模型和机制模型占主导地位。模型所用数据主要涉及种群动态与种群统计特征、疾病监测、宿主的流行病学特征与传播能力、气象，以及土地利用和土地覆盖等数据。此外，多数研究聚焦于家禽或野生鸟类，主要采用区域空间尺度和季节、年度或多年时间尺度，在种群或多种群层次开展研究，并以针对过去传播事件的回溯性建模为主。 机器学习模型和决策模型的应用较少。宿主免疫、行为与生活史、群落组成、形态特征、病毒遗传学及病毒存留时间受到的关注较少。以非人类哺乳动物为对象、在个体或群落层次开展的建模研究，以及采用局地或比区域更大的空间尺度、以日为时间尺度的研究也相对较少，前瞻性建模同样不足。文献作者经常指出数据获取受限、监测中的采样与报告偏差，以及模型简化等方面的局限，并普遍建议提高数据质量，增加模型复杂度，使模型更贴近实际。 未来研究可围绕明确界定的病毒传播过程，协调并整合建模方法、数据和模型结构，同时考虑研究过程中的不确定性，使模型复杂度与实证证据相匹配。重点方向包括利用模型指导疫病监测并考虑漏检的影响，更广泛地纳入研究不足的宿主和传播过程，增加前瞻性研究，以及在适当情况下拓展机器学习和决策模型的应用。对于跨越时空尺度和生物组织层次的研究问题，可能需要采用基于主体或个体的模型进行多尺度、多层次整合，并辅以分层贝叶斯推断，或围绕共同目标设计相互衔接的模型模块。
n677b20e24d13: Seagrasses support highly productive ecosystems in both temperate and tropical waters and provide essential ecosystem services. Despite their importance, the vertical structure of seagrasses (i.e. the canopy) remains poorly characterised at the microscale, even though it is a strong predictor of ecological processes that influence both biological and physical interactions in coastal environments. This study develops and validates a practical, scalable workflow to map canopy height (CH) across a large Posidonia oceanica meadow using low‐cost underwater Structure‐from‐Motion (SfM) photogrammetry acquired by Scuba Diver Propulsion Vehicle (DPV). Three‐dimensional georeferenced point clouds (PCLs) were analysed to develop an effective workflow, encompassing acquisition settings and optimal processing steps for accurately classifying PCLs and generating SfM‐based canopy height models (CHMs) of seagrass meadows. A testing site was identified to evaluate 3D positioning accuracies and three automated ground‐filtering methods (Metashape, CSF, CANUPO). Results were compared with manually classified PCL and in situ canopy measurements. An analysis of patch morphology, volume, and canopy height, based on model residuals, was conducted to provide an in‐depth assessment of accuracy and method effectiveness before expanding the workflow to a meadow‐wide scale (12,800 m2). Automated classifiers (CANUPO) yielded CHMs and patch metrics that were statistically similar to those from manual filtering. The ground‐filtered PCLs produced centimetre‐scale CHMs with accurate georeferencing, yielding 3D RMSE values of ~0.13–0.22 m depending on survey extent and ground‐control‐point configuration. The application of the proposed method at the meadow‐wide scale reported a higher mean CH at the Cala di Mezzo than at the Subielli bank site, indicating natural variability in seagrass associated with the depth gradient and substratum type. This study presents a new and scalable workflow for generating CHMs from SfM‐derived PCLs, enabling direct analysis of meadow canopy complexity and for deriving key seagrass descriptors, including mean and maximum CH, total canopy area and volume. This approach represents a significant advancement in ecological monitoring, offering the potential to streamline fieldwork and reduce reliance on labour‐intensive manual surveys. Overall, the findings highlight the promise of cost‐effective, open‐source tools for improving efficiency and replicability in underwater monitoring of marine seagrass ecosystems.
nc43018afc744: Natural sounds have been recorded for millions of hours over the previous decades using passive acoustic monitoring. Improvements in deep learning models have vastly accelerated the analysis of large portions of this data. While new models advance the state‐of‐the‐art, accessing them using tools to harness their full potential is not always straightforward. Here we present bacpipe, a collection of bioacoustic deep learning models and evaluation pipelines accessible through a graphical and programming interface, designed for both ecologists and computer scientists. Bacpipe streamlines the usage of state‐of‐the‐art models on custom audio datasets, generating acoustic feature vectors (embeddings) and classifier predictions. A modular design allows evaluation and benchmarking of models through interactive visualizations, clustering and probing. We believe that access to new deep learning models is important. By designing bacpipe to target a wide audience, researchers will be enabled to answer new ecological and evolutionary questions in bioacoustics.
n55355e8d2da1: The biodiversity crisis demands new approaches to describing and characterising species that can scale beyond the capacity of professional taxonomists alone. Hundreds of millions of specimen images are now openly available, yet almost none carry structured information about the morphology they depict. We present the Descriptron‐GBIF Annotator, a free, zero‐installation tool that runs entirely in a web browser and lets anyone create structured, ontology‐linked morphological annotations of specimen images drawn directly from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and the taxonomic literature. AI‐assisted outlining is provided by the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), and a library of anatomical templates covering 25 major taxonomic groups guides the annotator to standardised body regions and traits. Annotations can be exported in widely used formats: Darwin Core, COCO, a flat traits table and a linked‐data (JSON‐LD) knowledge graph, and published directly to Zenodo as citable, FAIR datasets with DOIs. We position the tool as the public‐facing first tier of a two‐tier system that complements a professional workbench (the Descriptron Portal) used by taxonomists, creating a feedback loop in which public annotations help train AI models and expert‐validated outputs improve the public tool. In roughly 5 months of quiet availability the tool has logged 2248 usage events, including 280 AI‐assisted segmentations across 43 anatomical regions with high mask confidence (median 0.92). We describe the tool, walk through a complete worked example, report this early usage and discuss what wider adoption will require. The annotator is available at https://www.descriptrongbifannotator.org and the source code at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18888577 and https://github.com/alexrvandam/Descriptron‐GBIF_Annotator.
n93a3f8ce8de7: As long‐read amplicon sequencing becomes routine for fungal metabarcoding, species‐level abundance estimation from ITS amplicons remains limited by naive best‐hit classification. Assigning each read to its single highest‐scoring reference misattributes reads among closely related species that share similar ITS sequences, and divides the reads of one species across the several redundant entries that represent it in the reference database, so that no single entry reflects its true abundance. Expectation–maximization (EM) approaches developed for full‐length 16S rRNA, notably EMU (Curry et al., 2022), have recently been benchmarked for fungal ITS metabarcoding (Graetz et al., 2025), but applying EMU to ITS requires custom reference database construction and uses parameters originally tuned for 16S. Here we present EMITS, a Rust‐based tool that applies EM to iteratively resolve ambiguous read‐to‐reference mappings from minimap2 alignments against the UNITE database, producing probabilistic species‐level abundance estimates. EMITS provides UNITE‐native header parsing with automatic accession aggregation, empirically tuned platform presets for current Oxford Nanopore (R10.4.1, R9.4.1, Duplex) and PacBio HiFi chemistries, and integration with ITSxRust (O'Brien et al., 2026b) for upstream ITS region extraction. We validated EMITS using three complementary approaches and benchmarked it against both naive best‐hit counting and EMU (with a UNITE‐formatted reference database). In controlled simulations, EM reduced L1 error by 80%–92% compared to naive counting under realistic noise conditions. For the ATCC fungal ITS mock community, EMITS provided superior within‐genus species resolution in taxonomically challenging genera: it correctly identified Trichophyton mentagrophytes (2.21%) where EMU misattributed substantial abundance to T. tonsurans (1.54%); it suppressed Penicillium rubens false positives (0.002% vs. EMU 0.58%); and it more accurately consolidated Nakaseomyces glabratus abundance across UNITE accessions (12.40% vs. EMU 9.95%). On a 21‐species synthetic UNITE community lacking substantial within‐genus difficulty, all three methods detected expected species at 100% sensitivity, with aggregate L1 errors of 8.64% (naive), 7.30% (EMITS), and 6.71% (EMU). Together with ITSxRust for upstream ITS extraction, EMITS provides an extraction‐to‐abundance workflow tuned for long‐read fungal amplicon profiling. The tool's UNITE‐native handling and ITS‐specific parameter presets address concrete adoption barriers for ecologists working with long‐read sequencing, while its demonstrated advantage in within‐genus species resolution targets the taxonomically challenging fungal genera of greatest clinical, agricultural and ecological importance. Resumen A medida que la secuenciación de amplicones de lectura larga se vuelve rutinaria en el metabarcoding de hongos, la estimación de abundancia a nivel de especie a partir de amplicones ITS sigue limitada por la clasificación ingenua por mejor coincidencia. Asignar cada lectura a su única referencia de mayor puntaje atribuye erróneamente lecturas entre especies estrechamente relacionadas que comparten secuencias ITS similares, y reparte las lecturas de una misma especie entre las múltiples entradas redundantes que la representan en la base de datos de referencia, de modo que ninguna entrada individual refleja su abundancia real. Los enfoques de esperanza‐maximización (EM) desarrollados para el gen 16S rRNA completo, en particular EMU (Curry et al., 2022), se han evaluado recientemente para el metabarcoding de ITS de hongos (Graetz et al., 2025), pero aplicar EMU a ITS exige construir una base de datos de referencia a medida y emplea parámetros originalmente ajustados para 16S.…
n35c8e1473dd0: Tree crowns are complex, three‐dimensional structures whose morphology varies among species, individuals and environments. Although light detection and ranging (LiDAR) provides high‐resolution, single‐tree point clouds that advance species discrimination and the assessment of intraspecific variation in situ, crown shape is still commonly reduced to low‐dimensional metrics (e.g. crown diameter or crown base height), losing much of its three‐dimensional geometric complexity. We introduce a fully 3D geometric morphometric framework that captures crown shape directly from LiDAR point clouds at both species and individual levels. Pre‐segmented LiDAR single‐tree point clouds of eight temperate forest species were converted into three‐dimensional shape representations using radial bounding volumes (RBVs), which partitioned each crown into a standardized set of vertical layers and radial sectors. Surface points automatically digitized from each RBV formed geospatially aligned, 3D pseudolandmark configurations representing geometric morphometric crown shapes. These configurations served as the input data for multivariate analyses of crown shape variation within and between species. Twelve structural traits, including crown and stem dimensions, were extracted from the same RBVs and integrated into analyses of trait–shape associations. The morphospace of crown shape was structured along different axes of variation in broadleaf species than in conifers. Within these groups, species pairs—such as Fagus versus Quercus and Picea versus Pinus—exhibited contrasting intraspecific morphological gradients, with different structural traits driving shape variation in each. Crown base height and total crown height emerged as the strongest predictors of crown shape. Differences in crown shape among species were primarily captured by symmetric components, with asymmetry providing a negligible signal. Interspecific differentiation was largely driven by architectural variation rather than pure size differences. Morphological differences derived from pseudolandmarks and convolutional neural network features exhibited stronger correlations in conifers than in broadleaf species. We present a reproducible, LiDAR‐native framework for quantifying and comparing 3D crown morphology within and across species. Using the RBV approach, geospatially aligned pseudolandmarks can be derived from any pre‐segmented, single‐tree LiDAR point cloud, enabling scalable, multi‐regional analyses of intraspecific variability. This framework provides a robust foundation for integrating crown shape into ecological, evolutionary, silvicultural and modelling studies, including assessments of environmental effects and architectural constraints.
nf6d2662d214c: Many ecological decisions are slowed by the gap between collecting and analysing biodiversity information. Edge computing moves data processing closer to the sensor, with edge artificial intelligence (AI) using AI models for data processing and selective data transfer. edge AI extends the scope of biodiversity monitoring by complementing retrospective ecological analysis with real‐time sensing, enabling responsive and adaptive decision‐making. However, the adoption of edge AI systems in ecological research remains fragmented because deploying efficient and reliable systems is complex. Edge hardware, on‐device AI models and network configuration are tightly linked, such that optimising any one component shapes the performance and feasibility of the others, demanding holistic system design. For the uptake of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring, it is essential to understand the design trade‐offs, performance constraints and implementation challenges faced by current systems. Here, we analyse 82 studies published between 2017 and 2025 that use edge AI systems for biodiversity monitoring across acoustic, vision‐based, tracking and multi‐modal sensing. We synthesise hardware platforms, AI model optimisation and wireless communication to assess how these design choices influence ecological inference and determine the practicality and longevity of field deployments. Annual publications rise moderately from 3 in 2017 to 19 in 2025. Across these studies, we identify four system types that represent distinct patterns of edge computing adoption in ecological monitoring. These include low‐power microcontrollers (MCUs) for single‐taxon or rare‐event detection (Type I: TinyML), single‐board computers (SBCs) supporting multi‐species classification and real‐time alerts (Type II: edge AI), distributed systems coordinating processing across multiple devices (Type III: Distributed edge AI) and network‐connected devices for cloud processing (Type IV: Cloud AI). Each type illustrates different trade‐offs among power consumption, computational capability and communication requirements. Our analysis reveals the evolution of edge AI systems from proof‐of‐concept to robust, scalable tools. We argue that edge AI systems enable timely and scalable ecological observations, but realising their full potential depends on closer collaboration between ecologists, engineers and data scientists to align AI model development and system design with ecological needs and field realities.
nd52cc2ab0f90: Trait‐based ecology increasingly relies on measures of intraspecific trait variability to estimate how trait diversity within species varies across species and environmental gradients. Yet variance and related metrics are often interpreted without considering their intrinsic dependence on the mean, as described by the empirical Taylor's power law. Several approaches have been considered to remove the effect of trait mean, for which we hypothesize that their effectiveness will depend on the skewness in traits. Here we used a hierarchical plant trait dataset with intensive sampling campaign (>5500 individuals), including three key functional traits (leaf area, specific leaf area and flower size), to test mean–variance scaling across scales and regression methods, from mean and variance within individuals to across species within communities. We focussed on alternative variability metrics: variance and standard error, coefficient of variation metrics (CVs), slope of Taylor's power law. We assessed the relative influence of trait mean on trait variability metrics against predictors associated with environmental and biotic gradients. Results show a consistent mean–variance scaling across traits, scales and regression methods. Coherent with expectations for skewed distributions, log transformation already substantially reduced mean–variance dependence, but its effectiveness depends on the variability metric used. CVs on untransformed data and variance of log‐transformed traits showed the lowest dependence on the mean. Our results show that the mean–variance scaling of the Taylor's power law controls patterns of intraspecific trait variability and should be taken into account when assessing trait diversity within species. However, results also highlight that the choice of variability metrics and transformation may help strengthening ecological conclusions.
na3d44d29b8b4: Understanding biodiversity patterns requires integrating information across the interrelated dimensions that organize life. Species occupy specific regions in geographic space, respond to environmental conditions and vary within attribute (or trait) spaces that are shaped by their ecological and evolutionary histories. However, most analyses address these dimensions independently, limiting our ability to understand how constraints in one space interrelate to patterns in another. Developing approaches that explicitly quantify and connect the geometry of these spaces should unify the study of biodiversity across scales and dimensions. We implement such a framework in the letsR R package by constructing a triad of presence–absence matrices (PAMs) representing geographic, environmental and attribute spaces. A concise set of functions computes geometry‐aware descriptors such as centrality, frequency, isolation and border proximity, and allows these descriptors to be propagated among spaces through explicit connectors. This design builds on the letsR architecture and integrates with functions to facilitate macroecological analysis. Using global terrestrial mammals as a model group, we illustrate how descriptors derived from environmental space can be mapped back into geographic and attribute spaces. This approach reveals where particular regions of climatic space are common or rare, how isolated they are and how these properties influence species richness across dimensions. This novel implementation lowers the barrier to reproducible, geometry‐aware analyses and enables direct tests of how constraints in one space influence diversity in others, advancing a more integrated understanding of macroecological and macroevolutionary patterns. Resumo Compreender os padrões de biodiversidade requer considerar conjuntamente as diferentes dimensões que organizam a distribuição e a diversidade da vida. Em cada uma dessas dimensões, as espécies ocupam posições particulares que refletem suas histórias ecológicas e evolutivas: distribuem‐se em determinadas regiões geográficas, estão associadas a diferentes condições ambientais e apresentam combinações específicas de atributos. Ainda assim, essas dimensões são frequentemente analisadas de forma isolada, o que limita nossa capacidade de compreender como as restrições que atuam em um espaço se refletem nos padrões observados em outros. Abordagens capazes de quantificar e relacionar explicitamente a geometria desses diferentes espaços podem, portanto, contribuir para uma visão mais integrada da biodiversidade, abrangendo diferentes escalas e dimensões. Neste trabalho, implementamos esse arcabouço metodológico no pacote letsR para a linguagem R, a partir da construção de uma tríade de matrizes de presença e ausência (PAMs) que representam os espaços geográfico, ambiental e de atributos. As funções do pacote permitem calcular descritores que levam em conta a geometria desses espaços, incluindo centralidade, frequência, isolamento e proximidade às bordas. Esses descritores podem então ser transferidos entre os diferentes espaços por meio de conexões explícitas entre as matrizes. A implementação aproveita a arquitetura já existente do letsR e se integra às demais funções do pacote voltadas à análise macroecológica. Utilizando os mamíferos terrestres do mundo como grupo modelo, mostramos como descritores obtidos no espaço ambiental podem ser projetados nos espaços geográfico e de atributos. Essa abordagem permite identificar quais regiões do espaço climático são mais comuns ou mais raras, avaliar seu grau de isolamento e investigar de que forma essas propriedades se associam aos padrões de riqueza de espécies nas diferentes dimensões consideradas. Essa nova implementação torna mais acessível a realização de análises reprodutíveis que incorporam explicitamente a geometria dos diferentes espaços ecológicos e biogeográficos.…
n2cc570f89aab: The fundamental unit of spatial ecology is a species range: the geographical area that it occupies. Species ranges are delineated by range edges (also known as boundaries or limits). Why range edges occur where they do and not elsewhere, and what makes them move, has been an active area of research since the 19th century. In the present day, range edge dynamics are an important metric of biodiversity's response to climate change, as species shift toward the poles to track their climatic niches. Yet there are many methods for measuring range edges and quantifying their displacement. Here I describe common methods for describing range edge positions and apply them to example data for a bird species and a fish species, using some of the most popular datasets in climate biogeography: the Audubon Society Christmas Bird Count and a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration bottom trawl survey. I show that the choice of range edge metric influences where range edge positions are estimated to occur; whether they are estimated to be shifting over time; and the estimated rate of shift. The lack of standardized metrics for range edges has likely shaped statistics reported in synthesis studies that measured overall biodiversity responses to climate change and global rates of range shifts. Through simulation, I found that reliably detecting range edge shifts may require decades of data or more, suggesting that many global change studies in this field are underpowered. Pairing metrics to research questions, sharing raw data and code, and conducting power analyses before reporting statistically significant results will all help to minimize this issue. Going forward, the field of biogeography should confront the degree to which ad hoc methods have influenced our understanding of range edge dynamics and move towards standardized metrics.
n07fb46680fcb: Understanding plant behaviour requires the integration of multiple phenotypic and physiological signals measured over time under controlled conditions. However, different plant signals are typically studied using separate experimental setups, limiting temporal alignment and integrative analyses. We present Mind(the)Plant, a modular experimental facility designed for the synchronized, long‐term acquisition of multimodal plant data, including three‐dimensional shoot kinematics, above‐ and below‐ground volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and root imaging. Its modular architecture is designed to accommodate additional acquisition modules, such as electrophysiological signalling, as future extensions. The platform integrates a controlled growth environment with stereovision imaging, high‐resolution time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry and custom rhizocameras. These components are connected through a unified network infrastructure that ensures synchronized acquisition and centralized data handling. We validate the performance of each acquisition module through multi‐week recordings, demonstrating high‐temporal stability, reliable stereovision synchronization, effective isolation of VOCs signals and robust operation of below‐ground imaging. We further illustrate the analytical potential of the platform using a one‐day continuous multimodal acquisition combining shoot kinematics, above‐ground VOC emissions, rhizocameras observations and environmental data. Mind(the)Plant provides a novel methodological framework for studying plant behaviour, signalling and phenotypic plasticity in ecological and evolutionary research. By enabling coordinated measurements of multiple plant response modalities, the platform supports investigations of dynamic plant‐environment and plant–plant interactions from a behavioural perspective.
ndedaac2636b1: Tropical dry ecosystems (TDEs) cover half of the tropics and play a key role in global carbon dynamics. TDEs present distinct canopy and ground layers that often exhibit contrasting phenological patterns. On‐the‐ground observations of phenology by the human eye, though valuable, may suffer from limited temporal resolution and observer biases. Satellite data offer broad coverage but are limited by cloud interference and low spatial resolution. Phenocameras have emerged as a cost‐effective, high‐frequency monitoring tool, yet most studies rely on tower‐mounted set‐ups that may miss ground‐layer dynamics. Here, we developed a standardized protocol for simultaneously monitoring the leaf phenology of canopy and ground‐layer vegetation in TDEs, using pole and tree‐mounted trail cameras (phenocameras). The protocol was tested across savanna, dry forest and woodland sites in Brazil and Angola. We demonstrated that phenocameras mounted on trees or poles can effectively capture canopy and ground‐layer phenological patterns, that cameras should be mounted on fixed poles and, where not possible, on large trees. We found that the seasonal patterns of ground‐layer phenology captured by cameras mounted at 1 versus 2 m above the ground are strongly correlated. We recommend installing at least three cameras per site to provide more precise estimates of community‐level patterns and to maintain continuous time series in the case of camera failure or loss. Our protocol enables scalable, replicable phenological monitoring of plant communities and the canopy and ground layer, including in remote areas, enhancing our capacity to detect and interpret vegetation responses to environmental variability in tropical dry ecosystems.
na1dca9e4f343: Geometric morphometrics (GM) is widely used to study phenotypic variation in ecological and evolutionary research, but the throughput of manual landmark digitization limits how large morphometric datasets can practically become, especially in field studies that would benefit from rapid on‐site feedback. We introduce Theia, an edge‐AI mobile framework that performs end‐to‐end GM workflows directly on‐device, including image acquisition, automated landmark detection and morphometric analysis. The system integrates a dual‐stage deep‐learning pipeline with an offline analytical engine implementing generalized procrustes analysis (GPA) and principal component analysis (PCA), enabling field‐based analyses on low‐cost mobile hardware. Validation against the geomorph R package demonstrated near‐perfect computational fidelity (|r| > 0.999). Comparisons with expert manual digitization across 268 held‐out specimens showed close morphospace concordance, with biological variation accounting for 92.9% of total shape variance and the method effect (AI vs. manual) for 0.5%. The method effect is small, so the shape ordination used in downstream analysis is preserved. Theia enables standardized, reproducible morphometric data collection directly in the field. It complements established desktop workflows and suits studies that need portability and on‐site quality control, such as large‐scale spatial sampling and long‐term monitoring. RESUMEN La morfometría geométrica (MG) se utiliza ampliamente para estudiar la variación fenotípica en investigaciones ecológicas y evolutivas. Sin embargo, el rendimiento limitado de la digitalización manual de puntos de referencia (landmarks) restringe en la práctica el tamaño que pueden alcanzar los conjuntos de datos morfométricos, especialmente en estudios de campo que se beneficiarían de disponer de información rápida in situ. Presentamos Theia, un sistema móvil basado en inteligencia artificial en el dispositivo (edge AI) que permite realizar flujos de trabajo completos de MG directamente en el propio dispositivo, incluyendo la adquisición de imágenes, la detección automatizada de landmarks y el análisis morfométrico. El sistema integra un proceso de aprendizaje profundo en dos etapas con un motor analítico que funciona sin conexión e implementa el Análisis Generalizado de Procrustes (GPA) y el Análisis de Componentes Principales (PCA), permitiendo realizar análisis directamente en el campo mediante dispositivos móviles de bajo coste. La validación frente al paquete geomorph de R mostró una fidelidad computacional prácticamente perfecta (|r| > 0.999). La comparación con la digitalización manual realizada por expertos en 268 especímenes independientes mostró una estrecha concordancia en el morfoespacio: la variación biológica explicó el 92.9% de la varianza totalde la forma, mientras que el efecto del método (IA frente a manual) explicó el 0.5%. El efecto del método espequeño, por lo que se conserva la ordenación de las formas utilizada en los análisis posteriores. Theia permite una recopilación estandarizada y reproducible de datos morfométricos directamente en el campo. Complementa los flujos de trabajo convencionales realizados en ordenadores y resulta especialmente adecuado para estudios que requieren portabilidad y control de calidad in situ, como los muestreos espaciales a gran escala y los programas de seguimiento a largo plazo.
n858ec512adab: Consumer cameras are not designed to be scientific instruments, yet they are increasingly used in science not just to see, but to measure. This is possible because camera sensors respond approximately linearly to the light they receive, a property that can, in principle, support quantitative measurements of colour. Whether that quantitative measurement potential is preserved depends on what happens to the image after capture. Minimally processed sensor images, commonly known as RAW, retain the approximately linear response needed. Instead of RAW, however, the default output of most cameras is a heavily processed image optimized for visual appearance, compact storage and immediate use, typically saved as a JPEG file. The convenience offered by an in‐camera processed image comes at a scientific cost. RAW capture requires more storage and processing effort but leaves calibration choices open. Processed images reduce those demands at acquisition and in post‐processing but transfer irreversible decisions about colour manipulation from the researcher to the camera. The preservation of RAW sensor data is necessary but not sufficient for quantitative colour measurement. Pixel values must also be calibrated to account for the light conditions under which the image was acquired. Underwater, this calibration is more challenging than in clear air, because light is absorbed and scattered as it travels through water, resulting in effects that depend on both wavelength and distance. Consequently, colour distortions vary across the scene and generally cannot be corrected with a single global colour transformation like white balancing; instead, calibration requires information about the imaging distance. We explain the consequences for quantitative imaging and introduce the 3P Protocol for distortion‐free colour imaging underwater: Preserve RAW sensor data, place a known colour reference in the scene and plan acquisition to control or measure imaging distance. Calibration and reconstruction methods will evolve but cannot recover information discarded at acquisition. Preserving the measurement today keeps image datasets open to the questions and methods of tomorrow.
nd2910d57b14c: Accurate spatial localisation of free‐flying echolocating bats is foundational for resolving fine‐scale flight and echolocation behaviour, prey interception and spatial decision‐making in natural environments. Acoustic localisation using microphone arrays is widely employed for this purpose, yet array geometries in field studies are typically chosen heuristically rather than systematically optimised. As portable multichannel ultrasonic recording systems become increasingly accessible, principled design guidelines are needed to ensure reliable localisation performance under practical deployment requirements. I introduce an iterative array optimisation algorithm that designs microphone geometries by maximising localisation reliability within a predefined three‐dimensional field of interest. The method evaluates candidate geometries using simulated acoustic emissions and time‐difference‐of‐arrival localisation, quantifying performance as a volumetric pass rate: the proportion of source locations that meet a user‐defined accuracy threshold. Microphone positions are iteratively perturbed and accepted based on improvements to this task‐level metric, while enforcing practical constraints on array aperture, inter‐sensor spacing and deployability. Across canonical polyhedral geometries, random initialisations and arrays comprising 4–12 microphones, optimisation consistently produced rapid early gains followed by geometry‐dependent performance plateaus under the specified stopping criterion and iteration budget. Under fixed‐aperture constraints, increasing the microphone count yielded diminishing returns, and optimised low‐order arrays—particularly four‐microphone configurations—matched or exceeded the volumetric localisation performance of higher order arrays with suboptimal geometry. Analysis of optimisation trajectories further revealed that convergence dynamics scale with array order, whereas volumetric performance under the tested conditions is dominated by geometry rather than sensor number. These results demonstrate that array geometry is the primary determinant of volumetric localisation reliability, and that efficient, portable arrays can be systematically designed using optimisation rather than heuristic rules. The proposed framework is broadly applicable to bioacoustic localisation problems beyond echolocating bats, including avian tracking, passive acoustic monitoring and conservation‐oriented sensing, and provides a general approach for designing task‐optimised acoustic sensor arrays for a wide range of applications.
na1045f3c626e: Ancestral adaptive variation is thought to play an important role in facilitating adaptation to insular environments. However, to properly evaluate its role, we need to determine the age of genetic variation. In this study, we investigate the Iago sparrow (Passer iagoensis), a generalist endemic to the Cabo Verde archipelago, to understand how genetic diversity is maintained in an island lineage where populations are likely ephemeral and adaptation to environmental extremes is ongoing. Using whole‐genome sequencing and phenotypic data, we inferred the species' evolutionary history, population structure, and signatures of selection. Our results show that the Iago sparrow diverged from its closest mainland relative approximately 4.26 million years ago, although the colonisation likely occurred only around 2 million years ago. Population structure analyses reveal three distinct lineages, corresponding to geographic divisions within the archipelago, with the Rombos islets population exhibiting significant phenotypic divergence, particularly in bill morphology. Genome scans and phenotypic measurements identified signatures of divergent selection in genes associated with bill size (HMG20B) and bill shape (ALX1), suggesting adaptive evolution in response to local environmental conditions. Our ancestral recombination graph analysis provided temporal estimates for adaptive variation associated with these genes, suggesting that adaptive haplotypes observed in the Rombos population arose after colonisation of the archipelago. This contrasts with patterns described in Darwin's finches, where ancestral variation likely originated prior to colonisation. Our findings highlight the interplay of genetic drift, gene flow, and selection in shaping island species' genetic diversity. The Iago sparrow, a generalist thriving across diverse habitats, provides insights into the mechanisms that maintain genetic diversity in island lineages despite small population sizes and pronounced environmental heterogeneity.
n9bcbb14ed8d1: Understanding how genetic novelty arises and contributes to population divergence is central to evolutionary biology. On short evolutionary timescales, the relative roles of new mutations and standing variation remain underexplored among structural variation. Here, we compare the contributions of chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplications and single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to early genomic differentiation in a recently colonized island population, Drosophila yakuba mayottensis, from the island of Mayotte. By comparing the relative impacts of these mutation classes, along with the involvement of transposable elements (TEs), we assess whether certain mutations are more likely to contribute to rapid divergence. We show that TEs are disproportionately involved in the formation of novel structural variants shortly after colonization, particularly through direct insertions. Our results suggest that TE‐associated rearrangements may bypass the clocklike pace of SNP accumulation and divergence, where the contributions of coding SNPs, tandem duplications and TE‐facilitated ectopic recombination are constrained to standing variation on short timescales. Although TEs can drive the rapid emergence of novel variants, their full contribution to adaptation likely depends on evolutionary context and time since colonization. Together, our findings reveal time‐dependent mutational dynamics and highlight the importance of structural variation, particularly TE‐associated rearrangements, in shaping early genomic divergence following habitat shifts.
n568621708714: Working model for Zea mays ARF27 mediated primary root growth in maize Summary Auxin is a central phytohormone that mediates root development. This study investigated the genetic basis of auxin‐mediated primary root growth in Zea mays (maize) seedlings, which is not well‐understood in this key cereal crop. To address this knowledge gap, 618 accessions from the Wisconsin Diversity panel were leveraged for a genome wide association study (GWAS) followed by reverse genetics and in silico gene regulatory network reconstruction (GRN). The GWAS identified several candidate genes associated with variation in root growth responses, including RAMOSA2 and multiple members of the AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR (ARF) gene family. Maize AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR27 (ZmARF27), an ortholog of Arabidopsis ARF7 and ARF19, was prioritized for functional characterization. A reduction in ZmARF27 levels led to short primary roots, insensitivity to exogenous auxin, and altered transcriptional responses. Reconstruction of an ZmARF27 GRN included known maize classical root development genes, such as ROOTLESS CONCERNING CROWN ROOTS, numerous auxin pathway genes, and genes associated with cell wall biogenesis. Altogether, this study identifies ZmARF27 as a novel genetic driver of auxin‐mediated root growth and gene expression in maize.
n6ada37d49d95: Conceptual overview of the perennial extensions implemented in CPlantBox, implemented for Vitis vinifera. Summary Perennial root systems develop over decades and exhibit continuous turnover of structural and absorptive components, yet most root architecture models treat woody roots as permanent and neglect root age structure. We developed an empirically constrained modelling framework that explicitly represents age‐structured demography, growth regulation and dormancy in perennial root systems (Vitis vinifera). We extended the functional–structural plant model CPlantBox to simulate perennial root development over decades by integrating age‐dependent survival, secondary radial growth and climate‐driven dormancy. The model was parameterised using unique three‐dimensional (3D) root system data from young and mature grapevines, together with dendrochronological root age measurements, and coupled to root hydraulic properties. Empirical analyses revealed multicohort age distributions and substantial turnover of lignified structural roots, contradicting the assumption of a static woody scaffold. The model reproduced age distributions, order‐specific survival probabilities and fine‐to‐structural root length ratios, and generated realistic, genotype‐specific 3D architectures. Simulated uptake profiles and hydraulic scenarios showed strong age‐ and architecture‐driven effects. Explicitly representing woody root age distributions and age‐dependent processes may fundamentally change predictions of perennial root system architecture and function. The framework advances root modelling beyond annual paradigms and provides a transferable tool for analysing long‐term architectural and hydraulic consequences of genotype × climate interactions in perennial crops.
nf5cccb3f969a: Schematic diagram illustrating the associations between ant nesting and the ant–aphid mutualism. Summary Ants are ubiquitous ecosystem engineers, yet the mechanisms through which their nesting activity regulates mutualistic interactions remain elusive. Here, we provide evidence consistent with the hypothesis that ant nesting initiates a soil–plant–herbivore cascade that reinforces a tripartite mutualism. Using the invasive fire ant Solenopsis invicta as a model system in both laboratory and field settings, we show that ant nesting increases soil nitrate and ammonium concentrations, which are associated with enhanced plant growth. These nesting‐related changes coincide with shifts in the host plant's hormonal signaling network: auxin signaling is systemically elevated, whereas salicylic acid defense pathways and jasmonate signal transduction are suppressed. Plants associated with ant nests exhibit compromised defense responses to aphid herbivory. This shift toward a growth‐biased physiology supports larger aphid populations, which in turn provide increased carbohydrate rewards for ants, augmenting ant colony survival and brood biomass. Collectively, our findings suggest a potential terrestrial feedback loop in which ants indirectly enhance their own performance through nesting‐associated changes in soil nutrients and plant physiology, which ultimately benefit a mutualist herbivore. In doing so, this study establishes a tripartite ant–plant–herbivore mutualism that extends beyond the ‘food‐for‐protection’ paradigm as classically defined.
n3396aaa153dd: China's complex river basins constitute a critical biogeographic setting for investigating genetic differentiation and lineage divergence in freshwater fishes. Opsariichthys bidens is broadly distributed among multiple, hydrologically isolated river basins, rendering it a well-suited system for assessing mitochondrial phylogeographic structure across major river basins. Here, we used newly generated mitochondrial data to characterize broad-scale genetic variation in O. bidens across China's major river basins. We analyzed 379 cytochrome b (cyt b) sequences sampled from 13 geographically distinct populations, including seven populations from the Yangtze River and one population from each of six other major rivers, complemented by complete mitochondrial genomes from one individual from each population. Mitochondrial diversity was high at the species level (haplotype diversity, H d = 0.942; nucleotide diversity, π = 0.02526), but varied markedly among populations, with some populations showing haplotype fixation and others retaining divergent haplotypes. Genetic differentiation was pronounced, with 83.84% of variation attributable to differences among populations; 93.6% of pairwise F st values exceeded 0.25. Haplotype-network and phylogenetic analyses showed two deeply divergent mitochondrial lineages, broadly distributed in northern and southern China, respectively, with further substructure broadly associated with major river basins. Complete mitochondrial genomes exhibited high structural conservation across lineages, and the clearest lineage-associated annotation differences were observed in the termination codons of nd1 and cox3. Overall, these results provide a broad-scale mitochondrial phylogeographic assessment of O. bidens and reveal a general association between river-basin geography and mitochondrial lineage structure across China.
n46145bd63db7: Open science aims to improve research transparency, reuse and societal impact, yet its adoption and reach ultimately depend on people. Understanding how personal characteristics such as gender, work experience or professional role influence familiarity with, attitudes toward and engagement in open science is critical for the effective, widespread implementation of open science practices. We surveyed 342 individuals who produce, mobilise or use scientific knowledge in ecology and evolutionary biology. Their engagement was analysed using the open science change framework, which conceptualises open science as a progression from familiarity and perceptions to practices and support for societal goals, as outlined in the UNESCO Recommendations. Familiarity with open science emerged as a strongest and most consistent predictor of engagement: higher familiarity was associated with more positive attitudes, greater participation in open science practices and stronger agreement with UNESCO principles. Although these relationships are correlational and likely bidirectional, they highlight the central role of familiarity in open science engagement. Years of professional experience were associated with slightly less positive perceptions of open science, particularly among knowledge creators, while gender effects were weak across all stages of engagement. Stakeholder groups differed most in their familiarity with open science, while attitudes and support for broader goals were more similar once familiarity was considered. Together, these findings suggest that increasing familiarity with open science may be more effective than managing resistance or targeting specific demographic groups. Aligning incentives and practical support to increase familiarity offers actionable opportunities to strengthen open science engagement across the research ecosystem in ecology and evolutionary biology and enhance its societal impact.
n1c5ab7419f60: Ancient tea agroforestry landscapes in Southwest China are structurally complex systems that may support high arthropod diversity, yet their biodiversity value remains poorly documented. We used COI metabarcoding of Malaise‐trap bulk samples to assess flying arthropod assemblages at four tea‐associated sites in the Mengku Ancient Tea and Cultural System, Yunnan, China: a wild ancient tea tree community, a village‐adjacent cultivated ancient tea garden, a forest‐adjacent cultivated ancient tea garden, and a young‐shrub tea plantation. Samples were collected from May to October 2024 and analyzed using OTU‐based diversity and community‐composition approaches. We recovered 5669 arthropod OTUs. Diptera dominated the assemblages, accounting for 57.5% of total OTU richness, followed by Hymenoptera, Lepidoptera, Hemiptera, Coleoptera, and other arthropod groups. OTU richness, alpha diversity, and community composition varied among the four sites. WJC had the highest total OTU richness and mean alpha‐diversity values, whereas DXS yielded the most compositionally distinct assemblage and the largest number of OTUs detected exclusively at that site during this survey. Dominant families included natural enemies, herbivores, and mixed‐function taxa. Seasonal patterns showed higher OTU richness in early summer and September, but lower richness during the main rainy‐season months and October. These findings document marked spatial and seasonal variation in Malaise‐trap‐sampled flying arthropod assemblages. Because each landscape context was represented by a single site, the observed differences cannot be attributed independently to forest association, habitat heterogeneity, or management.
n8cfb6dab9d46: Small‐ and medium‐sized mammals are vulnerable to temperature extremes due to their high surface‐area‐to‐volume ratios and elevated metabolic rates. Shelter sites that buffer ambient temperatures are critical for thermoregulation; however, shelter resources may be limited in agricultural landscapes. We examined shelter site selection and the thermal buffering capacity of rufous bettong (Aepyprymnus rufescens) shelters in a grazed tropical savanna woodland in Queensland, Australia. We radio‐tracked 15 rufous bettongs (nine females, six males) across five grazing strategies at Wambiana Station (2020–2021) to locate diurnal shelters. We assessed fine‐scale habitat composition at 133 shelter sites and 224 paired random locations using a MANOVA and NMDS ordination. We deployed iButton data loggers to record hourly temperatures within shelters and at paired ground‐level points 2 m away across wet and dry seasons, isolating the thermal effect of the constructed shelter at the locations the animals selected. Rufous bettongs selected shelter sites characterized by thorny shrubs (Carissa ovata), logs, and termite mounds. Grazing intensity did not significantly affect shelter site selection, though bettongs tended to avoid heavily grazed paddocks. Daytime shelter temperatures (0600–1800 h) were substantially less variable than those at random sites, with thermal buffering most pronounced during the day (0900–1700 h), when random sites exhibited 2–3 times greater temperature variability than bettong shelters. Shelters provided critical thermal refugia, buffering daily temperature extremes by over 20°C in a hot, seasonally variable environment. Retention of dense shrub thickets (C. ovata), logs, and adequate grass cover should be prioritised in grazing landscapes to support rufous bettong persistence under current and future climate conditions.
na3fafdb66c5d: To avoid competition, species partition resource‐use along various niche axes. However, variable resource availability, especially within dynamic environments, may influence this partitioning. Theory predicts that species will contract their ecological niche to limit competition during times of resource scarcity. We analysed blood δ13C and δ15N composition in four albatrosses, four penguin, two giant petrel and two fur seal species breeding on sub‐Antarctic Marion Island, during two seasons (autumn and summer) over 3 years. Using the species' seasonal stable isotopic niche space as a proxy for trophic niche space, we investigated their trophic dynamics and maintenance of inter‐specific resource partitioning. There were significant variations in the seasonal and inter‐annual trophic niches of these predators. However, despite this high seasonal and annual variability, resource partitioning among the species was maintained over time. Between years, there was greater variability in the species' trophic niches in autumn than in summer. This might reflect species being better able to track productive dynamic oceanographic features during autumn, when most species are less spatially constrained by breeding commitments compared to during summer. Our results indicate that most of these marine predators have foraging behaviours that are either sufficiently flexible or general to cope with resources that are variable in space and time. Their foraging strategies minimise inter‐specific overlap in food or foraging habitat preferences, potentially resulting from historic or present competition for resources.
n64627b90f8ea: Individuals vary in resource use, generating trophic niche variation that shapes a population's niche width (PNW). Interspecific interactions are predicted to constrain PNW, though individual responses are often heterogeneous. The keystone niche individual (KNI) framework identifies individuals that disproportionately expand PNW by exploiting resources beyond the population's realized niche, but whether interspecific interactions limit their emergence is unknown. We tested this by comparing an allopatric and sympatric population of brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). Fatty acid profiles from repeatedly sampled individuals were used to quantify individual trophic niches and their contributions to PNW. Individuals in sympatry exhibited more negative contributions to PNW (−2.70% ± 1.7%) than individuals in allopatry (−0.47% ± 1.8%) and showed a continuum of contributions rather than discrete KNI, indicating that interspecific interactions constrained niche expansion by reducing disproportionate contributions to PNW. Across both populations, individuals with greater contributions to PNW exhibited reduced trophic overlap with competitors and lower body condition, revealing energetic costs of niche expansion. These findings suggest that, in this study system, interspecific interactions can limit niche differentiation by reshaping how individuals contribute to population‐level trophic diversity, highlighting the need to evaluate the generality of these mechanisms across ecological contexts.
n91f1bd0f438a: The Indochinese leopard (Panthera pardus delacouri) is one of the most endangered leopard subspecies, restricted to < 4% of its historical range across Southeast Asia. With severe declines driven by poaching, habitat loss and fragmentation, and prey depletion, recovery requires urgent, spatially informed conservation action. This study presents the first connectivity analysis for the Indochinese leopard across its extant and former range, aiming to identify core habitats, priority connectivity areas and opportunities for population restoration. We used resistant kernel modelling through the CoLa Decision Support System to evaluate landscape connectivity across 14 forest complexes in the extant range and 11 potential reintroduction areas, considering scenarios of extant, reintroduction and combined range connectivity. Importance to connectivity was assessed based on Kernel Extent, Kernel Sum, movement density and protected area overlap. Our results confirmed the Dawna–Tenasserim landscape, spanning parts of Thailand and Myanmar, and Peninsular Malaysia as the most critical strongholds. In the former range, our analysis revealed potential for large‐scale metapopulation structural connectivity across Cambodia and Lao PDR, despite recent extirpations. We stress that reintroduction opportunities will require actions such as reducing poaching, restoring prey and improving habitat management. In some complexes, intensive landscape restoration may be needed to reconnect major core areas with smaller reintroduction complexes that could be critical for meta‐population connectivity. Despite increasing human pressure in the region, substantial habitat and connectivity potential remain. Our framework provides a spatial foundation to prioritise actions for preventing extinction of this subspecies and guiding large carnivore recovery across fragmented tropical landscapes.
ne118bc4abce6: Floral color polymorphism is widespread among flowering plants, yet the mechanisms underlying its maintenance remain poorly understood, particularly in food‐deceptive orchids where pollinator‐mediated selection may differ from that operating in rewarding species. Here, we investigated the relationship among floral color polymorphism, ploidy variation, floral scent composition, and pollination in the Mediterranean deceptive orchid Anacamptis pyramidalis. Cytotypes were determined by flow cytometry, and floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were analyzed using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) in white‐ and pink‐flowered individuals from multiple populations. VOC profiles were compared using multivariate and univariate statistical approaches. Pollination success was assessed in mixed‐color diploid and tetraploid populations by quantifying the number of mature fruits produced per individual. Floral color morph was significantly associated with floral scent composition, accounting for approximately 6.5% of the total multivariate variation. Five VOCs differed significantly in relative abundance after correction for multiple comparisons, whereas total VOC emission did not differ significantly between morphs when cultivated in a common garden. No significant association between VOCs and cytotype was detected. White morphs consistently showed higher pollination success than pink morphs, producing significantly more fruits. By showing that floral color polymorphism is associated with both scent differentiation and differences in pollination success, our study highlights the importance of considering floral polymorphism as an integrated phenotype rather than a simple variation in flower pigmentation and helps explain its maintenance in the natural populations of this orchid.
n732347c5a314: Although classic models of size‐dependent sex allocation (SDS) generally predict that among animal‐pollinated plants, female allocation increases with individual size, male‐and female‐biased allocation patterns have also been reported. We hypothesized that Capparis spinosa growing in resource‐poor desert habitats would exhibit a female‐biased sex allocation with increasing plant size, and that this pattern would be directly regulated by resource availability, because female function is generally more resource‐demanding to verify this conjecture. We examined SDS patterns at the flowering stage in the andromonoecious desert plant C. spinosa and assessed the role of resource availability in shaping these patterns through resource supplementation and pruning treatments. The results indicated that male plants with a low biomass occurred at low frequencies (0.021–0.051) in seven of the nine assessed populations. Among andromonoecious individuals across the nine populations, with increasing plant size, we recorded increases in the numbers of male and hermaphroditic flowers, the proportion of hermaphroditic flowers, and values of Lloyd's phenotypic gender index. These findings indicate a strong female‐biased sex allocation in C. spinosa plants of larger size. In addition, 2‐year resource manipulation experiments revealed that both the supplementation of water and nutrients and pruning treatments significantly enhanced the proportion of hermaphroditic flowers, thereby indicating that floral sex allocation is directly regulated by resource availability. Our findings in this study highlight the role of resource availability in shaping size‐dependent sex allocation patterns, particularly for plants in resource‐poor desert habitats, and sheds light on the evolution of sexual systems in plants.
n8c3bd16abb08: Transparency could be considered the idealized version of camouflage, capable of producing effective concealment across heterogeneous habitats. However, although examples of highly transparent species do exist, ‘transparent’ species are highly variable and are often either only partially transparent or better described as translucent. Exactly how these different forms of ‘imperfect’ transparency may act as camouflage remains largely unknown. The glass frogs (Centrolenidae) have long been thought of as a classic example of transparent camouflage due to their see‐through ventral skin. Yet even in these seemingly exemplary cases, glass frogs are better described as translucent due to the presence of obligate opaque structures, such as the internal organs, within the body and opaque color patterns in their dorsal skin. These opaque patterns could be predicted to detract from transparency, with the potential to increase detectability and therefore predation risk. One potential explanation is that the addition of opaque patterning could help to conceal the internal organs from view while maintaining the cryptic effects of translucency. Here we tested whether the presence of opaque spots could reduce predation risk for translucent frogs by presenting model frogs, which differed in opacity and dorsal patterning, to wild birds and recording the rate at which these models were attacked. We found that the addition of opaque dorsal patterning reduced predation risk but there was no effect of translucency on survival. These data suggest that opaque patterning in glass frogs may help to conceal conspicuous internal structures but that partial translucency does not necessarily guarantee effective concealment. Future work is needed to explore the full range of dorsal patterning found in translucent glass frogs and to further examine how patterns comprised of both opaque and transparent elements may function as camouflage in a wider range of taxa.
n4a864dc59409: Climate change is rapidly altering ecosystems worldwide and can modify the demographic rates of long‐lived vertebrates. For seabirds, which rely on ocean productivity, reproductive success is particularly sensitive to climatic variability. Identifying the scale and stability of climate drivers is therefore critical for predicting population dynamics. Previous work on Leach's storm‐petrels (Hydrobates leucorhous) breeding on Kent Island, New Brunswick, showed that Annual Global Mean Temperature (AGMT) best explained hatching success between 1955 and 2010, with a nonlinear response peaking in the late 1980s. Here, we extend this dataset through 2024 to test whether AGMT remains a reliable predictor given the recent rise of ocean temperatures. Using mixed‐effects models, we compared hatching success with multiple climatic indices at regional, basin, and global scales. While AGMT retained some explanatory power, the best performing model for predicting variation in hatching success for the historical dataset (1955–2010) also included the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), which was not evaluated in the original analyses, and the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) for the full dataset (1955–2024). Different pathways may be involved: SOI could reflect non‐breeding conditions and have a carry‐over effect, whereas AMO could change prey availability and foraging conditions during egg formation and incubation. The relationships of hatching success with environmental indices changed over time. These results provide evidence that climate–biology relationships can be temporally dynamic, with the effects of some climatic drivers on hatching success changing over the study period. The AMO has also been linked to variation in adult survival for this population; its emerging importance for hatching success implies a compounded demographic impact with consequences for the population vulnerability.
nb2b348f23a9f: Understanding ancient trophic dynamics and human integration in terrestrial high-latitude ecosystems requires moving beyond traditional taxonomic lists to evaluate structural biological interactions. This study presents the first probabilistic, trait-based bipartite network reconstruction of ancient predator-prey assemblages in northern Tierra del Fuego, Southern South America, based on archeological records. By integrating a comprehensive zooarcheological dataset spanning 50 spatial-temporal contexts from the late Pleistocene through the late Holocene across steppe and forest habitats, we model trophic interactions including human subsistence strategies. In this region, dominated by grassy steppes and the forest-steppe ecotone, terrestrial hunter-gatherer societies were embedded in a complex predator-prey network in which the guanaco (Lama guanicoe) played a central role. However, the trophic structure of these interactions and how the introduction of humans as an unprecedented predator affected community-level properties is poorly understood. Our results reveal a significant chronological transformation in network architecture and diet composition. During the late Pleistocene, communities exhibited lower interaction diversity and high specialization centered around megaherbivores and multiple large predators. Following megafaunal extinction and island isolation during the mid-Holocene, the guanaco emerged as an enduring keystone herbivore and dietary anchor, while marine-derived carrion and littoral resources (mollusks and pinnipeds) provided critical energy subsidies. Humans acted as highly plastic generalist consumers, influencing network architecture across diverse habitats. In the steppe, foragers employed broad-spectrum strategies, whereas forest assemblages reflected specialized reliance on coastal resources. Ultimately, this community-level framework demonstrates that despite intense environmental shifts and insularization, the guanaco and marine necromass served as foundational trophic stabilizers, maintaining ecosystem and subsistence resilience over millennia.
n55d5d3b67d60: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract In terrestrial ecosystems, plant residues can reach the soil as senesced leaf litter or green leaves, and both types can be transformed by invertebrates into detritivore or herbivore faeces. Yet, the consequences of this conversion on decomposition rates and soil fertility are largely unknown. To fill this knowledge gap, we collected faeces from caterpillars (Historis odius; herbivores) and millipedes (Anadenobolus monilicornis; detritivores), which were fed green and dead leaves of Cecropia schreberiana, respectively, in a tropical ecosystem context. We then incubated green leaves, herbivore faeces, dead leaves and detritivore faeces in a microcosm experiment for 180 days to measure their decomposition and underlying soil parameters. Our results showed significant effects of (1) leaf senescence, with green leaves decomposing faster than leaf litter, and of (2) leaf conversion to invertebrate faeces, with faeces decomposing faster than intact leaves for both herbivore and detritivore faeces. However, contrasting patterns emerged between carbon and nitrogen dynamics, as nitrogen cycling was generally slower for faeces than for litter, with a particularly notable reduction in nitrogen losses for herbivore faeces. Consequences for the biogeochemistry of the underlying soil, specifically soil mineral nitrogen, were also observed. This pioneering study on faeces decomposition in a tropical context suggests that leaf‐feeding invertebrates, whether herbivores or detritivores, accelerate decomposition processes by converting leaves into faeces. This consistent acceleration of decomposition could have important consequences for soil organic matter formation and nutrient returns to plants. Résumé Dans les écosystèmes terrestres, les résidus végétaux atteignent le sol après la sénescence des feuilles sous forme de litière qui peut être consommée par les détritivores. Une autre voie de restitution est la chute des feuilles vertes suite à des événements météorologiques intenses (pluie, vent, sécheresse) ou à leur consommation par les herbivores dont les déjections atteignent le sol. Cependant, l’impact de ces transformations sur la dynamique de décomposition et le fonctionnement du sol demeure largement méconnu. Afin de combler ce manque de connaissance, nous avons mené une expérience en conditions contrôlées dans un écosystème tropical humide, en utilisant deux espèces d’invertébrés et une espèce végétale collectées en Martinique. Nous avons ainsi collecté des boulettes fécales produites par des chenilles herbivores (Historis odius) et des diplopodes détritivores (Anadenobolus monilicornis), nourris respectivement de feuilles vertes ou de litière de Bois Canon (Cecropia schreberiana). Ces quatre types de matière organique (feuilles vertes, boulettes fécales d'herbivores, litière et boulettes fécales de détritivores) ont ensuite été incubés en microcosmes pendant 180 jours afin d’évaluer leur décomposition et les effets sur les propriétés du sol sous‐jacent. Nos résultats montrent que la sénescence des feuilles influence fortement leur décomposition : les feuilles vertes se décomposent plus rapidement que la litière. De plus, la transformation des feuilles en boulettes fécales accélère significativement leur décomposition, que ce soit pour les herbivores ou les détritivores. Toutefois, nous avons observé des dynamiques contrastées entre la décomposition du carbone et celle de l’azote. Le cycle de l’azote s’avère généralement plus lent dans les boulettes fécales que dans les feuilles, avec une réduction particulièrement marquée des pertes d’azote pour les boulettes fécales d’herbivores. En outre, cette transformation influence significativement le fonctionnement du sol sous‐jacent, notamment en modifiant les niveaux d’azote minéral.…
n294796aec6b7: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Hypoxic events (i.e. reduction of dissolved oxygen in water) are natural events, which intensity and frequency have been amplified by human activities. As oxygen fuels aerobic metabolism, species unable to avoid those events must maintain their functions through phenotypic adjustments, that could occur both at the individual level (plasticity) and population genomic level (adaptation). To examine the adaptative and plastic responses to hypoxia, we exposed two generations of three‐spined sticklebacks, Gasterosteus aculeatus, from wild populations historically exposed to different oxygen levels, to two different experimental oxygen conditions (normoxia or intermittent hypoxia with 12 h normoxia: 12 h hypoxia; with nighttime O2 level at 20% for wild‐caught F0 during 4–6 weeks and at 35% for F1 throughout their entire 19‐month lifetime). By comparing the two generations, early‐life programming of the mitochondrial aerobic metabolism was revealed, conditioning the adult‐stage phenotypic and plastic response: F0 fish from the wild hypoxic environment had elevated pectoral muscle mitochondrial respiration and were able to increase their mitochondrial OXPHOS control efficiency under normoxia conditions at the adult stage. Signs of adaptations towards mitochondrial suppression were found in F1 hypoxia population fish livers while no differences were observed in their pectoral muscle, suggesting a downregulation of the hepatic, but not the pectoral muscle, aerobic activities through generations. In opposition to the adaptative trend, the plastic responses to experimental hypoxia were a decreased mitochondrial respiration in the pectoral muscle and an elevated liver mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation of the F1 fish, suggesting that inherited divergence rather countered than reinforced plastic responses. While both signs of adaptation and plasticity were found in the antioxidant defences of F1 fish, the absence of significant differences between experimental groups in terms of oxidative damage revealed that these fish were able to maintain oxidative balance. Our findings highlight that plasticity to hypoxia depends on the full organism life‐cycle, with the adult ability to face hypoxia depending on their early‐life environmental experience and provides valuable information on the potential evolutionary process of fish facing hypoxia. nbff730fcc7e8: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Established plants affect directly and indirectly the success of juvenile plants recruiting in their close vicinity, what is defined as a canopy–recruit interaction. Such interactions affect plant species demography and community dynamics. Root‐associated fungi (RAF) can influence plant performance and survival, thus contributing to the sign and intensity of canopy–recruit interactions. Pathogenic RAF negatively affect individual plants and their neighbours, while mycorrhizal fungi can positively counteract those effects. Additionally, saprotrophic RAF decompose organic matter, modifying nutrient availability in the soil, possibly enhancing recruitment. Therefore, understanding the role of RAFs in canopy–recruit interactions will help us understand their potential effect on the dynamics of natural plant communities. We combined information on canopy–recruit interactions for 24 woody species in two Mediterranean mixed forests with high‐throughput sequencing of root DNA from each species. We determined the relationships between plant recruitment and the similarity and richness of RAF communities among woody species associated with different mycorrhizal types. The probability of canopy–recruit interactions decreased between plants sharing more similar pathogenic RAF communities. However, their effect on the frequency of recruitment was modulated by the mycorrhizal association of the recruit, being negative for plant species associated with AM fungi but not significant for those associated with ECM. At the plant species level, plants hosting higher richness of pathogenic RAF presented scarcer recruitment and recruited under a narrower set of canopy species; on the other hand, canopy species associated with ECM fungi or hosting higher richness of saprotrophic RAF promoted denser recruit banks of any species in their vicinity. Our findings provide evidence of the importance of RAF for plant recruitment in natural habitats, and thus for plant population and community dynamics. They support the hypothesis that pathogenic RAF interact with mycorrhizal associations, and that plant species susceptibility to multiple pathogens limits its recruitment success. They also suggest that the positive effect of certain plant species on the recruitment of others (i.e. nurse effect) is likely mediated by a higher diversity of saprotrophic RAF.
