n8707be1520e2: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Climate change is altering both the amount and temporal distribution of precipitation, yet drought is often simplified to a single gradient of water reduction. As a result, how experimentally imposed variation in water amount and watering frequency jointly shape root‐associated microbial communities and their links to plant performance remains poorly understood. Using a 3‐year full‐factorial drought experiment in a dry grassland system, we disentangled the individual and interactive effects of water amount, watering frequency and plant composition (conspecific stands versus two‐species mixtures) on root‐associated microbiome and tested whether microbial variation was linked to plant performance. Water amount emerged as the dominant driver of microbial structure, strongly shifting bacterial and fungal composition and reducing bacterial diversity. Watering frequency had weaker but detectable effects, acting mainly on bacterial communities and partly interacting with water amount, whereas the specific contrast between conspecific stands and two‐species mixtures had limited effects. Bacterial community composition was associated with root trait variation and plant fitness, suggesting that drought‐driven bacterial reassembly formed part of the pathway through which water regime influenced plant performance. Together, our results show that water amount and watering frequency represent distinct dimensions of experimental drought with partly independent effects and highlight bacterial reassembly as an important component of grassland responses to increasingly severe and temporally variable drought. nc327a5a4e8ad: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Mature trees exhibit distinct vertical gradients in temperature and light. These within‐crown microclimatic gradients have been linked to spatial variation in leaf chemistry and herbivory. However, phytochemical variation and resulting herbivore responses are also strongly influenced by tree phenology and genetic differences among individuals. In this study, we tested whether crown position influences the chemistry of mature leaves and whether these effects vary between distinct phenological stages within a growth cycle. We also examined whether microclimatic or growth‐stage‐related changes in phytochemistry influence herbivore performance. We exposed clonal pedunculate oak (Quercus robur) saplings within three crown strata (ground, middle and upper canopy) of mature trees at two forest sites in Germany and Switzerland. We measured targeted and untargeted leaf chemistry across growth stages and conducted bioassays with generalist spongy moth caterpillars (Lymantria dispar). We found that vertical crown position was a major driver of mature leaf chemistry. Growth stage had a significant additive effect on phytochemistry but explained less variation than crown position. We did not detect any interaction between crown position and growth stage on phytochemistry. Targeted analysis of flavonoids revealed differences among crown positions and between the two growth stages, with compounds showing distinct yet additive responses to these factors. Untargeted metabolomics revealed similar additive patterns, largely reflecting shifts in phenolic and terpenoid‐related metabolite classes. The relative growth rate of caterpillars (RGR) was affected by growth stage, declining during shoot elongation compared to the steady growth stage, but not by crown position. Among the measured metabolites, quercetin 3‐O‐glucuronide was negatively associated with caterpillar RGR, whereas higher triterpenoid levels were positively associated with RGR. Our findings demonstrate that within‐crown microclimatic variation and oak growth stage jointly shape mature leaf phytochemistry, but have only limited consequences for the performance of the generalist herbivore Lymantria dispar. Rather than reflecting broad metabolomic shifts, herbivore performance was associated with only a limited subset of measured metabolites, highlighting that pronounced chemical variation within‐tree crowns does not necessarily translate into equally strong ecological effects. n213f95ba36d0: Rainfed agriculture covers roughly 80% of global cropland and supplies more than half of global food production, yet uncertainty in how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone water deficits and crop losses impedes robust risk assessment. Here, we establish an integrated, production‐weighted assessment framework coupling SPEI, SSI, and 12 GGCMI3 crop models to trace how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone deficits and crop losses, explicitly separating affected area, conditional yield loss, and accumulated production loss across rainfed maize, soybean, and wheat. By 2070–2099, opposing‐direction SPEI–SSI change classes occupied 6.8%–28.4% of rainfed area across crops under SSP1‐2.6/default CO2 and 26.6%–48.2% under SSP5‐8.5/default CO2. Comparison with fixed‐2015 CO2 experiments (7.5%–27.6% and 21.7%–34.9%, respectively) indicates that elevated CO2 substantially expanded the spatial footprint of this hydrometeorological decoupling. Historically, SSI‐defined drought affected 12–16 million ha year−1 and was associated with annual production losses of 5–12 Mt year−1 (1.6–2.0% year−1). Under default CO2, affected area increased to 14–21 million ha under SSP1‐2.6 and 19–27 million ha under SSP5‐8.5, with production losses of 6–12 and 9–12 Mt year−1, respectively. Under SSP5‐8.5, median loss rates were higher under fixed‐2015 than default CO2 for maize (3.33 vs. 1.96% year−1), soybean (4.22 vs. 2.84% year−1) and wheat (5.41 vs. 2.90% year−1), as elevated CO2 reduces stomatal water loss and thus mitigates drought impacts, whereas SSP1‐2.6 estimates were similar. Severe drought became the largest loss contributor under both pathways and CO2 settings. Under default CO2, loss increases clustered in Central America, northeastern Brazil, western Europe and southern Africa; fixed‐2015 CO2 broadened the area of robust grid‐cell loss increases. These results show that drought‐related production losses are spatially uneven and sensitive to the modeled CO2 response, highlighting the value of crop‐ and region‐specific risk assessment.
nb520de1a385c: Soil organic carbon (SOC) pools reflect the net balance of plant‐ and microbial‐derived inputs, transformation, and loss, yet a global‐scale assessment of distribution patterns, relative contributions, and hierarchical environmental correlates of microbial necromass carbon (MNC) and plant‐derived carbon (PdC) remains incomplete. Based on 1167 site‐level observations (1235 pool‐level records) across four ecosystem types, we applied variance partitioning, random forest, linear mixed‐effects models, and structural equation modeling to quantify global patterns and associative pathways of the two carbon pools. Unadjusted pooled comparisons showed higher MNC concentration and SOC contribution than PdC. However, covariate‐adjusted linear mixed‐effects models revealed significantly higher PdC. Paired observations showed the same directional trend, although statistical significance was not reached due to limited paired sample size (concentration: p = 0.104; contribution: p = 0.140). The apparent MNC dominance constitutes a Simpson's paradox driven by uneven ecosystem sampling, rather than a consistent within‐ecosystem pattern. Instead, the relative contribution of MNC and PdC was ecosystem‐dependent: MNC was marginally higher in forests, whereas PdC dominated in croplands and wetlands, with no significant difference in grasslands in paired observations. Edaphic variables were the strongest predictors (independent explanatory power: 61.1% for MNC, 47.4% for PdC), with total nitrogen, C:N ratio, pH, and mean annual temperature as key correlates. Our results reveal a hierarchical associative cascade in which geographic factors covary with climate, which in turn correlates with edaphic properties as the strongest direct predictors. Climate shows a weak but significant negative direct association with MNC only. This synthesis provides a hierarchical correlative framework and biome‐specific baseline parameters to support explicit representation of plant‐ and microbial‐mediated SOC pathways in Earth system models.
n5d9673679ba7: No authors have evaluated how the resource dispersion hypothesis applies to solitary herbivores although it may explain group formation and contribute to management. We found grouping behaviour of black rhinos, a solitary megaherbivore, largely adhered to predictions associated with the hypothesis, with implications for management of this critically endangered species. Abstract The resource dispersion hypothesis (RDH) predicts that when resources are abundant and heterogeneously distributed, multiple individuals may satisfy their resource needs in a shared area without imposing large costs on one another. Under such conditions, groups can form even in the absence of other benefits, and other life history traits may not entirely explain group composition. For example, groups forming under conditions associated with the RDH may not display a biased sex ratio even if otherwise expected. Solitary herbivores, which are unlikely to gain benefits from grouping, may be strongly subject to the RDH, especially during growing seasons when there is an abundance of resources. However, to the best of our knowledge, no study has evaluated whether grouping behaviours in any solitary herbivore follows RDH predictions. To explore this, we used 48,678 sightings of black rhinos (Diceros bicornis) from 13 reserves in southern Africa to assess whether grouping behaviour in this solitary megaherbivore aligned with predictions of the RDH, or reflected predictions informed by the species ecology. We found that group formation and size largely followed RDH predictions where groups were more likely to form when resources were heterogenous and of high quality. Additionally, groups were larger during the growing season and when resources were heterogeneous. In contrast, as resource quality increased, group size decreased. Similarly, two of the four group composition results followed RDH predictions, where increasing group size was associated with decreasing within‐group familiarity and an unbiased sex ratio in opposition to usual expectations. The other two followed species ecology predictions wherein increasing group size was associated with an increasing proportion of subadults and all large groups included at least one cow–calf pair. Ultimately, our results show that, in solitary herbivores, the RDH may be useful in predicting group formation and size and may explain instances when group composition diverges from species‐specific expectations. Understanding grouping behaviour in endangered solitary species such as black rhino may improve management by allowing managers to identify conditions under which individuals are more tolerant of conspecifics.
n319027e215e0: The zeta diversity of bird assemblages in the Zhoushan Archipelago highlights the importance of dividing overall assemblages into separate ecological groups as the results of zeta diversity are different among bird groups. Our study also provides a transferable framework for other land‐bridge archipelagos and fragmented landscapes. Abstract Species turnover, the spatial dissimilarity in species composition, is a central concept in island biogeography and community ecology. Traditional pairwise beta diversity metrics are limited to two‐site comparisons and cannot fully resolve the mechanisms driving turnover across multiple communities. Zeta (ζ) diversity overcomes this limitation by quantifying multi‐site species sharing and capturing how both rare and widespread species contribute to species turnover along a continuum. However, existing applications of zeta diversity to birds have focused mainly on continental, urban or land‐use gradients, and have not examined island systems while simultaneously comparing phenological periods and migratory groups, nor have they separated richness differences from species replacement. As a typical land‐bridge archipelago containing multiple bird groups, the Zhoushan Archipelago of China provides an ideal system for addressing these research gaps. We surveyed forest bird assemblages across 40 islands in this archipelago. We combined zeta diversity, multi‐site generalized dissimilarity modelling (MS‐GDM) and generalized additive models, using both Sørensen and Simpson normalizations to distinguish the contribution of richness differences from that of species replacement. We classified forest birds by season (breeding vs. wintering) and by migratory strategy (resident vs. migrant), yielding five ecological groups: all forest birds, breeding birds, wintering birds, residents and migrants. We then tested whether the relative importance of island characteristics varied among these five bird groups. Zeta decay followed a pure power‐law form in all five bird groups, indicating a scale‐invariant pattern of species loss across sites. Comparing MS‐GDM results based on Sørensen‐normalized and Simpson‐normalized zeta diversity revealed a fundamental duality: island area primarily drove richness differences through selective species loss on small islands, whereas distance to the nearest mainland consistently governed true species replacement across all bird groups. Overall, our results demonstrate that deterministic assembly operates through two distinct pathways, that is area‐driven environmental filtering and isolation‐driven dispersal limitation, which jointly structure multi‐site species turnover. The richness difference and replacement duality identified here can be generalizable to other land‐bridge archipelagos and fragmented landscapes where area and isolation jointly shape community assembly, and provides a mechanistic framework for interpreting multi‐site species turnover beyond simple richness gradients.
n054318ecc572: We show that juvenile exposure to a danger can not only prime individuals to be more responsive to that same danger later in life but also to an ostensibly unrelated danger. These patterns of behavioural cross‐sensitization can have important ecological implications for how animals respond to multiple and novel stressors. Abstract Behavioural responses to multiple stressors play a major role in survival and fitness. In this context, an important issue that has rarely been tested is fear generalization, where responses to disparate threats are correlated at the individual level. Furthermore, while sensitization to stressors is well studied, cross‐sensitization, where exposure to one threat increases behavioural responsiveness to unrelated threats, is under‐studied. We exposed juvenile Physid snails (Physa acuta) to one of two disparate threats throughout their developmental period: predator cues and ash, a wildfire‐derived environmental stressor. We then assayed snails' responses, relative to control snails that had no experience with either threat, to three acute exposures of each stressor. We documented consistent individual differences in snails' avoidance of predation cues and of ash. Exposure to either stressor led to sensitization at short‐ and long‐term timescales. Importantly, snails exhibited fear generalization; individuals that avoided predation cues more strongly also avoided ash more strongly. We also documented cross‐sensitization; snails reared with ash showed heightened responses to predator cues while snails reared with predator cues showed heightened responses to ash. To our knowledge, this is the first study documenting behavioural cross‐sensitization for threats as disparate as predation risk and fire residue in a non‐human animal.
n1045fa9b5f0d: of behavioural and physiological responses of plains zebra (Equus quagga) and blue wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus) during the cool drought, hot drought, and recovery periods in Etosha National Park, Namibia. Arrows illustrate relative changes in movement, while temperature diagrams depict seasonal variation in minimum (T min) and maximum (T max) body temperatures and daily temperature amplitude (T max − T min). Despite behavioural adjustments during drought, both species experienced substantial physiological challenges, with drought-associated mortality reaching 27% in zebra and 15% in wildebeest. Following rainfall, improved resource availability coincided with reduced body temperature variability, indicating physiological recovery. Background photographs courtesy of Wendy Turner and Bernd Brell. Abstract Climate change is expected to increase the frequency and severity of droughts in dryland ecosystems, yet the mechanisms determining whether large herbivores survive these events remain poorly understood. We investigated how an extreme drought influenced movement, water use, body temperature and survival of two water-dependent grazing herbivores, plains zebra (Equus quagga) and blue wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus), in Etosha National Park, Namibia. GPS collars and abdominal temperature loggers were deployed on free-ranging animals during the most severe drought on record. We quantified changes in movement, drinking behaviour, thermoregulation and survival across seasons classified as cool drought, hot drought and rainy season recovery periods. Both species exhibited substantial behavioural plasticity as drought intensified, including shifts in diel activity, shorter median intervals between visits to perennial water sources and highly variable drinking schedules among individuals. Zebra increased daily travel during the hot drought, whereas wildebeest reduced daily travel and shifted activity toward cooler periods of the day, reflecting contrasting strategies for balancing resource acquisition with thermoregulation. Despite these behavioural adjustments, both species exhibited their greatest body temperature variability during both the cool and hot drought periods, indicating that these behavioural responses were insufficient to fully buffer the physiological consequences of the drought. Following rainfall, increased vegetation greenness was associated with higher minimum body temperatures and reduced daily temperature amplitudes, consistent with physiological recovery. Nevertheless, drought-related mortality reached 27% in zebra and 15% in wildebeest, differences that were not statistically significant. Although this drought was considerably more severe than those reported from other African protected areas, grazer mortality was comparable to or lower than that documented during less severe droughts, suggesting that behavioural flexibility together with the large, heterogeneous landscape of Etosha partially buffered drought impacts. Our findings demonstrate that behavioural responses can delay, but not fully prevent, the breakdown of physiological homeostasis during extreme drought. Integrating movement, physiology and survival provides a mechanistic framework for identifying populations approaching their resilience limits as climate change increases the frequency of extreme drought events. Resumen El cambio climático ha causado el aumento de la frecuencia e intensidad de las sequías en zonas áridas. Sin embargo, aún se desconocen algunos mecanismos que determinan si los grandes herbívoros sobreviven a estos eventos. Investigamos cómo una sequía extrema afectó el movimiento, uso del agua, temperatura corporal y supervivencia de dos herbívoros pastadores dependientes del agua, cebra de llanura (Equus quagga) y ñu azul (Connochaetes taurinus), en el Parque Nacional de Etosha, Namibia.…
n30e3bc99286c: The effects of mobile organisms on community structure and assembly are poorly understood. Distributional data show that seasonal migration in birds drives a complex continental redistribution of phylogenetic community structure. These results reveal a dynamic continental landscape of community structure directed by the movements of migratory birds. Abstract Seasonal migration in birds involves a substantial spatial redistribution of avian biodiversity each year and drives seasonal changes in community composition. Migrants experience different combinations of species interactions over space and time, generating regular disassembly and reassembly of bird communities throughout their annual cycles. However, the effects of seasonal migration on phylogenetic community structure remain poorly understood. We assess spatiotemporal variation in phylogenetic community structure of North American passerines to test how seasonal migration restructures the evolutionary relatedness and dominant assembly mechanisms in bird communities throughout the annual cycle. Using distributional projections, we calculated metrics describing the phylogenetic dispersion of passerine communities each week of the year. We then tested the relationship between seasonal turnover in community phylogenetic dispersion and seasonal variation in species richness and proportion of migratory species. Seasonal migration, by changing spatial patterns of avian diversity, simultaneously drives a complex continental redistribution of phylogenetic community structure. We find evidence of taxonomic scale dependency to our results, wherein throughout North America, the seasonal influx of migrant passerines yields communities that are overall more phylogenetically clustered, yet also exhibit greater phylogenetic overdispersion at smaller taxonomic scales. Seasonal shifts in phylogenetic dispersion, though complex, track changes in diversity, manifesting as fluctuations in phylogenetic dispersion between northern and southern regions as seasonal migrants move between these regions. Our findings reveal a dynamic continental landscape of phylogenetic community structure directed by the movements of seasonal migrants.
n6ca0aef8126a: The roles of morphology and phylogeny in thermoregulation were studied in mimetic Heliconius butterflies across habitats. Buffering ability differed among habitats, likely due to morphology. Live heating rate decreased with iridescence and forewing length. No phylogenetic signal was detected. This suggests Heliconius wing patterns may contribute to thermoregulation. Abstract Temperature determines butterflies' physiological processes and performance. It varies strongly across time and space, with tropical butterflies experiencing temperatures close to their thermal limits. Climate change with more frequent heat waves may push species closer to these limits. Butterflies are known to thermoregulate, which is influenced by their morphology and behaviour. However, in tropical butterflies, little is known about how thermoregulatory abilities vary across habitats and if morphology or species relatedness are their drivers. We conducted a field and laboratory study on buffering ability—the ability to regulate body temperature with respect to air temperature—, take‐off temperature and heating rate of mimetic Heliconius butterflies from different habitats. We tested whether butterfly thermoregulation varies across habitats and morphologies. We also tested whether closely related species exhibit more similar thermoregulatory abilities and explored the importance of behaviour. Mimetic Heliconius pairs are two species that have nearly identical wing coloration and are often in different phylogenetic clades. Studying these pairs allows us to quantify the contribution of morphology and phylogenetic relatedness to thermoregulation. Because mimetic species pairs are often restricted to specific habitats, thermoregulatory abilities can be compared across habitats. We found that butterflies from different habitats differed in their buffering ability, likely due to differences in morphology, such as wing colour. Take‐off temperature was lowest in the only high‐altitude species we studied, whereas species from lowland habitats did not differ. Live heating rate did not differ across habitats, yet it decreased with iridescence and forewing length. There was no phylogenetic signal in thermoregulatory abilities, indicating that more closely related species did not thermoregulate more similarly than expected by chance. Our results showed that the convergent wing patterns in Heliconius butterflies may contribute to thermoregulatory ability and that thermoregulation should be considered when investigating the habitat specificity of mimetic pairs. Furthermore, Heliconius thermoregulation is not constrained by shared ancestry, suggesting that the morphological traits observed in the different mimetic pairs may be advantageous in certain thermal environmental conditions. Overall, species differences in thermoregulatory abilities may shape how Heliconius distributions respond to climate change‐driven temperature shifts. Resumen La temperatura determina los procesos fisiológicos y el rendimiento de las mariposas. Esta varía considerablemente en el tiempo y el espacio, y en los trópicos las mariposas experimentan temperaturas cercanas a sus límites térmicos. En un escenario de cambio climático, las olas de calor más frecuentes podrían acercar aún más a las especies de mariposas a estos límites. Se sabe que las mariposas termorregulan y que su capacidad termorreguladora está influenciada por su morfología y comportamiento. Sin embargo, en las mariposas tropicales se sabe poco sobre cómo varían las capacidades termorreguladoras entre hábitats y si la morfología o el parentesco filogenético entre especies son sus factores determinantes.…
n58b80f5450d7: Adaxial and abaxial stomatal densities in amphistomatous plants follow a phylogenetically structured allometric scaling relationship, with species‐specific departures (ASR) associated with climate–soil context. Summary Amphistomatous plants distribute stomata between the adaxial and abaxial leaf surfaces, but whether this dual‐surface allocation follows a predictable scaling relationship, and why species deviate from it, remains poorly understood. Here, we compiled a global dataset of adaxial and abaxial stomatal densities for 559 species across 380 sites and 63 families. We quantified their allometric relationship using phylogenetic reduced major axis regression and calculated amphistomatal scaling residuals (ASR) as signed perpendicular deviations from the fitted scaling relationship. We then examined variation in ASR among plant functional groups and across climatic and edaphic gradients. Adaxial and abaxial stomatal densities showed a significant allometric relationship after accounting for phylogenetic nonindependence, with a slope significantly > 1. ASR showed a significant phylogenetic signal but did not differ significantly between woody and herbaceous species, evergreen and deciduous woody species, or annual and perennial herbs. Individual environmental associations with ASR were generally modest, whereas the selected phylogenetic model retained multiple interaction terms, indicating that associations between ASR and environmental conditions were strongly context‐dependent. By quantifying departures from adaxial–abaxial scaling, our study identifies a distinct dimension of stomatal allocation that is structured by evolutionary history and associated with multidimensional climatic and edaphic context. This framework provides a basis for testing the physiological and evolutionary mechanisms underlying variation in amphistomatous stomatal allocation.
n1633c271b655: Yellow‐cedar has experienced widespread decline as climate change reduces the snowpack that insulates its roots, but the mechanism of injury is unknown. We tested two competing hypotheses in roots of four conifers: loss of xylem conductivity from freeze‐thaw embolism, or loss of radial conductivity from direct freezing injury that forms cortical lacunae. Embolism caused little loss of conductivity in any species or treatment (a–c). In contrast, extreme freeze–thaw pushed radial conductivity loss in yellow‐cedar beyond the 50% threshold for lethal hydraulic dysfunction (f). Root freezing injury, not embolism, may explain why yellow‐cedar is especially vulnerable to snowpack loss. Summary Winter snowpack loss exposes fine roots to freeze–thaw cycles at high latitudes and elevations, but the mechanisms of injury and reasons for species differences in vulnerability are not well understood. Motivated by yellow‐cedar decline, we evaluated competing mechanisms of freeze–thaw hydraulic dysfunction (xylem embolism and cortical lacunae) and whether root economics strategy predicts susceptibility. We subjected 96 seedlings of four co‐occurring Pacific Northwest conifers (mountain hemlock, western hemlock, western redcedar, and yellow‐cedar) to seven daily temperature cycles with minima of 3, −3, or −9°C, quantifying xylem and radial conductivity loss, cortical lacunae, and root economics traits. Xylem conductivity loss was low in all species and treatments (mean 11–14%). Yellow‐cedar averaged 58% simulated radial conductivity loss at −9°C, with lacunae occupying 20% of cortical area. Hemlocks (with pervasively lignified cortical walls) rarely formed lacunae, whereas cedars (with largely unlignified walls reinforced by phi‐thickenings) were more susceptible. More acquisitive roots were more vulnerable, among and within species. Our results indicate that cortical lacunae, not xylem embolism, drive interspecific differences in freeze–thaw hydraulic dysfunction, which was most severe in yellow‐cedar. Vulnerability corresponded to cortical wall construction and root economics strategy, providing a mechanistic basis for yellow‐cedar's unique susceptibility to snowpack loss.
ncc1f73cb2b15: Schematic presentation highlighting role of PP‐InsPs in orchestrating diverse physiological functions and an illustration highlighting the putative roles of InsP and PP‐InsPs in plant terrestrialization. Summary Diphosphate‐containing inositol phosphates, also known as inositol pyrophosphates (PP‐InsPs), are energy‐rich signaling molecules that orchestrate an ever‐expanding repertoire of cellular processes in eukaryotes. Recent advances in analytical methodologies have been instrumental in detecting these messengers in plant extracts and characterizing the enzymology underlying PP‐InsP metabolism in plants. Collectively, these developments have been critical to establishing PP‐InsPs as emerging cellular messengers that control a broad spectrum of physiological processes, including immunity, nutrient homeostasis, growth, and development in plants. In this Tansley insight, we synthesize current knowledge on the molecular basis of PP‐InsP metabolism and their physiological functions, and outline potential future research directions. We further discuss the putative role of PP‐InsPs in plant terrestrialization, a pivotal evolutionary transition that fundamentally reshaped Earth's biosphere approximately half a billion years ago.
n7dab515eeef7: Modelling of Ca2+ effects at the micro, macro, and cellular levels. (a) Ca2+ binding to a calcium-binding protein (CBP) with two EF hands. (b) Four basic Ca2+ sensor modules. (c) Combining Ca2+ decoding modules with opposite properties can restrict the activity of the target protein (TP) to frequency islands. Summary Calcium signals are fundamental for plants and play crucial roles in developmental processes and in rapid responses to environmental stimuli and stress factors. Nevertheless, the mechanisms underlying the decoding of calcium signals in plants are still largely unclear. We have addressed the question of Ca2+ signal decoding in a bottom-up modelling approach starting with the thermodynamics of Ca2+ binding to EF hands (EF: Glutamic acid–Phenylalanine) in Ca2+-binding proteins (CBPs). On this basis, we identified four universal, fundamental Ca2+ decoding modules, in which a CBP modulates the activity of a target protein (TP). Representatives of these basic modules are omnipresent in plant cells. Their Ca2+ dependent properties are mainly determined by the interaction of the CBP with the TP rather than the Ca2+-binding properties of the EF hands. Combinations of the modules generated complexes that are also observed in plants, which decode not only the amplitude but also the frequency of Ca2+ signals by setting specific ‘frequency islands’ in which a TP is active. The modelling approach presented here addresses the decoding of Ca2+ signals from the microscopic to the systemic level and could help to find the ‘Rosetta Stone’ for Ca2+ signalling in plants. Resumen Las señales de calcio son fundamentales para las plantas y desempeñan funciones cruciales en los procesos de desarrollo, así como en las respuestas rápidas a los estímulos ambientales y los factores de estrés. Sin embargo, los mecanismos implicados en la decodificación de las señales de calcio en las plantas siguen sin estar claros en gran medida. Hemos abordado el tema de la decodificación de las señales de calcio mediante un enfoque de modelado ascendente (bottom-up), partiendo de la termodinámica de la unión de Ca2+ a los dominios EF-hand (EF: ácido glutámico–fenilalanina) en proteínas con unión de calcio (CBP, por sus siglas en inglés, Ca 2+ -binding proteins). Sobre esta base, identificamos cuatro módulos universales y fundamentales de decodificación de Ca2+, en los cuales una CBP modula la actividad de una proteína diana (TP, del inglés target protein). Los representantes de estos módulos básicos son omnipresentes en las células vegetales. Sus propiedades dependientes de Ca2+ están determinadas principalmente por la interacción de la CBP con la TP, más que por las propiedades de unión de Ca2+ de los dominios EF-hand. Las combinaciones de estos módulos generaron complejos que también se observan en las plantas, lo que permitió decodificar no solo la amplitud, sino también la frecuencia de las señales de Ca2+, al establecer «islas de frecuencia» específicas en las cuales una TP está activa. El enfoque de modelado presentado en este trabajo aborda la decodificación de las señales de Ca2+ desde el nivel microscópico hasta el sistémico, y podría ayudar a encontrar la «piedra Rosetta» de la señalización por Ca2+ en las plantas.
nfe3d3a1ef95e: PELOTA (PELO), a conserved ribosome surveillance factor underlying the tomato resistance allele ty-5, plays key roles in TYLCV susceptibility and reproductive development. Complete loss of PELO function (pelo-1CR ) confers strong resistance to TYLCV but causes severe floral defects, impaired male and female fertility, and complete sterility. While ty-5 reduces disease severity, it also decreases fruit size. CRISPR-mediated promoter editing generates novel PELO alleles, with reduced expression that confers resistance while maintaining normal fertility and fruit size (PELOpro-31 ). Fine-tuning PELO expression therefore offers a promising strategy to improve tomato resistance without compromising reproductive development. Summary Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is a major threat to tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) production, and durable resistance remains challenging to achieve. We show that complete loss of function of PELOTA (PELO), a conserved ribosome surveillance factor underlying the resistance allele ty-5, confers near-immunity to TYLCV. Unexpectedly, PELO is also required for reproductive development; pelo mutants display severe floral defects, impaired male and female fertility, and complete sterility, revealing a previously unknown role for PELO in tomato plant fertility. Using CRISPR-mediated promoter editing, we generated novel PELO alleles with reduced expression that maintain fertility while conferring enhanced resistance to TYLCV, providing a new strategy.
n059ba7ef9946: Stem increment, sap flow and leaf phenology. Summary Savannas are ecosystems with hot and wet summers and warm and dry winters. How and why savanna trees partition their physiological activity through this seasonal cycle is unknown; yet it is important to understand this temporal partitioning in order to anticipate how anthropogenic climatic change will impact the functioning of savannas. In a South African savanna ecosystem, we examined the temporal pattern of leaf deployment, sap flow and stem increment phenology over three growing seasons for six species. We found that although the phenologies varied between years, there was a high degree of temporal overlap in leaf, sap flow and stem increment phenology between the six study species. Further, we found that a surprisingly large proportion of days on which the measured soil water potential was sufficient for physiological activity remained unused. Although our data are consistent with convergent selection for deciduousness, the unused soil water niche we detected suggests that climate should select for evergreen strategies. Possible explanations for the dominance of deciduousness in these savannas relate to the costs of leaf construction coupled with the risk of leaf destruction due to fire and/or foliovory.
nb7463866a33e: Although restoration science increasingly considers social–ecological complexity, many restoration projects still fall short of their ecological or social goals. We argue that such failures often stem from a lack of attention to long-term social–ecological dynamics within the target system. To overcome this problem, we propose ‘regenerative transformation’ as a new paradigm to guide ecosystem restoration. Regenerative transformation foregrounds the thriving of human and other forms of life and emphasizes healthy endogenous social–ecological dynamics rather than exogenous interventions. Facilitating regenerative transformation through restoration will require changes in how restoration is conceptualized, practiced, and governed—moving from a focus on abstract targets and simple outcome indicators toward developing supportive conditions for the long-term, equitable coevolution of healthy social–ecological dynamics.
n977eb12aac01: To achieve Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) Target 3, the selection of protected areas must consider the condition of ecosystems at sites in addition to the GBF 30% area target. Implementing this consideration for coral reef ecosystems is challenging because data describing condition are patchy and limited. Thus, there is uncertainty in how effective coral reef condition data are for informing conservation priorities. To address this uncertainty, we evaluated whether including ecosystem condition data changed conservation priorities when the objective was to protect reefs and implement Target 3. We tested multiple static and modeled temporal coral reef condition datasets for the Great Barrier Reef and found that including reef condition significantly altered spatial planning priorities (p < 0.001), with effects varying according to the condition indicator used. Almost half of the reefs prioritized for protection when condition metrics were included became low priority when they were excluded. Ignoring information about condition missed conservation targets for ∼22% of reef habitats once condition measures were included, highlighting how presence‐only approaches can overestimate conservation benefits by treating lower‐condition reefs as equal contributors to biodiversity protection. These differences in priority areas highlight the need to develop and use effective condition metrics for designing marine protected area systems for coral reefs globally. Making such data available and usable for managers and practitioners is a priority for coral reef conservation. Incorporación de la condición de los arrecifes a la planeación de la conservación para cumplir con los resultados de sitio bajo el Marco Mundial para la Biodiversidad Resumen Para alcanzar la Meta 3 del Marco Mundial para la Biodiversidad (GBF) de Kunming‐Montreal, la selección de áreas protegidas debe tener en cuenta el estado de los ecosistemas en los distintos emplazamientos, además del objetivo del GBF de cubrir el 30% de la superficie. Aplicar esta consideración a los ecosistemas de arrecifes de coral supone un reto, ya que los datos que describen su estado son pocos y están fragmentados. Por lo tanto, existe incertidumbre sobre la eficacia de los datos sobre el estado de los arrecifes de coral a la hora de establecer prioridades de conservación. Para abordar esta incertidumbre, evaluamos si la inclusión de datos sobre el estado de los ecosistemas modificaba las prioridades de conservación cuando el objetivo era proteger los arrecifes y cumplir la Meta 3. Analizamos varios conjuntos de datos estáticos y temporales modelados sobre el estado de los arrecifes de coral de la Gran Barrera de Coral y descubrimos que la inclusión del estado de los arrecifes alteraba significativamente las prioridades de planificación espacial (p <0.001), con efectos que variaban según el indicador de estado utilizado. Casi la mitad de los arrecifes que se consideraban prioritarios para su protección cuando se incluían los indicadores de estado pasaban a tener baja prioridad cuando se excluían dichos indicadores. Cuando ignoramos la información sobre el estado, no se alcanzaron los objetivos de conservación en aproximadamente el 22% de los hábitats de arrecifes una vez que se incluyeron las medidas de estado, lo que resalta cómo los enfoques basados únicamente en la presencia pueden sobreestimar los beneficios de conservación al considerar que los arrecifes en peor estado contribuyen en igual medida a la protección de la biodiversidad. Estas diferencias en las áreas prioritarias ponen de manifiesto la necesidad de desarrollar y utilizar métricas de estado eficaces para diseñar sistemas de áreas marinas protegidas para los arrecifes de coral a nivel mundial. Poner dichos datos a disposición de los gestores y profesionales, y garantizar que sean utilizables, es una prioridad para la conservación de los arrecifes de coral.
n0c1252e15036: Understanding how climate change affects insect distribution is critical for biodiversity conservation, particularly in the case of range‐restricted and ecologically sensitive species. The glacial Apollo, Parnassius glacialis (Lepidoptera: Papilionidae), is a high‐altitude butterfly of notable scientific and esthetic value, yet its ecological response to climate change remains poorly understood. Here, we model the current and future distribution of P. glacialis across China and identify key environmental drivers shaping its habitat. We developed an ensemble species distribution model using 45 occurrence records and 10 bioclimatic variables, integrating outputs from multiple algorithms to enhance predictive robustness. Temperature—particularly seasonal variation—emerged as the strongest determinant of habitat suitability, followed by precipitation. At present, suitable habitats are concentrated in northern, southwestern, and eastern China. However, projections under future climate scenarios reveal a marked reduction in suitable range, with the habitat centroid shifting to lower elevations in Hubei Province. The direction and extent of this shift vary among scenarios, highlighting the species' vulnerability to both climatic and socioeconomic trajectories. These findings raise urgent conservation concerns, suggesting that P. glacialis may face significant habitat loss and range contraction under projected climate conditions. We recommend the establishment of targeted protected areas, the integration of insect responses into climate adaptation policies, and the implementation of long‐term ecological monitoring. This study provides crucial insights into climate‐driven range shifts in high‐altitude butterflies and underscores the broader need for adaptive conservation strategies in a warming world.
n920340a8d182: Simple sequence repeats (SSRs) are ubiquitous components of eukaryotic genomes that contribute to genome evolution, genetic variation, and gene regulation. Although genome‐wide SSR landscapes have been extensively characterized across vertebrates, the cross‐species distribution and functional associations of exonic SSR‐containing genes remain poorly understood, particularly in non‐model birds. To address this knowledge gap, we performed a comparative analysis of chromosome‐level genome assemblies from three diving duck species (Aythya ferina, Aythya marila, and Netta rufina) to investigate genome‐wide SSR patterns and the cross‐species sharing and functional characteristics of exonic SSR‐containing genes. Comparative analyses of genome‐wide SSRs revealed pronounced interspecific variation in SSR abundance and repeat composition, whereas exonic SSR abundance showed more similar values after normalization by total annotated exon sequence length. Cross‐species comparison identified 4336 exonic SSR‐containing genes shared among all three species, greatly outnumbering the species‐specific gene sets. Functional enrichment analyses identified four broad functional themes associated with these shared genes: (i) gene transcription and epigenetic regulation, (ii) protein homeostasis and the ubiquitin–proteasome system, (iii) development, differentiation and morphogenesis, and (iv) stress response and cellular maintenance. The most significantly enriched categories were associated with transcriptional regulation, chromatin remodeling, RNA processing, and epigenetic regulation, whereas autophagy‐ and other cellular‐maintenance pathways indicated additional associations with stress‐response processes. These functional associations should be interpreted cautiously because they may be influenced by cross‐species annotation limitations and gene‐architecture differences. Collectively, our results reveal distinct patterns for genome‐wide and exonic SSRs distribution among the three diving duck species and identify shared functional associations of genes containing exonic SSRs. These findings provide a comparative genomic framework for future investigations of exonic SSRs in waterfowl and other non‐model vertebrates.
nc483b69aa96b: Borrelia afzelii, a major causative agent of Lyme borreliosis in Europe, exhibits high polymorphism of the outer surface protein C (ospC) gene, which facilitates evasion of the vertebrate immune response. Among‐population differentiation was consistently lower at ospC than at IGS, and while IGS exhibited a significant isolation‐by‐distance pattern, no such signal was detected for ospC. Collectively, these findings support the hypothesis that balancing selection maintains ospC polymorphism and counteracts geographic differentiation, with implications for the evolutionary epidemiology of Lyme borreliosis in Europe.
nbb51fae6acf2: Effective conservation of marine mammals depends on reliable demographic information, yet acquiring such data for highly mobile cetaceans is challenging. Harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) are widely used as sentinel species, but much of what is known about their demography comes from stranding and bycatch records. Using a stage‐structured MPM parameterised from published vital rates, we derived the stable stage distribution (SSD) and compared it with age‐class distributions from 10,863 harbour porpoise strandings (of 16,181 total records) in Danish and North Sea waters, bycatch and mixed‐mortality records, and hunting captures from Greenland and Denmark. Deviations from SSD, and from the composition expected among deaths, were assessed using goodness‐of‐fit tests, distance metrics, and tests of the juvenile proportion. Strandings showed strong and consistent departures from SSD expectations, with juveniles markedly over‐represented across spatial and temporal scales. Divergence from the asymptotic stage structure was moderate to strong, varied across space, and increased significantly over time in 2 of 6 regions. Bycatch, mixed‐mortality, and hunting captures showed comparable SSD divergence, indicating that juvenile‐heavy mortality composition is not an artefact of stranding sampling alone. Our results show that harbour porpoise stranding, bycatch, and even hunting data should not be assumed to be demographically representative of living populations. Separating sampling bias from higher juvenile mortality needs independent estimates of juvenile survival.
n2736231adbf7: Many vertebrates that live in seasonal climates moult once or twice a year, with the effect of refreshing worn coat or plumage, increasing insulation or improving camouflage. Using the individually‐monitored red deer from the Isle of Rum, in which summer and winter coats are easily distinguished, we (a) test for traits that are predictive of moult timing, (b) explore traits that moult timing is predictive of and (c) analyse covariances between moult timings and calving dates at the individual, annual and residual level. We show that adult female moult timing in July and November is associated with age, reproductive status and parasite burden, and has been getting earlier over time in November. A female's moult timing also predicts the overwinter survival of herself and her current calf as well as her future fecundity. Moult timing varies among individuals and years. Covariances between calving dates and the timing of each moult shed light on the temporal patterns of condition within individuals and across years, for example, across years, winter moult covaries with the following calving date but not the summer moult that occurs shortly after. The timing of moult appears to be a non‐invasive measure of condition. Monitoring moult timing across years at the population level may shed light on year‐to‐year variation in population health and variation within populations is likely indicative of the relative conditions among individuals. Increased knowledge of population and individual condition may be of benefit for ungulate population management and conservation.
n14f0d6569174: The relationship between rodents and oak trees has attracted considerable attention. The interaction spans a wide range of outcomes, from extreme predation, in which rodents consume acorns, to forms of collaboration that approach mutualism. This study examines the influence of third species on rodent–oak interaction by using raptor models. The main objective is to determine whether raptors in the treetops can deter rodents from feeding on acorns, thereby reducing acorn dispersal. To achieve this objective, we monitored acorns' dispersal by four rodent species, Algerian mouse, wood mouse, common vole, and garden dormouse, in 10 m × 10 m semi‐wild enclosures with oak trees in the four corners, two of them with raptor models. Beneath the 4 oaks, 60 acorns, 15 acorns per tree, were provided daily for 15 days, and the acorns in situ consumption and dispersal were tracked to determine whether the presence of raptor models altered the dispersal by any of the rodent species. The results show that species that are actively involved in acorn dispersion through transport (Algerian mouse, wood mouse) modify their behavior in response to the presence of raptor models in the treetops. The garden dormouse also modifies its behavior, although this species does not transport or bury acorns; however, it does move them around on the surface and consumes most of the acorns whole by preying on them. Therefore, it does not participate in the acorn dispersion process. The common vole typically occupies open habitats without oaks and does not modify its behavior, probably because raptor models are not perceived as a threat.
n7cae52aaf556: Eye size influences captured light and visual resolution and is used as an indicator of the relative importance of vision. Although vision‐related sexual dimorphism is subtle among vertebrates, Cervids exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size, antler development, and reproductive strategies. We collected skull morphological, ocular biometric, and refractive error data from 69 semi‐domesticated reindeer (0.5–12.5‐year‐old; 27 females, 42 males) living year‐round under extreme high‐latitude seasonal variation in photoperiod in south‐central Norway. The relationships between eye size, mandible length, interorbital distance, and orbital diameter were analyzed, and binocular overlap and anterior blind zones were calculated. Eye size increased with measures of skull size, while refractive error remained minimal across all ages. Although male calves had significantly larger mandibles and interorbital distances, their orbital diameters were the same as in female calves. However, in adults, males also had larger orbital diameters. After controlling for differences in skeletal measures, males were found to have relatively smaller eyes than females, whereas binocular overlap and blind zones were similar. These findings demonstrate vision‐related sexual dimorphism in reindeer.
n58f0f8ba0bc7: The ‘social microbiome’ conceptualises gut microbial communities as ‘islands’ of host social organisation. Yet, in comparison to broader aspects of social organisation such as animals' group membership and composition, the impact of inter‐individual differences in sociality on microbiome community ecology remains less well studied. Bipartite network analysis showed that bacterial communities among macaques were nested rather than segregated or modular structures. Joint Species Distributions Models showed that macaques' sociality, particularly their dominance rank and their connectedness or centrality within their social grooming network, had the strongest impact on taxa abundance, followed by their demographic characteristics, and finally their exposure to both anthropogenic and abiotic environmental factors. Phylogenetically distant taxa were more likely to co‐occur within the same macaque hosts than phylogenetically related taxa. These findings confirm that microbiome communities are strongly influenced by the social status and connectedness of individual hosts. Nevertheless, the finding that some taxa were more prevalent among high‐ranking or well‐connected macaques, while others were more prevalent among low‐ranking or socially peripheral macaques, warrants further investigation into how individual differences in social microbiomes might affect their health and fitness. Future studies, through the collection of behavioural and microbial data on additional macaque groups, may provide further insights into the relative effects of animals' social organisation and social behaviours on microbiomes.
n575429602f79: Urban plant communities assemble from a regional species pool shaped by both ecological processes and horticultural trade, yet how these two forces jointly structure its functional composition remains poorly understood. Using a trait database covering life‐history strategies, morphology, environmental preferences, and human use, we examined functional trait space using principal component analysis and quantified functional richness, dispersion, and originality. We further tested which traits were associated with wild establishment among non‐native species and invasive status among overlapping species using Firth logistic regression. Commercial species were unevenly distributed across growth forms, dominating among trees (67.9%) and shrubs (59.7%) but less represented among herbs (17.9%). Functional differentiation was strongest along an environmental niche axis, with commercial herbs associated with drier conditions and commercial woody species with warmer conditions. Commercial species consistently had the lowest functional richness, dispersion, and originality across all growth forms. Wild establishment was associated with multiple environmental, reproductive, and ecological traits, whereas invasive status was associated with warmer temperature preference and anthropogenic tolerance, although the latter analysis was exploratory. These results indicate that commercial availability creates a functionally selective pool of species that may influence later urban community assembly. By shaping the functional possibilities available before local assembly occurs, horticultural trade may therefore leave an important human imprint on urban biodiversity, with potential downstream consequences for ecosystem functioning and trophic interactions.
n2daf077e23a0: Invasive bullheads of the genus Ameiurus are actively expanding across Eastern Europe, yet accurate species identification remains problematic owing to phenotypic plasticity and high intraspecific morphological variability. Our findings establish an ecological baseline for range forecasting and risk assessment of Ameiurus in European inland waters, underscoring the urgent need for coordinated molecular monitoring at the leading edges of freshwater biological invasions.
nd85f33289762: Understanding the impact of changing temperature on population densities is necessary to predict the likely impact of climate anomalies (e.g., marine heatwaves) or forecast distribution shifts under future climate scenarios. Population densities are often analyzed using spatio‐temporal models (STMs), which typically predict densities based on local habitat conditions while also estimating latent spatial and spatio‐temporal variation. Recent research extends STMs by also estimating density responses to habitat conditions at nearby locations using a “spatially distributed lag” (SDL) that averages habitat conditions in the vicinity of samples. Here, we extend the SDL by incorporating insights from diffusion‐enhanced STMs to simultaneously estimate spatially distributed and time‐lagged responses to nearby and past habitat conditions (a “spatio‐temporal distributed lag” STDL). We then use summer bottom trawl survey data from the eastern Bering Sea (1982–2024) to measure whether spatial and/or temporal lags are parsimonious when predicting population density from temperature anomalies for six ecologically important fishes. Results show that time‐lagged responses are parsimonious, positive, and substantial (correlation of 0.20–0.83 per year) for five species, and that density responses to temperature anomalies also diffuse outward over time for four species at 30–53 km per year. A self‐ and cross‐test simulation experiment shows that model selection can identify the appropriate model and that parameter estimates are approximately unbiased. We therefore conclude that temperature carryover effects arise in marine fishes and implement the method in the R package sdmTMB so that future studies can estimate nonlocal and time‐lagged responses when measuring density responses to habitat.
na6f8efeb497e: This study shows that stand development decreases soil nitrogen and phosphorus availability and results in a shift from nitrogen limitation to phosphorus limitation. In response, there was a clear transition from trees depending more on root nutrient scavenging to trees relying more on both nitrogen scavenging by ectomycorrhizal fungi and root phosphorus mining as stands developed. Abstract Soil nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) availability generally decrease with forest stand development, yet how tree species acclimate to this decline remains largely unclear. The functional coordination hypothesis proposes that trees concurrently improve leaf nutrient recycling and root nutrient acquisition to cope with nutrient deficiency. Conversely, the resource limitation hypothesis posits that trees prioritize either strategy, as simultaneous employment of both strategies is resource costly. Stand development reduced soil N and P availability and caused a shift from N to P limitation as evidenced by increasing needle N:P ratios and decreasing N:P‐acquisition enzyme ratios. There was no evidence of N or P retranslocation from old to young needles, and nutrient resorption efficiency was independent of soil nutrient availability, indicating that adjustments of needle nutrient recycling contribute little to mitigating nutrient deficiency. Root length density decreased exponentially with stand development, whereas cord‐forming ectomycorrhizal fungi (EMF), root phosphatase activity and rhizosphere effects on plant‐available soil P logarithmically increased, implying a shift from root nutrient scavenging to combined EMF nutrient scavenging and root P mining. Synthesis. Our findings suggest that tree species do not necessarily rely on both improved recycling and acquisition to acclimate to soil nutrient scarcity with stand development. However, trees can simultaneously depend on physiological adaptations of absorptive fine roots themselves, as well as on a constrained selection of EMF. This reveals that complex sets of adaptations, both root‐based ‘do‐it‐yourself’ and mycorrhizal‐based ‘outsourcing’, can be effectively used by trees to cope with changes in soil nutrient availability.
n8ed4edae1e01: Insect societies are characterised by a reproductive division of labour between queens that monopolise egg production and workers that perform all non‐reproductive tasks. However, the molecular changes that translate worker presence into queen behavioural specialisation remain unknown. Our transcriptomic analyses revealed that 123 genes were differentially expressed between the brains of queens maintained with and without workers. These genes were enriched for processes related to brain energy metabolism and neuronal plasticity and signalling. By investigating the response of selected genes of interest to further manipulations of the social environment, we identified four candidate genes that fully mirrored the queen behavioural changes. Specifically, their expression changes in response to worker presence were reversible and they did not respond to mere cues of the worker presence. These candidate genes included the transcription factor Krüppel‐homologue 1 and other genes in the juvenile hormone and insulin signalling pathways, both known to regulate multiple aspects of division of labour in social insects. By producing a robust, well‐replicated and well‐controlled investigation of the transcriptomic basis of the behavioural specialisation of ant queens, this study provides a better understanding of the emergence and maintenance of reproductive division of labour in insect societies.
n1df470aaa7c7: Sexual selection via honest (costly) signals of fitness can generate patterns in immunogenetic diversity at the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). We found population level support for a correlation between MHC diversity and Gyrodactylus prevalence, including an overall association between MHC supertype composition and prevalence. At the individual level, supertype (functional) diversity again emerged as a more informative measure than allelic richness alone. Predation was associated with Gyrodactylus prevalence and orange, but not black, colouration. Notably, some of these relationships differed between the individual and population levels. Further, much of this variation was explained by processes acting at a broader geographic scale within river drainages, which comprise divergent guppy lineages. These findings suggest that evolutionary history and processes such as genetic drift and gene flow contribute substantially to these relationships, but that ecological variation (i.e., predation) interacts with these processes. Our findings indicate that multi‐trait relationships between colour, immunogenetic diversity and infection are best examined within their broader evolutionary and ecological contexts.
ndc8be78818ef: The dose–time program of adventitious root (AR) formation. Summary Adventitious root (AR) formation is the developmental process that makes vegetative propagation possible, underpinning forestry, horticulture, and the clonal multiplication of elite and hard‐to‐propagate genotypes. Despite a detailed understanding of auxin's stage‐specific roles across the rooting program, propagation practice still treats auxin supply as a quantity to set rather than a profile to match. We argue that this produces a temporal mismatch between auxin supply and developmental demand: the available evidence shows that exogenous auxin availability frequently declines before the stages it should support are complete, particularly in slow‐to‐root and recalcitrant species, where developmental timelines are longest. New delivery tools, such as slow‐release conjugates, encapsulation systems, and selective auxin agonists, now make time‐structured delivery profiles feasible, but realizing their potential requires a different starting point. Rather than optimizing auxin dose empirically against rooting outcome, the field should characterize the spatiotemporal auxin demand curve across AR stages and design delivery profiles to match it. We outline the conceptual framework for this shift and the experimental approaches now available to support it.
ncb40714d4211: Piecewise structural equation model and decomposition of standardized effects. Summary Aridity is a primary driver of plant community assembly, yet most trait-based studies focus on mean traits rather than trait dispersion. Soil microbes may mediate plant responses to aridity, but whether leaf and root trait dispersion responds to aridity through shared or distinct microbial pathways remains unclear. Using 535 species-by-plot records (247 species) along an aridity gradient in north-west China, we quantified four leaf and four root traits, soil properties, microbial diversity and composition, and microbial carbon use efficiency. We tested whether aridity differentially regulates leaf vs root functional dispersion (FD is ), and whether these responses are associated with different microbial predictors. Leaf traits shifted more consistently with aridity and were more tightly linked to environmental variation than root traits. Leaf FD is negatively correlated with CUE, whereas root FD is negatively correlated with fungal diversity and bacterial community composition. These associations weakened toward less arid sites. Structural equation modeling further showed that leaf FD is linked primarily to microbial functioning, whereas root FD is linked more strongly to microbial diversity and composition. Our results reveal that aridity reshapes trait dispersion through organ-specific plant–microbe pathways, highlighting that predicting dryland community responses to increasing drought must treat above- and belowground traits separately.
n7c27a8b0d4cc: Here, we reveal that fruit color and size traits signaled macronutrient reward specifically relating to bird‐, mammal‐, and mixed‐dispersed dispersal syndromes. Birds prioritize fruit color, while mammals prioritize fruit size to achieve optimal macronutritional reward, and these signal‐mutualist relationships are shaped by associated disperser traits, demonstrating co‐evolutionary mechanisms driving adaptive differentiation of fruit morphological and macronutrient traits. Our findings connect classical dispersal‐syndrome research with more recent developments in signal theory, trait‐matching theory, optimal foraging theory, and nutritional geometry theory, thus advancing the seed disperser mutualism paradigm. Summary Fruit color and size provide vital cues for determining seed dispersers' preferences; however, any consistent underlying link between these traits and fruit macronutritional rewards remains to be established by large‐scale analyses. We collated a global database comprising 2626 observations of 1626 fruiting plant species from 460 global sites to test whether fruit color and size traits do indeed consistently signal macronutritional rewards to frugivores. We found that consistent fruit color and size signaled macronutrient reward specifically relating to bird‐, mammal‐, and mixed‐dispersed dispersal syndromes. Lipids were the predominant macronutrient in black, blue, red, orange, and yellow fruits with birds (27.24%), whereas sugar predominated in mammal‐dispersed fruits (72.55%). Fruits dispersed by mammals (25.55 mm) were consistently larger than those dispersed by birds (10.17 mm) regardless of fruit color, and total macronutrient mass per fruit increased with fruit size. These signal‐mutualist relationships are shaped by associated disperser traits, demonstrating co‐evolutionary mechanisms driving adaptive differentiation of fruit morphological and macronutrient traits. By integrating the disperser syndrome hypothesis and signal theory with nutritional geometry theory and trait‐matching theory, our study expounds the role of seed disperser selective preferences in the evolution of fruit traits, thus advancing the seed disperser mutualism paradigm.
nc43553da59b6: Phenotypes of 43‐d‐old wild‐type (WT), Osbzip11‐KO, and OsbZIP11‐OX seedlings grown under control N and low N conditions. Summary Nitrogen (N)‐deficiency responses, which are closely linked to plant biomass and crop yield, differ between plant tissues. A previous in silico analysis suggested that four transcription factors, including OsbZIP11, play vital roles in the gene regulatory network governing N‐deficiency responses (NDRs) in rice roots. To investigate the role of OsbZIP11 in NDRs, the phenotypes, functional responses, and gene expression of rice plants that either lacked functional OsbZIP11 or overexpressed OsbZIP11 were analyzed. Contrary to expectations, OsbZIP11 function showed an overwhelmingly stronger association with photosynthetic gene expression than with any other physiological process, including the expression control of N‐related genes. OsbZIP11 directly suppressed numerous photosynthetic genes as a transcriptional repressor. N deficiency increased OsbZIP11 expression in shoots, consistent with N deficiency‐reduced photosynthetic activity. Furthermore, removing functional OsbZIP11 and OsbZIP11 overexpression produced opposite effects on the expression of genes involved in the light‐dependent reactions of photosynthesis and carbon dioxide fixation, as well as on growth and grain yield. These findings indicate that OsbZIP11 is a critical factor responsible for N deficiency‐induced decreases in photosynthesis in rice and provide new insights into the mechanism underlying the coordination of C and N acquisition. まとめ 植物のバイオマスや作物の収量と密接に関連する窒素(N)欠乏応答は、植物組織によって異なる。これまでに計算科学的手法により、OsbZIP11を含む4つの転写因子が、イネの根における窒素欠乏応答を制御する遺伝子調節ネットワークにおいて重要な役割を果たしていることが示唆されていた。 窒素欠乏応答におけるOsbZIP11の役割を解明するため、機能的なOsbZIP11を欠くイネおよびOsbZIP11遺伝子を過剰発現させたイネの表現型、機能的応答、および遺伝子発現を解析した。 予想に反して、OsbZIP11の機能は、窒素関連遺伝子の発現制御を含む他のいかなる生理的プロセスよりも、光合成関連遺伝子の発現と圧倒的に強い関連性を示した。OsbZIP11は転写抑制因子として多数の光合成関連遺伝子の発現を直接的に抑制しており、また、窒素欠乏による光合成活性の低下と一致して、地上部におけるOsbZIP11遺伝子の発現量は窒素欠乏により増加した。さらに、機能的なOsbZIP11の除去とOsbZIP11遺伝子の過剰発現は、光合成の光依存反応や二酸化炭素固定に関与する遺伝子の発現、ならびに生育や穀粒収量に対して、正反対の影響をもたらした。 これらの知見は、OsbZIP11がイネにおける窒素欠乏による光合成低下を担う重要な転写因子であることを示しており、植物における炭素と窒素の獲得の協調的制御を司るメカニズムに関する新たな知見を提供するものである。
nc2d700e190ef: Observed vs modelled relationships between (a) T opt and growth temperature and (b) normalised A opt and growth temperature for different species. Summary Leaf-level photosynthesis acclimates to growth conditions over days to weeks, with the instantaneous optimal temperature for photosynthesis (T opt) increasing with growth temperature (T growth). We investigated how this behaviour emerges in the P model, a primary production model based on eco-evolutionary optimality hypotheses. We evaluated the P model estimates against experimental data for three herbaceous species grown at different temperatures and examined mechanisms underlying the responses of T opt and the photosynthetic rate at T opt (A opt). The model yields a realistic increase in T opt with T growth and a peaked relationship between A opt and T growth. These responses emerge largely from adjustment of the stomatal sensitivity parameter ξ, which determines the internal-to-ambient CO2 ratio (c i : c a) and its sensitivity to vapour pressure deficit. Rubisco kinetics (K) does not acclimate in the model, but its temperature dependence enters acclimation through optimality, mainly via ξ, shifting T opt. The decline in A opt at high growth temperatures, often attributed to heat stress, reflects the narrowing gap between T opt and T growth because the T opt shift has a slope below one. The P model provides a mechanistic explanation for observed trends in T opt and A opt and a scalable approach for representing biochemical and stomatal acclimation in land-surface models.
n87045044542f: Climate change is driving increasingly frequent and severe weather events that can undermine the effectiveness of conservation interventions for threatened species, yet the extent and mechanisms of such impacts remain poorly understood. We assessed both peer‐reviewed and gray literature to determine how climate adaptation interventions have been affected by weather events across different land types, Australian bioregions, taxonomic groups, and intervention categories. Specifically, we evaluated 593 climate adaptation interventions for 145 threatened species in Australia. We found 36% of the interventions experienced impacts from weather events, with only 9% of these reporting positive outcomes, which were significantly associated with above‐average rainfall. Critically, our dataset was dominated by plant‐focused translocations, with drought and wildfire representing the primary stressors. Most taxonomic groups, despite being targeted by conservation interventions, experienced population declines and habitat loss following weather events. Inadequate mitigation of cumulative threats, such as grazing pressure and weed invasion, frequently exacerbated negative impacts and reduced the resilience of ecosystems to withstand and recover from weather impacts. Our findings suggested that although extreme weather risks have been recognized, they are not yet being systematically incorporated into the design and implementation of climate adaptation interventions in Australia. We recommend adopting adaptive and integrated management approaches to enhance climate adaptation success for threatened species, particularly by enabling the systematic management of multiple threats and facilitating flexible, evidence‐informed interventions in response to changing environmental conditions. Future research should prioritize adopting more rigorous, proactive experimental designs that bridge the gap between recognizing extreme weather risks and implementing robust mitigation strategies. Expanding the empirical basis for climate adaptation is also needed for less‐represented taxa such as reptiles, invertebrates, and freshwater fish, as well as in regions with limited data such as central and northern Australia where increased cyclone and flooding intensities are already occurring. Analizamos la literatura revisada por pares y la literatura gris para determinar cómo se han visto afectadas las intervenciones de adaptación climática por los fenómenos meteorológicos en diferentes tipos de terreno, biorregiones australianas, grupos taxonómicos y categorías de intervención.
