nc35559884222: Understanding drivers of plant rarity, especially for highly threatened and understudied tropical oceanic island flora, can improve conservation prioritization. Studies exploring trait–rarity relationships have the potential to identify species that may be more vulnerable, but inference is often limited by incomplete taxon sampling and failure to account for local ecological context. We used the complete Kauaʻi single‐island endemic angiosperm flora (240 taxa), combining known population sizes and robust population estimates determined for International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species assessments, and compiled data for 42 plant traits while accounting for elevation and habitat type to explore trait–rarity relationships. We tested for phylogenetic signals, accounted for correlation and log10‐transformed continuous trait data, and implemented phylogenetic linear models with a continuous response (log10(n + 1), where n is the population size) in the phylolm R package. Discrete variables were treated as fixed effects. We also tested multitrait models and individual confounding traits. We found that shorter species, species with shorter leaves, species with lower seed mass, and species with lower initial seed germinability were significant predictors of rarity. Species occurring at lower elevations and across narrower elevational ranges also tended to have smaller populations. Importantly, elevation influenced trait–rarity relationships, with plant height showing different relationships with rarity across elevation classes. Our findings demonstrated that traits associated with rarity are not universal predictors but context‐dependent indicators that may aid conservation prioritization. More broadly, our study highlights the value of more complete sampling and incorporation of local ecological context for trait‐based assessments of rarity, particularly for threatened oceanic island floras. Importancia del contexto ecológico en las relaciones característica‐rareza inferidas a partir de la flora angiosperma endémica de una sola isla Resumen Comprender los factores que determinan la rareza de las plantas, especialmente en el caso de la flora de las islas oceánicas tropicales, la cual está sumamente amenazada y poco estudiada, puede mejorar la priorización de la conservación. Los estudios que exploran las relaciones entre características y rareza tienen el potencial de identificar especies que pueden ser más vulnerables, pero las conclusiones suelen verse limitadas por un muestreo incompleto de los taxones y por no tener en cuenta el contexto ecológico local. Utilizamos la flora completa de angiospermas endémicas de la isla de Kauaʻi (240 taxones) junto con los tamaños de población conocidos y las estimaciones poblacionales robustas determinadas para las evaluaciones de la Lista Roja de Especies Amenazadas de la Unión Internacional para la Conservación de la Naturaleza (UICN) y recopilamos datos sobre características botánicas, considerando la altitud y el tipo de hábitat, para explorar las relaciones entre las características y la rareza. Comprobamos la presencia de señales filogenéticas, tuvimos en cuenta la correlación y los datos de rasgos continuos transformados en log10 e implementamos modelos lineales filogenéticos con una respuesta continua (log10 (n+1), donde n es el tamaño de la población) en el paquete phylolm de R. Las variables discretas se trataron como efectos fijos. También analizamos modelos multicaracterísticos y rasgos de confusión individuales. Observamos que las especies más bajas, las de hojas más cortas, las de menor masa de semillas y las de menor capacidad de germinación inicial de las semillas eran predictores significativos de la rareza. Las especies que se dan a menor altitud y en rangos altitudinales más estrechos también tendían a tener poblaciones más pequeñas.…
nbc0e7291593d: Periodically driven systems are ubiquitous in nature, and their stability against perturbations such as the introduction of a novel pathogens or invasive species is often a major concern. To better understand and control these systems, it is common to assess the sensitivity to changes in the model parameters of stability threshold quantities such as the basic reproduction number R0$$ {R}_0 $$, or the Floquet multiplier Λ$$ \Lambda $$, which determines stability against invasion of the disease/invader‐free system. However, traditional methods often assume that these parameter changes are permanent and constant in time, so they may over‐ or underpredict the cost‐effectiveness of management activities that can only be maintained for a limited time during each period, such as culling when most individuals are at an especially vulnerable life‐stage. Moreover, they cannot highlight important time junctures in the model dynamics. In this article, we address this problem by providing efficient algorithms to compute the sensitivities of objectives like Λ$$ \Lambda $$ and R0$$ {R}_0 $$ to periodic, time‐localised perturbations in the model parameters. These sensitivities provide information about when during each period interventions should have the largest effect on the objective, and can also be used to calculate the sensitivities to more general periodic perturbations. Hence, this article extends previous work on time‐dependent sensitivity analysis (TDSA) to a new class of problems relevant to stability analysis. Using empirically parameterised models for Lyme disease and hantavirus, we demonstrate that TDSA can provide useful and sometimes surprising insights that nonetheless have intuitive biological interpretations. Specifically, we find that culling at the optimal times of susceptible and infected non‐human hosts has additive effects in the hantavirus model, but opposite and nearly cancelling effects in the Lyme disease model, so that indiscriminate culling is predicted to be effective for hantavirus but ineffective for Lyme disease.
nea622f0975b1: Conceptual overview of the two hypotheses linking stomatal anatomy to closure kinetics. Summary In fluctuating environments, the kinetics of stomatal opening and closing influence the balance between carbon gain and water loss. Smaller guard cells may respond faster to fluctuating environmental conditions because of their greater surface area for osmolyte flux relative to cell volume. A related hypothesis is that operational stomatal conductance (gop$$ {g}_{\mathrm{op}} $$) is often well below its theoretical maximum (gmax$$ {g}_{\mathrm{max}} $$) because at this stomatal aperture, guard cell volume is poised to change rapidly with small changes in turgor pressure. We analyzed 2125 estimates of stomatal closure kinetics in response to an abrupt increase in vapor pressure deficit (VPD) among 29 diverse wild tomato populations in the genus Solanum. Leaves with small guard cells and a lower initial stomatal conductance (gi$$ {g}_{\mathrm{i}} $$) closed faster, but each explained variation in kinetic parameters at different levels of biological organization. Guard cell size had high phylogenetic heritability and varied relatively little within populations, whereas gi$$ {g}_{\mathrm{i}} $$ varied mostly among individuals and between light‐intensity treatments. Smaller stomata can be speedier, but the current physiological state of the leaf also affects the responsiveness of stomatal conductance to fluctuations. Selection on stomatal speed may influence not only anatomical traits like guard cell size but also physiological controls on gop$$ {g}_{\mathrm{op}} $$.
nf0e562b0f613: The Red List Index (RLI) is a key indicator for global biodiversity targets, but its application to freshwater fishes has been limited by infrequent reassessment and sparse monitoring data. To address this gap, we developed the first comprehensive RLI for freshwater fishes of the Western Palearctic (Europe, West Asia, and North Africa), based on two comparable global assessment rounds. We reconciled taxonomy, classified category changes as nongenuine (reflecting taxonomic revision or improved knowledge) or genuine, and calculated RLIs with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals. Of 1,157 native, described species, 727 (63%) had two comparable assessments and formed the index. The RLI declined across the region (−2.4%), with subregional declines ranging from −0.8% in West Asia to −7.1% in North Africa; genuine declines outnumbered improvements by approximately 6:1 and included losses to extinct in the wild or possibly extinct. Most species showed no change or a nongenuine change. The main constraint on the trend was not data deficiency (eight species) but the absence of a comparable earlier assessment for 337 species recently assessed. Of these species, the assessments showed that 163 were threatened and concentrated in West Asia, and coverage was lowest in West Asia (51%) and for small‐bodied, range‐restricted families. The index should therefore be read as a regional benchmark and not as a test of the RLI's sensitivity because the true number of genuine changes that should have occurred is unknown. Building on this analysis, we developed a prioritized, data‐informed agenda for strengthening future iterations: completing a second assessment of the already‐threatened species currently outside the trend, focusing the resurvey on under‐covered subregions and families, and matching monitoring technique to taxon. Documented recoveries show that targeted conservation can reverse declines, often in data‐poor areas, but without such effort, both decline and recovery of these faunas will be detected slowly. Índice de la Lista Roja de peces de agua dulce del Paleártico occidental Resumen El Índice de la Lista Roja (RLI) es un indicador clave para los objetivos mundiales de biodiversidad, pero su aplicación a los peces de agua dulce se ha visto limitada por la escasa frecuencia de las reevaluaciones y la escasez de datos de seguimiento. Para subsanar esta carencia desarrollamos el primer RLI exhaustivo para los peces de agua dulce del Paleártico occidental (Europa, Asia Occidental y el norte de África), basado en dos rondas de evaluación global comparables. Conciliamos la taxonomía, clasificamos los cambios de categoría como no genuinos (que reflejan una revisión taxonómica o un mayor conocimiento) o genuinos, y calculamos los RLI con intervalos de confianza del 95% obtenidos mediante el método bootstrap. De las 1,157 especies autóctonas descritas, 727 (63%) contaban con dos evaluaciones comparables y formaron parte del índice. El RLI disminuyó en toda la región (–2.4%), con descensos subregionales que oscilaron entre el –0.8% en Asia Occidental y el –7.1% en el norte de África. Los descensos genuinos superaron a las mejoras en una proporción de aproximadamente 6:1 e incluyeron pérdidas por extinción en estado silvestre o posible extinción. La mayoría de las especies no mostraron cambios o presentaron un cambio no genuino. La principal limitación de la tendencia no fue la falta de datos (8 especies), sino la ausencia de una evaluación anterior comparable para 337 especies evaluadas recientemente. De estas especies, el RLI reveló que 163 se encontraban amenazadas y concentradas en Asia occidental, y que la cobertura era menor en esta zona (51%) y para el caso de las familias de pequeño tamaño y área de distribución limitada. Por lo tanto, el índice debe interpretarse como un punto de referencia regional y no como una prueba de la sensibilidad del RLI, ya que se desconoce el número real de cambios genuinos que deberían haber ocurrido.…
n3d8d94f3f047: The mechanisms underlying the transition of juvenile sea turtles from oceanic to neritic habitats remain poorly understood, as the oceanic stage is rarely observed directly. Here, we report a 201‐day satellite track of a juvenile hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata, curved carapace length of 38 cm) that traveled 9129 km from the Mozambique Channel to Huvadhu Atoll, Maldives. Current reanalysis data indicate that 74% of this distance resulted from passive transport by regional ocean currents. However, upon approaching within 50 km of the atoll, the turtle showed a marked, active course correction, swimming against weak currents while positioned downwind and downstream of the atoll, a low‐lying landform (~1 m above sea level) that would have been invisible by eye at such a distance. This pattern raises the possibility of olfactory detection of the atoll and provides, to our knowledge, a first indication of olfactory‐based island detection guiding habitat recruitment in a juvenile turtle, a mechanism previously documented only in breeding females. This track suggests a potential two‐scale process of oceanic‐to‐neritic habitat transition: a broadly stochastic oceanic phase shaped by passive dispersal, followed by fine‐scale, sensory‐guided settlement once the turtle nears a suitable habitat.
na5755cd0257e: The proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus) is an endangered colobine endemic to Borneo, largely confined to mangrove, peat-swamp, and riverine forest and capable of swimming across the rivers and tidal channels that structure its habitat. How this riparian specialization influences the spatial distribution of genetic diversity across the species' range in Indonesia has not been characterized. We sequenced the mitochondrial control region from 32 individuals collected at 11 localities throughout North and East Kalimantan and combined them with published data from Sabah and Pulau Kaget. Twenty-six haplotypes (Hd = 0.986; π = 0.029) are divided into three haplogroups, with their geographic distributions only partially separated. AMOVA revealed significant population differentiation (Φ ST = 0.275, p = 0.018). Differentiation among localities was more accurately explained by least-cost distance calculated over a combined riverine–coastal network than by straight-line distance, supporting the idea that gene flow predominantly occurs along riparian and coastal corridors rather than crossing land. A haplotype found in Sembakung, Nunukan, and Sabah indicates mitochondrial continuity across the Indonesia–Malaysia border. The Pulau Kaget reserve population clusters with East Kalimantan rather than forming a separate southern lineage. Neutrality tests indicate a demographic expansion in the late Pleistocene within the most prevalent haplogroup. Calibrated Simias–Nasalis distances place the split between these sister genera in the Pleistocene (~0.74 Ma). These findings reveal regionally distinct and transboundary mitochondrial lineages, which should guide conservation efforts for this endangered primate.
ned8d96128bc6: Understanding the spatial dynamics of genetic ancestry is essential for elucidating historical and contemporary patterns of gene flow among populations. Honey bees in the United States have a 400‐year history of importation, management, and adaptation to diverse environments. Genetic diversity is a key factor for colony health and resilience. Notably, the most genetically diverse populations in the country originate from the invasive A‐lineage (Africanized or ‘Killer’ honey bees). In this study, we leveraged a nationwide community‐science platform to assemble an extensive genomic dataset of U.S. honey bee populations and used it to ask how this invasive lineage is spreading across the country and how its spread has impacted honey bee genetic diversity nationwide. Using RFMix, we assigned local ancestry across the genome to capture fine‐scale ancestry patterns and applied TreeMix to genome‐wide allele frequency data to infer directional gene flow among U.S. populations. Our analyses revealed patterns consistent with a strong northward migration, with major source populations in southern states such as Texas (TX), Arizona (AZ), and Florida (FL), and primary targets in northern states including Michigan (MI), New York (NY), and Vermont (VT). Covariance estimates indicated strong genetic connectivity, particularly from TX and AZ. Spatial visualization of migration edges highlighted key routes of A‐lineage expansion. Together, these results provide the first genome‐wide evidence for a nationwide spread of A‐lineage ancestry in the U.S., offering insights to guide breeding strategies and predict the future dynamics of honey bee genetic diversity.
n7c60a60b22a0: Our definition of a green list is rooted in the art of safeguarding plant genetic resources and relies on the ability to compile all the tools and information on conservation plans and management activities with the goal of de‐listing any taxon of special concern from the red lists.
n8f17a4bd7125: Ongoing recovery of large carnivore species into their former ranges increases the occurrence of interactions among them. The recovering Scandinavian wolverine (Gulo gulo) population has recently expanded southwards and is increasingly overlapping with the core of the brown bear (Ursus arctos) range. Both species are facultative scavengers that feed on moose (Alces alces) carcasses, which are an important resource all year round for wolverines and seasonally for bears. Reliance on the same resource may lead to interactions. We monitored five GPS‐collared wolverines in central Sweden to investigate feeding sites with food remains and determine bear activity. In addition, we used motion‐triggered cameras to monitor wolverine and bear activity at three wolverine rendezvous sites (i.e., temporary sites where females keep cubs) and at a recently bear‐killed adult moose carcass. We found 115 wolverine feeding sites, of which 25 (22%) showed signs of bear activity. At 24 sites we found remains from adult moose carcasses, five presumably bear‐killed of which two were fresh (< 1 week). Based on GPS‐data, wolverines repeatedly used these recently bear‐killed moose for periods ranging from a few hours to multiple days. Bear activity was documented at two of the three presumed rendezvous sites used by a female wolverine with cubs. Camera data also documented repeated visits by at least three different wolverines at the presumed bear‐killed moose carcass, including visits short before and after bear activity at the site. Our results illustrate that wolverines and bears overlap and share food resources, potentially leading to direct and/or indirect interactions. These observations suggest that co‐occurrence between these two species create both feeding opportunities and potential risks for wolverines, which deserves further research.
na3fbfd709164: Marine heatwaves are increasing in frequency and intensity worldwide, triggering coral bleaching events. While colony and community scale consequences of bleaching have been well documented, its consequence on reef structural complexity remains comparatively less studied. Using Structure‐from‐Motion (SfM), colony fate tracking of hermatypic scleractinians, and a cross‐scale, sequential approach, this study linked in situ thermal stress to coral colony‐scale bleaching and mortality and reef‐scale structural change during the 2023 bleaching event in the central Saudi Arabian Red Sea. Taxon‐specific bleaching thresholds were consistent with regional bleaching alert levels; however, ecological risk varied substantially among reefs. We further support that the relationship between thermal stress and change in reef‐building coral colony area is taxon‐dependent, and that bleaching‐driven coral mortality can rapidly alter reef structural complexity, with potential consequences for ecosystem function. This study represents the first mechanistic assessment of coral resilience across biological scales in the central Red Sea, and provides new insight into reef structural persistence under accelerating climate change.
n211dc2a3522b: Exploring multifaceted beta diversity, including its turnover and nestedness components, is crucial for elucidating the drivers of community assembly. Arid mountain ecosystems, with their strong environmental filtering and fragmented habitats, serve as a useful model system for testing how these drivers interact across multiple dimensions of diversity. Here, we compared taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic beta diversity in non‐volant small mammal communities across environmental gradients in arid areas of the western Tianshan Mountains, China, and inferred the associated community‐assembly processes. Species turnover predominantly structured beta diversity across all three dimensions. Decomposition of multifaceted beta diversity revealed a consistent pattern: functional dissimilarity was highest, followed by taxonomic and phylogenetic dissimilarity. Hierarchical partitioning identified elevational distance as the most significant factor influencing beta diversity and its turnover component, and nestedness was driven by multiple factors. We also confirmed a significant distance–decay relationship for overall community dissimilarity and its turnover component. Moreover, analyses of community‐assembly mechanisms suggested a synergistic interaction between deterministic and neutral processes, whereby the influence of environmental filtering weakened while that of limiting similarity strengthened as elevational distance increased. Collectively, these findings clarify the patterns and drivers of beta diversity in arid montane regions and provide a practical basis for biodiversity conservation in Central Asian mountain ecosystems.
n96188a094773: IntroductionBamboo exhibits a complex taxonomy due to polyploidy, hybridisation, and long flowering periods, which complicate species identification. Traditional morphological taxonomy often struggles with limited diagnostic traits and considerable phenotypic variability, leading to taxonomic ambiguities and misinterpretations. The convergence of similar traits among unrelated species further complicates phylogenetic classification. To address these challenges, integrative taxonomic approaches are needed to combine morphological, molecular, and ecological data for accurate bamboo classification. This review synthesises the current status, recent advances, and emerging trends in molecular identification and DNA barcoding of bamboo, highlighting their potential to improve taxonomy, conservation, and the sustainable utilisation of bamboo genetic resources.MethodTo provide a framework for the review, a scientometric analysis was performed using bibliographic records.ResultsThe review suggests that no single marker or combination of markers can currently serve as a universal barcode across bamboo. The performance of commonly used markers such as ITS, matK, rbcL, psbA-trnH, rps16-trnQ, and alternative plastid regions provides valuable insights into species identification. Comparative evidence indicates that barcode performance is strongly marker- and lineage-dependent. These markers have improved plant taxonomy by providing more reliable species identification than traditional morphological methods.DiscussionDNA barcoding has been effectively used to understand complex species relationships and identify cryptic species that are difficult to distinguish morphologically. Furthermore, next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have transformed genomic data acquisition, enabling species discrimination. Integrating machine learning with DNA barcoding further improves species identification accuracy and shows promise for improving conventional methodologies in bamboo systematics. However, the application of ML and NGS in bamboo is still in its early stages and will require substantial work on bamboo databases to achieve greater accuracy.
n7223340e883d: Sociality can improve access to information, cooperation, collective defense, parental care, collective decision-making, and social buffering, but it can also intensify competition and pathogen transmission, spread outdated information, and create dependence on particular partners, roles, or traditions. In this article, we propose the Intermediate Social Resilience Hypothesis (ISRH), which predicts that, under specified conditions, population resilience may be greatest at an intermediate value of a defined social dimension. We do not rank all animal societies on a single universal scale. Instead, low, intermediate, and high values must be defined within a measurable dimension, such as group size, cohesion, network connectivity, cooperative effort, or reliance on social information, and within a biologically comparable system. Resilience must likewise be specified as resistance, recovery, temporal stability, or persistence under a defined form and scale of environmental change. The distinctive contribution of the ISRH is not simply the recognition that sociality can generate both benefits and costs, but the explicit prediction that their balance can, under identifiable conditions, produce a testable intermediate maximum in population resilience. An intermediate optimum is expected only when social benefits initially increase but eventually saturate, whereas one or more relevant social costs continue to rise. Environmental harshness, variability, unpredictability, and the flexibility, modularity, redundancy, or multilevel organization of social systems may shift, flatten, or eliminate this relationship. The hypothesis generates two falsifiable predictions that can be tested through comparative, longitudinal, experimental, phylogenetic, network, and population-monitoring approaches. By integrating behavioral ecology, social evolution, resilience theory, and conservation, the framework explicitly recognizes the multidimensional nature of animal social systems while providing explicit criteria for distinguishing support for the ISRH from monotonic, threshold, flat, or context-dependent alternative relationships.
ne5f120c151b5: Wildlife damage is often expected to push national park residents toward new sources of income, but the appraisals that turn damage into a willingness to move into tourism remain unclear. Drawing on protection motivation theory and questionnaire data from 513 residents in and around the Wuyishan City section of Wuyishan National Park, China, this study distinguishes perceived tourism adaptive efficacy from tourism self-efficacy and examines how these two beliefs relate to intentions to shift household livelihoods toward tourism. Greater perceived wildlife damage was related to stronger threat appraisal of traditional livelihoods. Residents who perceived greater livelihood threat also reported stronger transition intentions and were more likely to view tourism as a workable livelihood alternative. However, no clear relationship emerged between livelihood threat and tourism self-efficacy, although both adaptive efficacy and self-efficacy were positively related to transition intention. As a moderator, perceived tourism development opportunity was more relevant to adaptive efficacy than to self-efficacy. When residents perceived greater tourism opportunities, the positive relationship between livelihood threat and adaptive efficacy was stronger, as was the corresponding indirect relationship with transition intention. In contrast, perceived opportunity made little difference to the relationship involving self-efficacy. These findings suggest that livelihood threat was associated with greater perceived usefulness and feasibility of tourism without a corresponding association with residents’ confidence in their own ability to engage in tourism activities. Policies aimed at encouraging livelihood diversification in national park communities may therefore need to combine the creation of tourism opportunities with training, skills development, and other forms of support that strengthen residents’ capacity to participate.
n3dde51d8a05b: This study reveals that host trophic strategy, not shared seasonality, drives gut microbiota plasticity in sympatric rodents. Herbivorous voles show tight diet–microbiome coupling; granivorous gerbils exhibit functional stability. This highlights gut microbiota as a potential key mechanism for niche differentiation and coexistence. Abstract The coexistence mechanisms of sympatric species have long attracted widespread research attention. However, it remains unclear whether sympatric species experiencing the same seasonal conditions exhibit convergent or host‐specific gut microbiota responses. We compared the herbivorous Brandt's vole (Lasiopodomys brandtii) and the granivorous Mongolian gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), two sympatric rodent species with divergent trophic strategies inhabiting the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, China. By integrating plant DNA metabarcoding, gut microbiota profiling and microbial functional output analyses across seasons, we investigated seasonal dietary–microbiome associations. Our results revealed that although seasonal dietary variation affects the composition of the host gut microbiota, the taxonomic and functional plasticity of gut microbiota is strongly influenced by host trophic strategies. Brandt's voles maintained a fermentation‐oriented microbiota tightly coupled with seasonal shifts in Poaceae and Cyperaceae intake, exhibiting coordinated changes in microbial taxa, short‐chain fatty acid production and cellulase activity. In contrast, Mongolian gerbils exhibited substantial seasonal dietary turnover between Chenopodiaceae and Caragana plants, while maintaining comparatively stable microbial functional outputs, suggesting metabolic buffering. Host trophic strategy, rather than shared environmental seasonality, is related to the strength and functional consequences of the coupling between diet and microbiome. Our results emphasize the gut microbiome as a potential key mechanism underlying trophic niche differentiation and ecological coexistence in wild mammalian communities.
n3235ec97f1d8: Biological invasions on islands provide a natural framework to study how dispersal and connectivity influence evolutionary and ecological processes. The avian nest parasitic fly, Philornis downsi—first recorded in Darwin's finch nests in 1997—causes high mortality in endemic land birds, yet its inter‐island and sex‐specific patterns of dispersal and genetic structure remain poorly understood. We use low‐coverage whole genome sequencing to investigate genome‐wide patterns of genetic diversity, directional migration and effective population size in P. downsi across five major Galápagos Islands and its native range in mainland Ecuador. We find evidence for a genetic bottleneck in the Galápagos, isolation by distance, and evidence that the island closest to the Ecuadorian mainland, San Cristóbal, is genetically divergent from the other four islands sampled, despite retaining the highest genetic diversity. No evidence was found for sex‐biased dispersal; however, sex‐biased genetic structure was detected using only markers from inferred autosomal scaffolds. We found asymmetric gene flow with higher migration rates from San Cristóbal westward to the other islands, matching the direction of both southeast trade winds and major cargo shipping routes. Our results suggest both natural and human‐mediated colonisation of P. downsi from the mainland through San Cristóbal to the other islands, followed by high inter‐island dispersal among closely situated sink islands. Our findings are critical for prioritising islands for control strategies that will reduce P. downsi impacts on vulnerable endemic birds and underscore the value of understanding directional migration patterns for managing invasive species in metapopulations.
n803debbb9bbf: Beneficial symbionts act as ecological stabilizers that mitigate differential pathogen susceptibility within natural plant populations. Summary Host genetic diversity shapes pathogen susceptibility within plant populations, raising the question of whether beneficial root microbes can buffer these differences. The fungal root endophyte Serendipita indica (Si) promotes plant growth and can mitigate disease caused by the pathogen Bipolaris sorokiniana (Bs). Here, we assessed how natural host genetic variation influences Si‐mediated protection against Bs in Arabidopsis thaliana. We screened 47 A. thaliana accessions for susceptibility to Bs with and without Si colonization and performed phenotypic, transcriptomic, and comparative genomic analyses of two genetically and geographically proximate Swedish accessions, T510 and T530, that differed strongly in Bs colonization. Si conferred consistent protection against Bs across all accessions, despite variation in baseline susceptibility and immune‐gene content. T510 and T530 differed in Bs colonization, disease symptoms, transcriptional responses, and immune‐gene repertoires, including presence–absence variation of the TIR‐NLR gene ISI. T530 lacks ISI, and mutation of ISI in Col‐0 increased Bs susceptibility, demonstrating that ISI contributes to root immunity. However, Si‐mediated protection was retained in the absence of ISI, demonstrating that ISI is not required for this protective effect. Beneficial fungal endophytes can thus buffer phenotypic consequences of natural variation in pathogen susceptibility, stabilizing disease outcomes across genetically diverse plant populations.
nd5bf8012fe59: Boreal forests store a large portion of global terrestrial carbon, primarily in soils, yet their sensitivity to environmental changes remains uncertain. Disturbance is one major agent of change, with dominance shifting from wildfire to forest management over the past century. Mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophic decomposition may be an important control on boreal soil carbon storage, but its occurrence and magnitude remain uncertain. Additionally, the distinct impacts of wildfire and clearcutting on decomposition and soil microbial communities remain largely unexplored. We quantified mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophs and decomposition in needle and humus litter through a root‐exclusion experiment in 31 sites across wildfire (4–375 yr since disturbance) and clearcut chronosequences (1–109 yr since disturbance) in northern Sweden. Mycorrhizas suppressed decomposition by 15.5 ± 5.9% overall, with no consistent change over time after disturbance. This pattern was linked to absolute fungal abundance but not to other microbial community shifts, soil temperature or soil moisture. Decomposition rates were stable across time since disturbance for all substrates and disturbance types. Our findings improve understanding of mycorrhizal‐decomposition interactions and highlight the need to further explore key fungal traits and compositional changes, especially at the soil surface, that regulate carbon storage dynamics in boreal soils.
naf02b8de760a: WRKY47 functions upstream of bHLH105 and bHLH115 to mediate iron (Fe) deficiency stress responses in Arabidopsis. Summary Iron (Fe) deficiency limits plant growth, yet its upstream regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify WRKY47 as a positive regulator of Fe‐deficiency responses in Arabidopsis. WRKY47 directly binds and activates bHLH105 and bHLH115, key IVc bHLH factors that trigger the Fe uptake cascade. We further show that RCD1 interacts with WRKY47 and suppresses its DNA‐binding and transcriptional activity. Fe deficiency also promotes the redistribution of RCD1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, suggesting a potential mechanism for modulating WRKY47 activity during the response. Our findings uncover a previously uncharacterized regulatory mechanism linking WRKY transcription factors and the bHLH cascade through RCD1‐mediated modulation, providing a conceptual framework for engineering crops with enhanced Fe acquisition and stress resilience.
n3b65c33cb86d: Field site and experimental set‐up with stemflow‐labelled European beech trees. Summary Stemflow of forest trees can contribute a significant fraction of water to forest's water fluxes; however, it is still unclear whether and to what extent trees and their neighbours use stemflow for water uptake and supply. We applied deuterium‐enriched stemflow equivalent to a 23‐mm throughfall event to adult Fagus sylvatica trees to trace stemflow through the soil and trees. We continuously measured in situ water stable isotopes in soil and xylem water and destructively sampled xylem water in the crowns of adult labelled, nonlabelled F. sylvatica and nonlabelled Picea abies, complemented by destructive xylem water sampling of neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica. Stemflow water supported up to 5.7 ± 2.1% of daily sap flux of adult F. sylvatica trees labelled at the stem base and was detectable in xylem water for several weeks. In the soil, deuterium‐enriched stemflow was present at a maximum distance of 0.40 m from the labelled tree. Moreover, nonlabelled juvenile trees within a distance of 2 m showed uptake of labelled water, indicating rooting into soil compartments affected by stemflow. We demonstrate the importance of stemflow as a water source for both adult and neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica, even when soil water is not limiting.
n6a804aa06e3a: Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. Researchers commonly compare the efficacy of specific control methods. However, invasive species control programs vary greatly in overarching goals and often occur over large areas, long timeframes, and varied environmental and social contexts. The success of these programs likely hinges on factors including organizational structures, concurrent restoration activities, geographic and temporal scope of control, and the invasive species’ biology. To enable assessment of the relative influence of these common features, we propose clearer definitions of success in invasive species control and explicit comparisons among control programs. Post hoc assessment of existing programs’ success will complement system-specific studies to guide strategies that work in real-world situations.
nf6ca3b58ab9a: Vessel strikes threaten many large whale species. Managers employ several mitigation measures to reduce vessel strike risk, including establishing or modifying vessel routing measures, such as shipping lanes. However, most studies utilized to inform the configuration of shipping lanes only consider a limited number of potential lanes, and in many cases, the criteria used to generate the lanes are unclear. We developed an approach to design, modify, or evaluate shipping lanes that involves clearly defining the objectives of the lanes and using the k least‐cost path (KLCP) algorithm, which identifies the KLCPs between two points on a cost surface, to identify all lanes that meet the objectives. We applied our approach to evaluate recommended shipping lanes in Cape Cod Bay, Massachusetts (United States), and off the Atlantic Coast of the southeastern United States with respect to the risk of vessel strikes to North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) and the time it takes vessels to travel the lanes. We identified all lanes with a risk of right whale strikes and a travel time less than or equal to that of the recommended lanes using the KLCP algorithm. In most cases, the lanes identified had similar spatial configurations to the recommended lanes and reduced the risk of strikes by <15%, which indicates that the existing recommended lanes are adequately, but not optimally, designed to reduce strike risk and travel time relative to potential alternative lanes. Our approach applying the KLCP algorithm provides a thorough, objective, and transparent way to identify vessel routing configurations that minimize whale–vessel strikes and meet other objectives. Reducción de las colisiones entre ballenas y embarcaciones mediante la planificación de rutas de tráfico marítimo con múltiples objetivos Resumen Las colisiones con embarcaciones suponen una amenaza para muchas especies de ballenas de gran tamaño. Los responsables aplican diversas medidas de mitigación para reducir el riesgo de la colisión, entre ellas el establecimiento o la modificación de medidas de trazado de rutas marítimas, como las rutas de navegación. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los estudios utilizados para definir la configuración de las rutas de navegación solo tienen en cuenta un número limitado de rutas potenciales y, en muchos casos, los criterios empleados para generarlas no están claros. Desarrollamos un enfoque para diseñar, modificar o evaluar rutas marítimas que consiste en definir claramente los objetivos de las mismas y utilizar el algoritmo k de las rutas de menor coste (KLCP), que identifica las KLCP entre dos puntos en una superficie de costos, con el fin de determinar todas las rutas que cumplen dichos objetivos. Aplicamos nuestro enfoque para evaluar las rutas marítimas recomendadas en la bahía de Cape Cod, en Massachusetts (Estados Unidos), y frente a la costa atlántica del sureste de Estados Unidos, con la consideración del riesgo de colisiones de buques con las ballenas francas del Atlántico Norte (Eubaleana glacialis) y el tiempo que tardan los buques en recorrer dichas rutas. Identificamos todas las rutas con riesgo de colisiones con ballenas francas y un tiempo de travesía inferior o igual al de las rutas recomendadas utilizando el algoritmo KLCP. En la mayoría de los casos, las rutas identificadas presentaban configuraciones espaciales similares a las de las rutas recomendadas y reducían el riesgo de colisiones en menos del 15%, lo que indica que las rutas recomendadas existentes están diseñadas de forma adecuada, aunque no óptima, para reducir el riesgo de colisiones y el tiempo de travesía en comparación con posibles rutas alternativas. Nuestro enfoque, basado en la aplicación del algoritmo KLCP, ofrece una forma exhaustiva, objetiva y transparente de identificar configuraciones de rutas para buques que minimicen las colisiones entre ballenas y buques y cumplan otros objetivos.
n840d60065a0c: Wildlife population dynamics change across time and space, but few studies use formal spatiotemporal statistical models to understand these patterns. The population distribution of mallards (Anas platyrhyncos) in the Prairie Pothole Region of central North America (PPR) has shifted dramatically over the past several decades as agricultural intensity and climate have changed. We examined spatiotemporal variation in survival, natural mortality, and harvest mortality rates for mallards in the PPR from 1974 to 2023 using intrinsic conditional autoregressive models in a Bayesian framework. There was substantial variation over time and space for all demographic rates, and relationships between mortality and habitat variables varied by age and sex cohort. Specifically, environmental relationships indicate that habitats with less agricultural activity and more wetlands decrease survival via increased natural mortality driven by reproductive risks. We also found a worrying trend: females exhibited declining survival probabilities since the late 1980s and early 1990s. Our analyses demonstrate major variation in survival rates of a well‐studied organism across an environmental gradient, reveal subtle but critical differences relative to inference obtained from pooled data, and provide a clear roadmap to future research that can inform spatially explicit conservation and management goals.
nd2faf2ef2641: A number of otherwise cryptic species have areas on their body of conspicuous colour that are hidden while stationary but displayed when moving. A suggested function of this conspicuous colouration is for flash behaviour, in which an otherwise cryptic prey exposes obvious colours during escape to disrupt the predators' ability to locate the prey when it stops moving and hides the colour. Experimental studies of artificial prey with human and avian predators have found that flash behaviour can increase ‘prey’ survival, but this has not been comprehensively tested using real prey. European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) display their white tail when running but are otherwise cryptic when resting or foraging. We experimentally tested whether flash behaviour inhibits detection by presenting videos of wild rabbits fleeing to human participants and manipulated the tail colour of the rabbits. We found that rabbits with unmanipulated white tails were neither more likely nor faster to be located than rabbits with tails digitally manipulated to be cryptic. This does not support the hypothesis that flash behaviour helps rabbits evade predators.
n0d6aa7877e32: Wildlife feeding through intentional or unintentional practices can result in increased human‐wildlife conflict, disease transmission, population growth, and altered behavior. We quantified how spatial and temporal variation in black bear (Ursus americanus) bait availability within home ranges influenced black bear diet composition as mediated by sex and age. We tested carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) isotopes in hair samples from hunter‐harvested bears during pre‐baiting (about 1 May–9 August) and baiting (about 10 August–26 October) periods in Michigan, USA, 2017–2021 and used isotopic mixing models to estimate how diet varied between sexes and with spatially‐varying bait distribution. We used linear models to determine whether intrinsic (i.e., sex, age) and extrinsic (i.e., region, bait quantity and distribution) factors were correlated with δ13C and δ15N enrichment of black bear hair during pre‐baiting and baiting periods while controlling for corn agriculture, distance from waste accumulation sites, and human population density. Proportion of anthropogenic food in black bear diet was greater during the baiting period, especially for female black bears, but bait density did not influence black bear diet composition. Black bear hair from the Northern Lower Peninsula was more enriched in δ13C as compared to the Upper Peninsula and had the greatest δ13C and δ15N enrichment at about 10 years of age. Bait density and distribution did not influence δ13C or δ15N enrichment in black bear hair, potentially due to bait availability. Our results demonstrate that anthropogenic food from intentional and non‐intentional sources contributes substantially to black bear diet in Michigan, which may affect body condition, behavior, reproduction, and abundance.
nb3a65652c521: Hierarchical and latent variable models are fundamental in ecology, fisheries science, and epidemiology, but fitting them efficiently relies on automatic differentiation (AD) combined with approximations such as the Laplace approximation. Template Model Builder (TMB) has become a standard tool for this kind of inference in R, but it requires users to write the objective function in C++, which is a potential obstacle for those unfamiliar with it, slows model iteration through compilation, and complicates debugging and simulation. We present RTMB, an R package that exposes the full power of TMB's AD machinery directly from plain R. Users write the joint negative log‐likelihood as an ordinary R function; RTMB traces it onto an AD tape and hands the result to TMB's existing optimization, Laplace approximation, and reporting routines. We describe the design of the package, illustrate its use through a worked example, and provide a side‐by‐side comparison with the equivalent TMB implementation of a theta‐logistic state‐space population model. The result is a transparent, debuggable, and pedagogically accessible interface to state‐of‐the‐art latent variable inference, with runtime performance comparable to native TMB.
nf2ec1ee0e0ed: Many seabird populations along the UK's East Coast have declined over the past three decades. A key concern is reduced availability of their primary breeding season prey, sandeel (Ammodytes marinus). While some seabirds have partially switched to sprat (Sprattus sprattus), this is not universal. Studying these predator–prey dynamics requires fine‐scale estimates of prey distributions that are both spatially and temporally resolved—yet such data are limited, especially for sandeel due to sampling challenges. We evaluate the utility of large‐scale ICES bottom trawl surveys to model sandeel distribution, combining them with winter dredge surveys designed specifically for this species. For sprat, we combine bottom trawl data with the Herring Acoustic Survey. Using hierarchical Bayesian spatiotemporal models (R‐INLA), we estimate the biomass of small and medium sandeel (≤ 16 cm) and sprat across the entire North Sea from 2000 to 2020, accounting for spatial and temporal dependencies. We validate our sandeel models by comparison with other modelling approaches and ICES stock assessments. Results reveal marked regional variation: sandeel increased in Area 3 (Norwegian EEZ), declined in Areas 1 and 2 and fluctuated in Area 4. Sprat biomass increased over time, with a modest northward expansion. This study provides the first North Sea‐wide, fine‐scale, multi‐decadal distribution models for these two key seabird prey species and identifies important regional drivers of their populations.
n3dafadaaf5cd: To investigate the growth and development mechanisms in Dermatophagoides farinae, it is essential to understand its gene expression profiles across different life stages, which are typically assessed by transcriptional profiling based on RT‐qPCR. Suitable reference genes are vital for ensuring reliable and accurate results; however, none have been established for this species across different developmental stages. Here, we analyzed expression profiles of ten frequently used reference genes (RPL18, RPS18, RPS9, EF1A, RPS28, Actin, V‐ATPaseB, GAPDH, RPL32, and α‐tubulin) to determine their stability across different developmental stages of D. farinae. Four algorithms (GeNorm, NormFinder, BestKeeper, and ΔCt) were employed to examine gene stability, and their results were subsequently integrated by RefFinder to yield a comprehensive assessment. The results indicated that RPL18 and RPS28 were the two top‐ranked stable reference genes, whereas α‐tubulin and RPL32 showed the lowest stability. To confirm the robustness of the chosen reference genes, we assessed cytochrome P450 3A8 expression at developmental stages of D. farinae using three independent biological replicates and three technical replicates per stage. Normalization against RPL18 and RPS28, individually or combined, produced expression patterns consistent with previously reported developmental trends of cytochrome P450 genes in mites and insects, namely higher expression in larvae and protonymphs, lower expression in later stages, and minimal expression observed in eggs. In contrast, unstable reference genes yielded inconsistent results, thereby confirming our findings. In conclusion, this study identifies two highly stable reference genes that will provide a robust foundation for precise gene expression normalization and functional studies in D. farinae.
nfc7c6c4d2934: Urban environments expose wildlife to anthropogenic hazards, including materials capable of causing physical injuries. Among urban birds, the rock pigeon (Columba livia) is highly adapted to urban environments. However, frequent reports of digit entanglement and foot deformities in these environments suggest that urban conditions expose birds to foot injuries. Despite widespread observations of “string foot”, quantitative assessments of deformity prevalence and severity across urban land-use types remain limited, particularly within African cities. This study assessed the prevalence and severity of foot deformities in rock pigeons across three land-use zones in Katima Mulilo, Namibia: the Central Business District (CBD), market areas, and residential areas. A total of 300 pigeons were visually inspected during systematic field surveys. Foot deformities were recorded as present or absent and classified into three severity levels (mild, moderate, severe). Forty-six (15.3%) pigeons exhibited foot deformities. The prevalence of foot deformities varied significantly among land-use categories, with the highest recorded in the residential areas (22.5%), followed by the CBD (12.4%) and least in the market areas (10.4%). Moderate deformities were the most prevalent injury category (60.9%), followed by severe (23.9%) and mild deformities (15.2%). Pigeons observed in residential areas had significantly higher odds of deformities compared with those in the CBD (OR = 2.05, p = 0.044). Fibrous wastes, which constitute the important potential sources of entanglement hazard, were prevalent in the environment of pigeons. Results of this study suggest that foot injury in urban rock pigeons varied across land-use types and highlight the potential role of human-derived materials on pigeon health in urban areas. Targeted management of fibrous wastes in the CBD and residential areas is recommended to reduce entanglement-related foot deformities, with emphasis on improved local waste handling and disposal behavior.
n8b28d1883135: Coral reefs are undergoing profound compositional changes driven by climate change, disease, and chronic human disturbance. Coral cover is the primary metric used to track reef condition, but it often fails to capture the contributions of different coral species to reef carbonate production, structural complexity, and associated biodiversity. Here, I review evidence showing that global change disproportionately removes competitively dominant and architecturally complex corals, driving non‐random changes and coral community homogenisation. These changes erode reef functionality, even when overall cover is maintained. Species‐specific contributions to calcification and structural complexity span orders of magnitude, such that targeted losses of framework‐building taxa collapse carbonate budgets and habitat architecture in ways not predictable from cover trends. These structural changes cascade through associated communities, undermining functional diversity and the ecosystem processes on which reef resilience depends. Critically, rebounds in coral cover frequently reflect the colonisation by fast‐growing opportunistic species, which yield slow or absent recovery of physical functionality, while reassembly and the re‐establishment of large, structurally complex colonies (and the physical functionality they provide) might lag by decades. Furthermore, as mass disturbance events occur at ever‐shorter intervals, recovery windows close before reef‐building potential and complexity can be fully restored. Monitoring, management, and restoration should therefore focus on trait‐ and species‐explicit assessments that prioritise protection and restoration of keystone reef‐builders, target sites with high functional potential, and reduce stressors at appropriate scales. Integrating functional metrics into policy and restoration planning is essential to safeguard reef geomorphic and ecological services under continued global change.
n311b75e6d0b9: Climate change and overexploitation are increasingly threatening sharks, with pelagic species among the most affected. The complex ecology and life histories of these species, however, pose major challenges for conservation planning. Here, we examine how integrating genomics and movement ecology can better inform the conservation of highly migratory sharks. The growing availability of reference genomes and expanding population genomic datasets in sharks, coupled with advances in biologging, creates unprecedented opportunities to integrate these approaches and link long‐term, population‐level evolutionary processes with short‐term individual, behavioural patterns. This mini review explores research applications that integrate both fields to overcome their individual limitations and strengthen the evidence and conclusions used to inform conservation. Then we discuss, based on previous studies, how this framework can address specific conservation objectives and lead to decision‐ready outcomes, including the delineation of management units, the design of spatial and stock‐specific fisheries management measures, and the assessment of species' vulnerability to climate change. We conclude by highlighting that the translation of this knowledge into practice requires engagement with the scientific and management bodies responsible for evaluating the evidence, advising decision‐makers, and implementing shark conservation measures.

naa2c7a227c7f: Model showing phyB‐mediated fine‐tuning of defence responses via NPR1. Summary Light perception by phytochromes controls different aspects of plant–environment interactions including plant immunity; however, the underpinning molecular mechanisms are less well‐understood. Upon localized attack on leaves by avirulent pathogens, the systemic accumulation of salicylic acid (SA) is required for the establishment of systemic acquired resistance (SAR) throughout the plant to curtail pathogen spread. We demonstrate that light‐mediated Small Ubiquitin‐like Modifier 1 (SUMO) conjugation to phytochrome B (phyB) is critical for increasing cellular SA levels to orchestrate SAR upon avirulent bacterial infection. SA promotes SUMOylation of phyB, which enables it to interact with the SA receptor, Nonexpressor of Pathogenesis‐Related 1 (NPR1) via its SUMO1‐interacting motif. SUMOylation of phyB is enhanced by the accumulation of SUMO‐Conjugating Enzyme (E2) (SCE1) and the degradation of SUMO protease Overly Tolerant to Salt 1 (OTS1) in SAR‐induced systemic tissues. Using confocal imaging, we show that SUMOylated phyB undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation together with NPR1 in nuclear bodies. We further validated through immunoprecipitation, ChIP and RNA‐seq analysis that SUMOylated phyB associates with NPR1 and TGA transcription factors in nuclear photobodies to induce the expression of PR1 gene. We reveal a post‐translational modification mechanism in which light‐induced SUMOylation of photoreceptors promotes SAR by regulating NPR1 function.
n89b3501e8c4e: Schematic of plant species range boundaries, some mechanisms that might set them, and some traits that might explain them. Summary Since around the year 2000, trait‐based ecology has become self‐aware as a strand of research within ecology. How did this happen? What is trait‐based ecology now? And where might it go in future? This paper offers selective answers to those questions. We first outline the history leading up to the emergence of trait‐based plant ecology during the 1990s. Second, we assess briefly what has been achieved up to mid‐2020s. Third, we discuss two challenges (among many) for trait‐based plant ecology over the next 25 yr. One is about the boundaries of species ranges along temperature gradients. Some of these boundaries may be decided by thermal tolerance, others by biotic interactions such as competition or pathogens. How can we identify which applies to which species? Which traits, feasible to measure across many species, might help with this? A second major challenge is about the global zonation of vegetation physiognomy or biome types. How well can we explain this in terms of traits, and from first principles, meaning via eco‐evolutionary models for why different trait values should be competent and competitive in different settings? First‐principle rules for how ecosystems are constructed should be central to ecology as a discipline. Resumen Desde aproximadamente el año 2000, la ecología basada en caracteres funcionales se consolidó como una línea de investigación autoconsciente y distintiva. ¿Cómo surgió, qué representa actualmente y hacia dónde avanzaría? Este artículo ofrece algunas respuestas selectivas. Primero, resumimos los antecedentes históricos que condujeron al desarrollo de la ecología vegetal basada en caracteres funcionales en los años 1990. Segundo, evaluamos los logros en la década de 2020. Tercero, examinamos dos desafíos (entre los muchos que existen) para los próximos 25 años. El primer desafío se refiere a los límites de distribución de las especies a lo largo de gradientes térmicos. Algunos pueden estar determinados por la tolerancia térmica y otros por interacciones bióticas, como la competencia o los patógenos. ¿Cómo podrían distinguirse estos mecanismos y qué caracteres, factibles de ser medidos en muchas especies, podrían ayudar? El segundo desafío involucra la zonación global de las fisonomías de vegetación y los biomas. ¿Hasta qué punto pueden explicarse mediante caracteres funcionales y primeros principios, es decir modelos eco‐evolutivos, cuáles valores de caracteres deberían ser competentes y competitivos en diferentes ambientes? Las reglas fundamentales que explican a partir de primeros principios cómo se construyen los ecosistemas deberían ocupar un lugar central en la ecología.
nf9ccd63706b8: Directed acyclic diagram (DAG) illustrating causal relationships between variables to estimate the effects of individual and neighborhood damage on delayed mortality. Summary Tropical forest resilience, biodiversity, and carbon sequestration depend on tree survival. Disturbance events, such as hurricanes, generate distinct forms of damage at the individual‐tree and neighborhood scale, providing a unique setting to disentangle the causal contributions of mortality drivers. Leveraging post‐hurricane census data for nearly 4000 trees in the Luquillo Forest Dynamics Plot, Puerto Rico, we used a causal inference framework combined with Bayesian multilevel models to estimate the effect of individual‐ and neighborhood‐scale damage on delayed tree mortality following Hurricane Maria (2017). Individual damage effects depended on species identity and tree size. Stem break emerged as the most lethal form of damage across the community. Neighborhood damage was associated with elevated mortality following Hurricane Maria, independent of focal tree damage. This effect was strongest among large trees, consistent with disproportionately high physiological stress resulting from greater inherent metabolic demands, refoliation energy costs, and evapotranspiration following canopy recovery. Severe biomass loss (> 75% crown loss) buffered large trees from negative neighborhood effects, revealing a positive pruning effect on survival. Our study advances mechanistic understanding of delayed tree mortality, while also suggesting how mortality patterns may shift with expected increases in disturbance severity under a warming climate. Resumen La resiliencia, la biodiversidad y el secuestro de carbono de los bosques tropicales dependen de la supervivencia de los árboles. Las perturbaciones, como los huracanes, generan distintos tipos de daño tanto a escala del árbol individual como de su vecindario, proporcionando un escenario único para desentrañar las contribuciones causales de los factores determinantes de la mortalidad. Utilizando censos de aproximadamente 4000 árboles en la Parcela de Dinámica del Bosque de Luquillo, Puerto Rico, usamos un método de inferencia causal combinado con modelos multinivel bayesianos para estimar el efecto del daño a escala individual y de vecindario sobre la mortalidad diferida de los árboles tras el huracán María (2017). Los efectos del daño individual dependieron de la identidad de la especie y del tamaño del árbol. La rotura del tronco resultó ser el tipo de daño más letal en toda la comunidad. El daño en el vecindario se asoció con un aumento de la mortalidad tras el huracán María, independientemente del daño sufrido por el árbol focal. Este efecto fue más fuerte entre los árboles grandes, lo cual concuerda con un estrés fisiológico desproporcionadamente alto debido a mayores demandas metabólicas inherentes, costos energéticos de refoliación y evapotranspiración tras la recuperación del dosel. La pérdida severa de biomasa (> 75 % de pérdida de copa) amortiguó los efectos negativos del vecindario sobre los árboles grandes, revelando un ‘efecto poda’ positivo sobre la supervivencia. Nuestro estudio avanza en la comprensión mecanística de la mortalidad diferida de los árboles y, además, sugiere cómo los patrones de mortalidad pueden cambiar con los aumentos esperados en la severidad de las perturbaciones bajo un clima en calentamiento.
n1fd6bc6202fd: The Brahminy blindsnake (Indotyphlops braminus), an all‐female, parthenogenetic, and triploid snake, is an informative species for studying polyploidy and asexual reproduction in vertebrates. In this study, we analyzed tissue expression patterns in I. braminus using a PacBio‐derived transcript reference and Illumina RNA‐seq. Differential expression and annotation over‐representation analyses were used to characterize tissue‐associated expression differences and over‐represented annotations across ovary, heart, liver, and skin from the same three individuals. The three overlapping eye‐spot pools were described at the library level. Weighted gene co‐expression network analysis (WGCNA) was used only as an exploratory analysis of the 12 four‐tissue libraries. A total of 835,353,682 clean read pairs were retained, and gene expression profiles showed broad differences among the four formally analyzed tissues. Of 30,224 tested genes, 13,849 showed a tissue effect, and 4228 candidate tissue‐enriched genes were identified by requiring higher expression in all three relevant pairwise comparisons. Six representative annotation terms remained significant in the sensitivity analysis, and 3 of 11 non‐gray co‐expression modules passed the prespecified stability rule across nine alternative networks. This study provides an additional multi‐tissue transcriptomic resource for I. braminus, with candidate sets that can guide future functional and comparative tests of hypotheses concerning parthenogenesis, triploidy, fossoriality, and visual reduction.
n1965a012fa57: Eucosma giganteana is a specialist herbivore on Silphium spp. and a major limiting factor to the commercialization of Silphium integrifolium, a perennial oilseed crop. Although it is known that (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate works as an attractant to E. giganteana, it is unknown whether it responds in a concentration‐dependent manner, and whether this cue works throughout the season. Also unknown is whether these moths behaviorally or physiologically respond to other important semiochemicals, such as those emitted by conspecifics or its host. This information is important for developing volatiles for use in behaviorally‐based management of E. giganteana. To address our questions, we performed field trapping with traps baited with (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate, characterized headspace emissions from E. giganteana, and used EAG and flight mill analysis to assess response to (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate and volatiles derived from S. integrifolium and conspecifics. Higher loadings of (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate in the field trapping studies conducted in 2024 resulted in increased captures of E. giganteana moths on sticky traps, which successfully monitored E. giganteana through their full flight period. EAG showed antennal depolarizations, which confirmed E. giganteana perceive (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate. In addition, female E. giganteana perceive volatiles emitted by S. integrifolium whereas males did not. Despite eliciting clear antennal responses and showing success in field monitoring, (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate did not influence flight behavior during the flight mill experiments under the tested conditions. Altogether this study shows (E)‐8‐dodecenyl acetate successfully monitored E. giganteana through the field season; more work is required to deploy it in behaviorally‐based management IPM tactics.
naf1783bd7c23: The Dinaric karst encompasses a network of over 10,000 caves and represents one of the world's most important subterranean biodiversity hotspots. It is inhabited by remarkably diverse and often endemic species, including planarian flatworms. Although cave planarians have long been known from the region, they have not yet been investigated using an integrative approach, and their evolutionary relationships with surface‐dwelling relatives remain unresolved. To address these gaps, we combined field sampling, phylogenetic analyses based on the COI and 18S genes, and phenotypic characterisation. Our results show that cave planariids in the Dinaric karst belong to at least three genera and are more widespread and diverse than previously assumed. We increased the number of cave records in the Dinaric karst from 26 to 37 and documented cf. Atrioplanaria and Phagocata in Croatian caves for the first time. Phylogenetic reconstructions are consistent with independent cave colonisation events, including multiple instances within the genera Crenobia and cf. Atrioplanaria. Variation in pigmentation and eye reduction, both within and between populations, further reveals heterogeneous evolutionary trajectories of cave‐associated phenotypes. Our molecular phylogeny and documentation of trait variability constitute a first step towards establishing Planariidae as a model for investigating the mechanisms underlying the convergent evolution of pigment loss and eye reduction in cave environments.
nd36b08c7ff0d: River corridors play an important role in maintaining the diversity and ecological functions of spontaneous plants. Within urban river corridors, spontaneous plant communities are exposed to both urbanization in the surrounding landscape and lateral hydrological variation between water and land. However, the relative contributions of the surrounding urban matrix and the lateral hydrological position to these community properties have rarely been examined within a common framework. Functional rarity was included because it complements conventional diversity metrics by identifying uncommon functional strategies. We surveyed spontaneous plants along six rivers and one lake in the central urban area of Changde, China, and combined analyses of plant functional traits with structural equation modeling to evaluate the associations of urbanization gradient and lateral hydrological gradient with species diversity, functional structure, and functional rarity. The results showed that species diversity (Shannon–Wiener) and functional diversity (FDis) showed unimodal patterns across urbanization levels, with the highest values at intermediate urbanization. Functional trait space was more clearly separated among lateral habitat types than among urbanization levels. Functional rarity increased with ISA but declined with WD. The structural equation models showed contrasting associations of the two gradients with community properties: higher ISA was associated with greater community‐weighted mean plant height and functional rarity but lower species diversity and FDis, whereas greater WD showed the opposite pattern. Functional rarity was positively associated with FDis in both models. This study provides a transferable framework for comparative research across urban river systems. The framework integrates urbanization at the landscape scale, lateral habitat variation within river corridors, and complementary species, functional, structural, and rarity metrics. The framework is helpful in identifying community patterns that assessments based on a single gradient or a single metric may overlook.
n0edafbbe2040: IntroductionScientific understanding of the spatio-temporal evolution of Production-Ecological-Living Spaces (PELS) and their driving factors provides theoretical support and practical guidance for territorial spatial planning. This study aimed to investigate the spatio-temporal evolution of PELS and explore its driving factors in the Funiu Mountain area.MethodsDigital elevation models (DEMs), multi-source datasets of natural, social, and economic driving factors, and the geographical detector method were used to analyze the spatio-temporal evolution of PELS and identify its driving factors.ResultsFrom 2000 to 2020, the area of production space showed a shrinking trend, whereas the areas of ecological space and living space expanded. Among these, grassland ecological space and urban living space expanded significantly. Across different elevation zones, production space decreased in area. Ecological space increased slightly in low-altitude areas (<400 m), while changes in medium- and high-altitude areas were relatively stable. Living space increased across all elevation zones. Urban living space and industrial production space underwent the most frequent changes. In terms of spatial transformation, exchanges between ecological space and production space were dominant, followed by those between living space and production space, whereas transformations between ecological space and living space were infrequent. The evolution of PELS was primarily influenced by natural background conditions, while the driving effects of socio-economic factors became increasingly prominent. The q value of economic density increased 26.4-fold (from 0.0064 to 0.1688), while that of population density increased 7.5-fold, highlighting the increasingly important role of socio-economic factors in shaping the spatial pattern.DiscussionUnlike existing regional-scale investigations, this study identifies the elevation-gradient differentiation of the driving mechanisms underlying PELS evolution in mountainous areas. These findings enrich the theoretical understanding of PELS in mountain regions and provide targeted support for territorial spatial optimization and sustainable, coordinated regional development in the Funiu Mountain area.
ncf0cca69bf06: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Climate change is driving shrub encroachment and treeline advance in the Arctic, increasing inputs of plant‐derived carbon (C) to soil. These inputs could enhance or reduce microbial decomposition of soil organic matter (SOM) (‘priming’), affecting the soil C balance. In nitrogen (N)‐poor subarctic soils, priming may arise due to selective microbial N‐mining. We investigated the susceptibility of soils to priming across a subarctic ecotone (four sites: birch forest, treeline, shrub‐dominated tundra, tundra heath). Fertilisation with N and phosphorus (P) in the field for 2 years was used to test how nutrient availability interacted with plant communities to modulate microbial responses to simulated rhizosphere input. Soils were incubated with either 13C‐glucose (simulating rhizosphere input) or water (control) for 1 week under controlled laboratory conditions to assess priming effects on soil C mineralisation, soil N mineralisation and microbial growth. Soil and foliar nutrient concentrations tended to decline from forest to tundra, reflecting shifts in vegetation composition and associated plant–soil‐microbial feedbacks. Soil C mineralisation was initially primed most strongly in tundra (+130%) and P‐fertilised treeline soils (+150%), but these effects largely disappeared within 24 h, resulting in no change to the overall soil C balance. In all soils, in the absence of added glucose, we found evidence for selective microbial use of N‐rich organic matter, suggesting high microbial demand for N. However, counter to expectation, glucose addition did not generally strengthen selective microbial N‐mining, likely because microbial use of N‐rich SOM was already near its stoichiometric limit (set by the lowest possible C:N ratio of organic compounds). This was with the exception of N‐fertilised soils, where glucose addition primed soil N mineralisation (up to +250%), resulting in intensified selective microbial N‐mining, with an effect size that tended to strengthen towards the forest. n1c9c268bfa69: Conceptual framework linking fire injury to immediate and delayed physiological effects and postfire tree outcomes. n238f24b6e623: Medicinal plants face growing threats from climate change, habitat fragmentation, selective harvesting, and other human-induced pressures that may diminish genetic diversity and weaken evolutionary resilience. ne828877f222b: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Plant litter input can affect soil organic carbon (SOC) decomposition, that is the priming effect.
