As land tenure provides critical insights into the spatial stability of populations and informs conservation planning, its limited integration into ecological studies remains concerning despite advances in population ecology and monitoring technologies. We attempted to build a foundation for future research that aims to measure population stability and species persistence. सारांश इलाके पर कब्ज़ा (लैंड टेन्योर) उन जानवरों के लिए एक बुनियादी पारिस्थितिक प्रक्रिया है जो अपने इलाके की रक्षा करते हैं; यह बताता है कि कैसे कोई जानवर जगह और संसाधनों तक अपनी पहुँच बनाता है और उसे बनाए रखता है। हॉर्नॉकर ने 1969 में सबसे पहले इस अवधारणा को पेश किया था, जिससे जनसंख्या गतिकी की गतिविधियों (पॉपुलेशन डायनामिक्स) को शुरुआती तौर पर समझने में मदद मिलती है। हालाँकि, किसी आबादी की स्थिरता, पूर्वानुमान और विशिष्टता को समझने के लिए इस अहम पहलू का शायद ही कभी मूल्यांकन किया जाता है। अब तक, ‘लैंड टेन्योर सिस्टम’ की कोई स्पष्ट पारिस्थितिक परिभाषा नहीं दी गई है। इस कॉन्सेप्ट को समझने के लिए, हम अपने इलाके पर कब्ज़ा रखने वाले मांसाहारी जानवरों पर पिछले 50 से ज़्यादा सालों की इकोलॉजिकल स्टडीज़ का रिव्यू करते हैं और यह समझते हैं कि अलग‐अलग तरह के जानवरों के लिए लैंड टेन्योर को कैसे मापा गया है। हम यह देखते हैं कि यह पहलू जनसंख्या गतिकी और डेमोग्राफिक प्रक्रियाओं को कैसे जोड़ता है, जिससे अलग‐अलग तरह के लैंडस्केप में प्रजातियों के संरक्षण में मदद मिलती है। इसका मकसद एक ऐसा तरीका विकसित करना है जो अलग‐अलग प्रजातियों और इलाकों में लैंड टेन्योर का मूल्यांकन करने के लिए एक ढांचा और जांचने योग्य परिकल्पनाएं प्रदान करे। चूंकि लैंड टेन्योर आबादी की स्थानिक स्थिरता के बारे में महत्वपूर्ण जानकारी देता है और संरक्षण की योजना बनाने में मदद करता है, इसलिए आबादी की पारिस्थितिकी और निगरानी तकनीकों में प्रगति के बावजूद पारिस्थितिक अध्ययनों में इसका सीमित एकीकरण चिंता का विषय बना हुआ है। हमने भविष्य के शोध के लिए एक आधार बनाने की कोशिश की है जिसका मकसद आबादी की स्थिरता और प्रजातियों के बने रहने को मापना है।
nb18daad1f74c: Our findings indicate that elevated plant colonisation drives shifts towards faster‐growing, decomposition‐oriented microbial communities. Associations between plant colonists and microbial communities were stronger at the late succession site, even though colonist cover was higher in the early succession site. Practitioners should therefore consider belowground impacts of plant colonisation across all grasslands, and not only where effects on plant community composition are most visible. Abstract Colonisation by previously absent plants is increasing under global environmental change. Colonist establishment can alter plant community composition and could subsequently affect soil microbial communities. Using a 9‐year seed addition experiment, we ask: (i) how do colonists influence plant community composition; and (ii) do these vegetation changes drive shifts in soil prokaryote and fungal communities? We introduced 23 colonist species, divided into ‘fast’ and ‘slow’ resource acquisition strategies, into two grassland sites that differed in successional age and community composition. We manipulated local disturbance and colonist seed additions and examined how site and colonist characteristics influenced microbial community composition. Plant and microbial communities were surveyed 9 years after initial seed addition. Colonist cover was higher in the early succession site. Across both sites, evidence indicated that higher colonist cover led to communities with faster growth strategies, altered belowground resource acquisition strategies, and—at the early succession site—lowered taxonomic diversity. Through these changes in plant community composition, higher colonist cover was associated with less diverse prokaryote communities characterised by elevated metabolic activity and cellular replication, and a higher abundance of fungal saprotrophs. Additional associations between colonists and microbial composition depended on site characteristics and colonist characteristics. Colonist cover was only weakly linked to other microbial functional groups at the early succession site, with no observed links to obligate fungi, despite colonist abundance being highest there. At the late succession site, higher cover of fast‐growing colonists was associated with prokaryote communities exhibiting lower metabolic activity and greater obligate fungal abundance. Also at the late succession site, plots with more colonist seed additions supported higher prokaryote diversity and greater abundance of fungal obligates than unsown plots, regardless of current plant composition. Synthesis: Our findings indicate that elevated plant colonisation drives shifts towards faster‐growing, decomposition‐oriented microbial communities. However, associations between plant colonists and microbial communities were stronger at the late succession site, even though colonist cover was higher in the early succession site. Practitioners should therefore consider belowground impacts of plant colonisation across all grasslands, and not only where effects on plant community composition are most visible.
n2aef9f241866: Exotic dominance can leave behind soil microbial legacies that favour exotic plants over natives. In a two‐phase greenhouse experiment, increasing exotic dominance enriched arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and progressively enhanced exotic growth, while competition strength remained unchanged. A complementary field survey showed that exotic abundance was positively associated with AMF richness, supporting a potential microbial feedback that reinforces invasion. Abstract Ecosystems worldwide are undergoing a pervasive transition toward exotic‐dominated states, a shift that threatens biodiversity and disrupts key ecosystem functions. Although positive abiotic feedbacks are frequently cited as drivers of these transitions, the microbial mechanisms involved remain poorly understood. In a two‐phase greenhouse experiment, we conditioned soils along a gradient of increasing exotic plant dominance using 10 exotic and 10 native species. We then assessed plant performance on these soil microbial inocula under no, intraspecific and interspecific competition. We found that increasing exotic dominance progressively reshaped soil microbial communities in ways that favoured exotic over native growth, without altering competitive strengths. This growth asymmetry was tightly linked to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF), whose richness increased with exotic dominance and was positively correlated with exotic performance. Complementary field surveys of the same exotic species confirmed a positive correlation between their abundance and AMF richness in natural communities. Synthesis. Our findings demonstrate that increasing dominance of exotic plants can generate microbial legacies that progressively favour exotic plants over native plants. These microbial legacies provide a mechanism linking changes in plant community structure to subsequent competitive interactions and offer a framework for understanding how biotic interactions, particularly those involving soil mutualists, can contribute to the persistence and spread of invasive plants. 中文摘要 全球生态系统正在普遍向外来植物占优势的状态转变，这一转变威胁生物多样性并扰乱关键生态系统功能。尽管正向非生物反馈常被认为是这类生态转变的驱动因素，但其中涉及的微生物机制仍知之甚少。 本研究开展两阶段温室实验，选取10种外来植物和10种本地植物，沿外来植物优势度递增梯度完成土壤驯化处理。随后在无竞争、种内竞争和种间竞争条件下，评估植物在上述土壤微生物接种环境中的生长表现。 研究发现，外来植物优势度的增加会逐步重塑土壤微生物群落结构，形成利于外来植物生长、而非本地植物生长的格局，且不会改变物种竞争强度。这种生长不对称性与丛枝菌根真菌密切相关:丛枝菌根真菌丰富度随外来植物优势度升高而增加，且与外来植物生长表现呈正相关。针对相同外来物种的野外补充调查进一步证实，自然群落中外来植物多度与丛枝菌根真菌丰富度存在显著正相关关系。 综上，外来植物优势度的增加可以形成有利于外来植物而非本土植物的土壤微生物遗留效应，而且这种作用会随外来植物优势度提高而增强。这些遗留效应揭示了植物群落结构变化影响后续竞争关系的潜在机制，并为理解生物相互作用，尤其是土壤互惠生物介导的相互作用，如何促进入侵植物的持续存在和扩散提供了理论框架。
nde9de303f3e6: Collectively, these findings provide direct experimental evidence that plants act as central hubs that reconfigure the biodiversity‐stability relationship by mediating green‐brown food web coupling, and emphasise that maintaining plant integrity is critical for sustaining high multifunctionality and biologically buffered stability under global change. Abstract Direct evidence of how plants regulate soil biodiversity–ecosystem stability relationships remains scarce, as the coupling between aboveground and belowground components makes it methodologically challenging to isolate plant‐mediated effects from the independent role of soil biota. Using a long‐term multifactorial semiarid grassland experiment with plant removal nested within grazing, nitrogen addition and water addition, we directly tested whether weakening plant‐derived green inputs reconfigures the soil biodiversity–ecosystem stability relationship through altered green‐brown food web coupling. By contrasting plant‐present and plant‐removal plots, we found that plants fundamentally reconfigured the biodiversity‐stability relationship. In the coupled state, plant presence shifted ecosystem stability towards biotic regulation: multifunctionality was supported by soil biota richness, while functional stability depended on biotic insurance via soil biota asynchrony and compositional stability. After plant removal, multifunctionality weakened and control shifted towards abiotic factors (soil pH/moisture); the observed increase in calculated stability reflected reduced temporal variability at a lower functional level rather than enhanced ecological resilience. Water availability was the strongest moderator of these plant‐mediated effects, whereas grazing primarily reduced the magnitude of multifunctionality and soil biota richness, and nitrogen addition had comparatively weak effects. Synthesis. Collectively, these findings provide direct experimental evidence that plants act as central hubs that reconfigure the biodiversity‐stability relationship by mediating green‐brown food web coupling, and emphasise that maintaining plant integrity is critical for sustaining high multifunctionality and biologically buffered stability under global change.
n462c1857a9cd: Context dependence can sometimes seem overwhelming in ecology, but—in this study—trends were largely predictable when we considered how causal drivers and limiting factors likely vary across different ecological conditions. Our study highlights the value of long‐term multifactorial experiments and suggests that the interplay of limiting factors can help predict mechanistic context dependence in plant colonisation. Abstract Context dependence can impede accurate prediction in ecology, including plant colonisation. Although it is well established that ecology is complicated, most studies in ecology focus on one or two factors at a time and most experiments run for less than 3 years. As such, most studies only provide a partial picture, and sometimes those pictures can appear contradictory, leading researchers and practitioners to question what factors are important and when. Using a 12‐year multifactorial grassland seed addition experiment, we tested whether we could accurately predict drivers of sown colonist abundance based on the species, sites and conditions in question. Up to 15 grassland species, divided into resource‐acquisitive (‘fast’) or resource‐conservative (‘slow’) life history groups, were added at two different seed rates, with and without the other colonist group, into grassland plots in Minnesota, USA. The plots represented early, mid and late successional communities, and half of the plots were regularly disturbed. We surveyed sown ‘colonist’ cover six times over 12 years. None of the five factors examined (colonist life history group, colonist group composition, seed rate, community successional age, disturbance—plus time) had a consistent relationship with colonist abundance, but general trends did emerge. Resource‐acquisitive colonists with fast life histories were most successful soon after seed addition while resource‐conservative slow colonists reached peak abundances in later years. Colonist cover was higher in early successional than late successional communities, reflecting soil N limitation in late succession. Physical disturbance facilitated colonisation when soil N was limiting, especially for resource‐acquisitive colonists, but disturbance otherwise impeded colonisation as it exacerbated effects of low soil moisture and reduced microhabitat suitability. When sown together into communities not already limited by resource competition, there was some evidence that fast colonists impeded slow colonists through niche pre‐emption. Synthesis: Context dependence can sometimes seem overwhelming in ecology, but—in this study—trends were largely predictable when we considered how causal drivers and limiting factors likely vary across different ecological conditions. Our study highlights the value of long‐term multifactorial experiments and suggests that the interplay of limiting factors can help predict mechanistic context dependence in plant colonisation.
ne1127af09c50: India is a major centre of rice diversity, where long‐term cultivation across contrasting environments has generated substantial genomic and phenotypic variation. We analysed genome‐wide SNP variation in 313 Indian rice accessions to resolve ancestry structure, regional diversity, spatial genetic processes, environmental associations and haplotype variation at key domestication and adaptation genes. Population structure analyses resolved eight ancestry groups corresponding to indica, aus, aromatic and japonica lineages. Ancestry explained substantially more genomic differentiation than biogeographic regionalization, while there is extensive historical connectivity among lineages and regions. Genetic diversity considerably varied across biogeographic zones. After balanced resampling, the Himalayan region showed the highest standardized allelic diversity and private‐allele richness, whereas the North‐East region retained high observed heterozygosity and broad ancestry representation. Isolation‐by‐distance was weak overall but strongly lineage‐ and region‐dependent. Spatial principal component analysis identified significant ancestry‐independent broad‐scale genetic gradients, demonstrating geography‐influenced structure beyond lineage composition. Redundancy analysis detected significant genome–environment associations (F = 3.07, p = 0.001), with climate explaining more independent genomic variation (2.7%) than soil (0.9%). District‐level tribal population proportion showed only a weak negative association with individual heterozygosity (Spearman ρ = −0.155, p = 0.006), although PTP classes exhibited low‐to‐moderate genetic differentiation. Haplotype analysis revealed strong locus‐specific ancestry and geographic structuring at sd1, Wx, GS3 and DRO1. Together, the results show that Indian rice diversity is a reticulate genomic mosaic shaped by ancestry, geography, historical gene flow and environmental heterogeneity. This study provides a landscape‐genomic framework for conservation and targeted germplasm utilization in breeding programmes.
n8cb3ea9ed3ae: Contact zones, where related taxa breed sympatrically, provide natural laboratories for studying phylogeography and speciation. In migratory species, these systems offer unique opportunities to disentangle the relative roles of genetic and social factors in migratory behaviour. Cory's (Calonectris borealis) and Scopoli's shearwaters (C. diomedea) are closely related long‐distance migrants that breed allopatrically across most of their ranges but occur sympatrically in the Alboran Sea. Here, we tested whether the migratory strategies of these shearwaters are determined primarily by their genetic ancestry or by the social environment of their breeding colony. We used light‐level geolocators to track the annual migration of 50 individuals (127 tracks) from six breeding colonies: four sympatric colonies within the Alboran contact zone and one allopatric colony of each species. We also generated whole‐genome sequencing data for 58 individuals (including all 50 tracked birds) to infer species ancestry and identify hybrids. Most Cory's shearwaters wintered in subtropical Atlantic upwelling systems along the African and South American coasts, whereas most Scopoli's shearwaters wintered in tropical waters off West Africa. The two taxa partially overlapped in the Sahelian upwelling and Angolan waters. Individuals breeding in the contact zone exhibited migration strategies that matched their genomic ancestry rather than the colony's predominant pattern. Most importantly, we identified seven recent hybrids between the two taxa, representing 17.5% of the sampled individuals in the contact zone. These hybrids exhibited intermediate migratory strategies, indicating a strong genetic determination of migratory behaviour. The overlap in wintering areas may increase opportunities for interspecific interactions before arrival at the breeding colonies, potentially promoting hybridisation. Our study demonstrates that migratory strategies are strongly influenced by genetic background in long‐distance migratory seabirds and suggests that weak migratory connectivity among populations facilitates hybridisation in contact zones.
neba55a94366d: Targets 1 and 3 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) require actions to focus on areas of importance for biodiversity—a prerequisite for reversing biodiversity loss and halting human‐induced extinctions as set out in the Mission and Goals of the KMGBF. There is a need to review progress on how countries are aiming to identify and conserve such areas of importance. We reviewed 97 national biodiversity strategy and action plans (NBSAPs) and 89 country submissions to the Convention on Biological Diversity's (CBD) Online Reporting Tool (ORT) to assess ambition across five targets of the KMGBF. We searched for evidence that countries were considering where to act for Targets 1, 2, 3, 14, 15, and 21. No country defined what constitutes an important area for biodiversity, and any stated focus of planning was limited largely to existing protected areas or ecosystems. Key Biodiversity Areas were identified in 40% of the NBSAPs, yet only 26% included specific targets, actions, or indicators for these globally significant sites. Ambition toward the 30% restoration (Target 2) and 30% protection (Target 3) targets was higher than previously reported but remained low overall. Only half of the countries planned to mandate or encourage business to measure its impacts on biodiversity (Target 15). Across six measures of ambition, an average of 29% of the countries submitting NBSAPs and 31% of the ORT target countries aimed to meet the KMGBF benchmarks, whereas 48% and 53%, respectively, showed no ambition to do so. European countries showed the lowest level of ambition of any region. Much greater levels of ambition and progress are needed to achieve the targets, goals, and vision for areas of importance for biodiversity in the KMGBF by 2030. Marco conceptual para la aplicación del componente de reducción de amenazas de la medida de Reducción de Amenazas y Restauración de Especies (STAR) Resumen Uno de los objetivos principales del Marco Global de Biodiversidad de Kunming‐Montreal (KMGBF) es detener la extinción de especies y reducir el riesgo de extinción diez veces para 2050. Con el fin de garantizar que las medidas adoptadas en el marco de los objetivos del KMGBF contribuyan a reducir el riesgo de extinción de las especies, se diseñó el indicador «Reducción de amenazas y restauración de especies» (STAR), que permite establecer objetivos basados en la ciencia para las especies. STAR cuantifica la contribución potencial de las medidas de reducción de amenazas o de restauración del hábitat a la reducción del riesgo de extinción de las especies en una zona. Para apoyar la aplicación efectiva de STAR, desarrollamos un marco que permite pasar de determinar el componente de reducción de amenazas de STAR (START) con datos globales a calibrar START utilizando datos locales, para finalmente establecer objetivos y calcular las puntuaciones START reales para medir el progreso. El marco describe los enfoques específicos que pueden aplicarse para calcular estas diferentes métricas START. Primero, las puntuaciones estimadas de START utilizan datos globales para proporcionar una indicación inicial de las especies y las amenazas que se espera que estén presentes en una zona. A continuación, las puntuaciones calibradas de START implican confirmar la presencia local de especies y amenazas y los datos verificados a nivel local permiten establecer objetivos sólidos de mitigación de amenazas que pueden articularse como puntuaciones objetivo de START. El START calibrado también puede servir de base para la gestión reactiva y proactiva de las amenazas. Por último, se supervisan los cambios en la intensidad de las amenazas y se utilizan para calcular el START realizado. Para alcanzar el START realizado, los actores deben no solo reducir las amenazas existentes, sino también evitar que surjan nuevas amenazas en la zona.…
nb3c0655fe6ef: The mismatch between the scale of ecological processes and management decisions represents a significant challenge in marine conservation. This misalignment can result in ineffective conservation measures and compromise the sustainability of marine ecosystems. The large spatial resolution commonly used to analyze food webs may obscure key ecological processes and their functioning, leading to inaccurate conclusions with important consequences for management and governance. To address this gap, we used a food web indicator, the survey‐based mean trophic level (MTL), covering an entire bentho‐demersal community across four subregions of the Northeast Atlantic. The indicator was developed at two spatial resolutions, subregional and local (0.2° × 0.2° cells), and we used a long‐term dataset to assess food‐web status. A set of 18 ecological scenarios, based on different trophic level (TL) thresholds and depth ranges, were established for each subregion, and linear models were applied to the historical series for each scenario. At the subregional scale, the results indicated potential recovery of top predators in the northern area; however, the stable patterns under various scenarios may have been attributable to ongoing fishing pressure rather than to true ecosystem stability or a genuinely balanced state. At the finer spatial resolution, local declining trends were revealed that had been masked in the broader‐scale analysis. These contrasting patterns underscore the importance of spatial resolution when assessing the status of marine food webs and highlight the need to consider multiple ecological scenarios. We recommend aligning management strategies with the natural processes that govern marine ecosystems to enhance the resilience and long‐term sustainability of ocean environments. Evaluación y cuantificación de las variaciones en el funcionamiento de las redes tróficas a través de escalas Resumen El desajuste entre la escala de los procesos ecológicos y las decisiones de gestión es un reto importante para la conservación marina. Este desajuste puede dar lugar a medidas de conservación ineficaces y poner en peligro la sostenibilidad de los ecosistemas marinos. La alta resolución espacial que se suele emplear para analizar las redes tróficas puede ocultar procesos ecológicos clave y su funcionamiento, lo que lleva a conclusiones inexactas con importantes consecuencias para la gestión y la gobernanza. Para abordar este vacío, utilizamos un indicador de la red trófica, el nivel trófico medio (NTM) basado en estudios de campo, que abarca toda una comunidad bentónica y demersal en cuatro subregiones del Atlántico nororiental. El indicador se desarrolló en dos resoluciones espaciales, subregional y local (celdas de 0.2° x 0.2°), y con un conjunto de datos a largo plazo para evaluar el estado de las redes tróficas. Establecimos un conjunto de 18 escenarios ecológicos, basados en diferentes umbrales de nivel trófico (NT) y rangos de profundidad para cada subregión y se aplicaron modelos lineales a las series históricas de cada escenario. A escala subregional, los resultados indicaron una posible recuperación de los depredadores superiores en la zona norte; sin embargo, los patrones estables observados en diversos escenarios podrían deberse a la presión pesquera actual, más que a una verdadera estabilidad del ecosistema o a un estado genuinamente equilibrado. A una resolución espacial más detallada, se revelaron tendencias locales de declive que habían quedado ocultas en el análisis a mayor escala. Estos patrones contrastantes subrayan la importancia de la resolución espacial a la hora de evaluar el estado de las redes tróficas marinas y resaltan la necesidad de considerar múltiples escenarios ecológicos. Recomendamos armonizar las estrategias de gestión con los procesos naturales que rigen los ecosistemas marinos para mejorar la resiliencia y la sostenibilidad a largo plazo de los entornos oceánicos.…
n968db71542d9: There is a persistent underrepresentation of marginalized voices in academic literature, including that for ecology and conservation. Such exclusion hampers career progression, perpetuating disadvantages for historically marginalized groups in the field, with implications for the direction of conservation research. Diverse perspectives foster novel thinking, strengthen innovation, and ensure research reflects the full spectrum of challenges faced by communities. To assess this underrepresentation, we analyzed self‐reported demographic data for authors of scientific articles to explore demographic trends and how they shifted between 2010 and 2020. The journals chosen were listed as conservation‐related by three or more of the five major journal indices. We used the same dimensions of diversity to assess editor demographics in 2021. In total, 2152 authors and 241 editors completed the survey (response rate: 21.5% authors; 29.5% editors). We found that overall author diversity across multiple traits (Rao's Q) increased between 2010 and 2020. Most notably, the representation of women increased from 29.5% to 35.6% of authors. However, women from lower‐middle‐ or low‐income countries still represented <1% of authors, and most dimensions of diversity saw little change over a decade. In 2020–2021, 80% of authors and 76% of editors self‐identified as White; over three‐quarters of respondents across years lived in high‐income countries; and nationals of three countries (the United Kingdom, the United States, and Australia) represented 34% of authors and 49% of editors (5% of the global population). Our study findings highlight the importance of considering intersectionality, as respondents spanning multiple marginalized identities were disproportionately underrepresented. Overall, our work highlights how a lack of representation continues to characterize academic publishing in conservation and ecology but shows signs of positive change. There is evidence that gender‐based initiatives are having a positive effect, yet more work is needed to enhance representation across other dimensions of diversity. Representación en la literatura sobre conservación Resumen Existe una infrarrepresentación persistente de las voces marginadas en la literatura académica, incluida la dedicada a la ecología y la conservación. Dicha exclusión dificulta el desarrollo profesional y perpetúa las desventajas para los grupos históricamente marginados en este ámbito, lo que tiene implicaciones para la orientación de la investigación en materia de conservación. La diversidad de perspectivas fomenta el pensamiento creador, refuerza la innovación y garantiza que la investigación refleje todo el espectro de retos a los que se enfrentan las comunidades. Para evaluar esta infrarrepresentación, analizamos los datos demográficos facilitados por los propios autores de artículos científicos con el fin de explorar las tendencias demográficas y cómo evolucionaron entre 2010 y 2020. Las revistas seleccionadas figuraban como relacionadas con la conservación en tres o más de los cinco principales índices de revistas. Utilizamos las mismas dimensiones de diversidad para evaluar los datos demográficos de los editores en 2021. En total, 2 152 autores y 241 editores completaron la encuesta (tasa de respuesta: 21,5 % de los autores; 29,5 % de los editores). Observamos que la diversidad general de los autores en múltiples características (Q de Rao) aumentó entre 2010 y 2020. Cabe destacar que la representación de las mujeres aumentó del 29,5 % al 35,6 % del total de autores. Sin embargo, las mujeres de países de renta media‐baja o baja seguían representando menos del 1 % de los autores, y en la mayoría de los aspectos relacionados con la diversidad apenas se observaron cambios a lo largo de la década.…
n0175f4fadfb6: Ancient pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics have transformed archaeological research on infectious disease by enabling the detection of pathogens, reconstruction of extinct lineages, and investigation of host responses in past populations. Yet pathogen identification alone addresses only part of retrospective diagnosis: whether an individual experienced disease, which tissues were affected, and how infection contributed to morbidity or death. Palaeoproteomics extends this enquiry through the recovery of pathogen proteins, host immune proteins, and tissue-associated molecules from ancient human remains and associated materials. This review evaluates its diagnostic contribution within the broader reconstruction of ancient disease ecology. Dental calculus provides a particularly rich record of oral host–microbe interactions, combining microbial signals with inflammatory and dietary proteins. Studies of mummified skin, muscle and other soft tissues, dental pulp, skeletal lesions, historical bloodstains, coprolites, and latrine residues further extend the range of evidence available for retrospective diagnosis. Protein-based investigations of intestinal infection also illustrate the need to distinguish antibody-based antigen detection from sequence-based proteomics. Published studies support several levels of inference, ranging from tissue identification and inflammatory processes to specific infection and, more cautiously, clinical disease. They also reveal continuing challenges involving peptide specificity, contamination, source attribution, and the interpretation of disease-associated proteins. Retrospective diagnosis is strongest when molecular findings are consistent with anatomical, archaeological, and historical evidence and help discriminate among plausible alternative diagnoses. Protein evidence therefore contributes not only to individual palaeopathological diagnosis but also to broader reconstructions of relationships among infection, diet, sanitation, care, and social conditions. Future progress will depend on comparative samples with and without independently supported pathological evidence, archaeological validation of diagnostic markers, transparent reporting, broader regional coverage, and sampling of finite human remains.
nc545f8543f9e: Accurate mapping of woody biomass and its temporal change is critical for understanding the global carbon balance, informing restoration and supporting evidence‐based policy on climate mitigation and livelihoods. The vegetation of the dry tropics, comprised largely of dry forests and savannas, holds substantial woody carbon stocks, but both stocks and change over time remain uncertain. Where Earth Observation (EO) data have been used to estimate change over time, different products give conflicting results on the direction, magnitude and location of change. We present pan‐dry‐tropical maps of aboveground carbon density (AGCD) and AGCD change at 100 m resolution for the years 2015–2024, developed using ALOS ScanSAR satellite radar observations calibrated with in situ measurements (n = 237). These maps suggest an aboveground woody carbon pool (AGC) in the dry tropics of 25.3 ±$$ \pm $$ 2.0 PgC, ~13.0% of global AGC. Net AGC has increased by 0.43 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.07 PgC yr−1, ~20.0% of the global net land sink. The overall net increase (0.43 PgC yr−1) is comprised of gross losses from deforestation and degradation (0.27 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.05 PgC yr−1) and gains due to densification and extensification of 0.59 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.1 PgC yr−1, with the balance accounted for by small changes (change < 20% of AGCD; 0.11 PgC yr−1). Losses are equally split between degradation and deforestation, while gains are divided roughly 2:1 between the densification of woody ecosystems and expansion into previously grass‐dominated areas. These new maps, created with a dry‐tropics‐specific EO method, highlight the importance of tropical dry forests and savannas in the global carbon cycle. The prominent role of degradation‐related losses suggests that climate change mitigation will need to focus much more on reducing losses from overharvesting than at present. The widespread increases in carbon density and the increase in tree biomass into open systems present major challenges for biodiversity conservation, restoration and livelihoods.
nfd62231b2efe: Climate change is widely expected to push many taxa beyond their biological limits, yet some populations persist in environments that routinely experience climatic extremes. This raises a fundamental question: does their thermal tolerance reflect species‐level thermal generalism (an evolved capacity to maintain performance across a broad thermal range) or population‐specific acclimation to local conditions (phenotypic plasticity)? Distinguishing between these alternatives is key for predicting whether tolerance to climatic extremes will generalise across species distributions or remain restricted to heat‐tolerant populations. To test these competing hypotheses, we quantified physiological performance (at cellular and organismal levels) in three economically important estuarine fish (Acanthopagrus australis, Sillago ciliata and Rhabdosargus sarba) collected from 20 sites across 15 estuaries along a ~1000‐km latitudinal gradient spanning their core and poleward range edges. Sites differed in thermal variability, including some that intermittently exceeded the severest end‐of‐century climate projections. We then experimentally exposed two of the fish species from low and high thermal variability sites to moderate (+2°C, 14 days) or extreme (+4°C, 7 days) simulated marine heatwave events, assessing 12 physiological and behavioural proxies. All three species collected in situ maintained comparable physiological performance across sites of contrasting thermal variability. Both experimental species, each collected from a single high‐ and low‐variability site, tolerated heatwave conditions regardless of thermal history or heatwave intensity, supporting species‐level thermal generalism rather than population‐specific acclimation. In the absence of heatwave conditions, S. ciliata from high‐variability sites also showed steeper allometric scaling and faster growth at 26 versus 24°C experimental control temperatures, suggesting this species may benefit from the warmer baseline temperatures projected under gradual climate change. Combined, our findings support thermal generalism as the primary driver of tolerance in estuarine fishes to climatic extremes, with important implications for the fisheries they support under climate change.
n6299c4a3aa98: Many species are responding to environmental change by shifting the timings of phenological events such as migration or reproduction. These shifts are typically reported as rates of change, which do not indicate when such shifts transcend their original states, nor consider whether species experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species at their phenological events. We present a new, generalizable approach to detect and contextualize shifts in phenological data regardless of taxonomic group or location by applying statistical and empirical Time of Emergence (ToE) metrics derived from climate science. Our approach conclusively identifies when species depart from their baseline phenological event timings and determines whether they experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species during their phenological event. In combination, these metrics detect emergence in timing, environment and community synchrony for species' phenological responses. We explore these metrics using simulations then apply them to a diverse set of example datasets (butterflies, marine plankton and cherry blossoms). We then develop community‐wide indicators of phenological emergence, environmental emergence and species mismatch, which can be applied to inform biodiversity policy at any scale and for any taxa. These methods are available via the phenometrics R package.
n23dbb4bb3a1f: Datasets derived from mixed‐template DNA amplification and sequencing (‘metabarcoding’) are common in environmental DNA (eDNA), microbiome or microbial ecology analyses. Such metabarcoding data have been broadly used to inform estimates of biodiversity, distribution and abundance across a wide range of species and habitats. Generally, data from metabarcoding consist of a table of read‐counts assigned to each of a set of taxa or sequence variants. As such, they appear to contain quantitative information about the environment under study, immediately eligible for traditional community ecology analyses. In fact, metabarcoding data are compositional, can be biased by variation in PCR amplification rates among taxa, and have other statistical attributes that are distinct from many other common ecological observations. The difficulty in understanding and accounting for the complexity of metabarcoding observations has hindered their ecological interpretation and limited their integration with other ecological data types. Here, we use both simulations and empirical observations to show that the variability among replicate metabarcoding observations is closely tied to the absolute quantities of DNA present in a sample. We then develop a general statistical model for estimating DNA abundance from metabarcoding observations using the relationship between mean and variance of metabarcoding reads. We demonstrate that the model can effectively estimate DNA abundances using simulations and from experimentally created DNA samples. The model can be applied to a single marker or to multiple markers simultaneously, allowing the direct integration of information from multiple genetic markers derived from a common biological sample. Estimates of absolute DNA abundance are the logical unit to connect DNA observations to organismal abundance or biomass. Our methods can be used to link together multiple types of DNA observations or to connect DNA observations with non‐genetic ecological methods for surveying ecosystems. However, important aspects of the ‘ecology of DNA’ remain unresolved and may limit our ability to link observed concentrations to organismal abundances in a general way.
nbf5db98f9e53: Tropical forest canopies host diverse tree and liana assemblages, yet key foliar and reproductive traits needed for taxonomic identification of canopy plants are often difficult to see from the forest floor, creating a bottleneck in inventories. We introduce a drone-based workflow that automatically acquires hundreds of close-up, ultra-high-resolution photographs (~0.4 mm pixel−1) of selected tree crowns per day, enabling efficient botanical and ecological studies of canopy plants (demo: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). The approach leverages a compact DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) with wide-angle and telephoto cameras to (i) generate a high-resolution digital surface model and orthomosaic via structure-from-motion photogrammetry and (ii) capture close-up photographs from ~6 m above the canopy at preplanned locations. Photographs are accurately (<13 cm error) geolocated with real-time kinematic (RTK) global navigation satellite system to support spatial co-registration with photogrammetric products. In field deployments, we acquired close-up photographs for up to ~300 selected canopy trees per day and maintained RTK corrections over operational distances up to ~3 km, illustrating the potential of the method for plot- to landscape-scale studies. The level of visual detail in the close-up photographs of canopy crowns was sufficient to support expert identification in a majority of cases in our tropical forest study sites despite their high taxonomic diversity. Although developed for tropical trees and lianas, the workflow is applicable to other forest and vegetation types for botanical, phenological and ecological applications. We outline strengths and limitations of the workflow to guide use and also provide harpia , an open-source Python library to program automatic close-up missions with the M3E (code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22116831). Resumen El dosel de los bosques tropicales alberga diversas comunidades de árboles y lianas. Sin embargo, las características foliares y reproductivas clave necesarias para la identificación taxonómica de las especies del dosel suelen ser difíciles de observar desde el suelo del bosque, lo que limita el progreso en los inventarios. Presentamos un flujo de trabajo basado en drones que adquiere automáticamente cientos de fotografías de primer plano de ultra alta resolución (~0,4 mm píxel−1) de copas de árboles seleccionadas por día, agilizando los estudios botánicos y ecológicos de las especies del dosel (demostración: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). Utilizamos un dron DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) compacto, equipado con cámaras gran angular y teleobjetivo, para (i) generar un modelo digital de superficie y un ortomosaico de alta resolución mediante fotogrametría de estructura a partir del movimiento (structure-from-motion) y (ii) capturar fotografías de primer plano desde ~6 m sobre el dosel en ubicaciones planificadas previamente. Las fotografías se georreferencian con precisión (error <13 cm) mediante un sistema global de navegación por satélite (GNSS) con posicionamiento cinemático en tiempo real (RTK), facilitando su corregistro espacial con los productos fotogramétricos. En campañas de campo, adquirimos fotografías de primer plano de hasta ~300 árboles de dosel diarios y mantuvimos correcciones RTK a distancias operativas de hasta ~3 km, lo que evidencia el potencial del método para estudios desde nivel de parcela hasta paisaje. La alta resolución de las fotografías permitió la identificación taxonómica por expertos en la mayoría de los casos, aun en ecosistemas de bosque tropical con elevada diversidad taxonómica. Aunque se desarrolló para árboles y lianas tropicales, el flujo de trabajo es aplicable a otros tipos de bosques y vegetación con fines botánicos, fenológicos y ecológicos.…
n228d8356b644: Individual‐tree segmentation from three‐dimensional forest point clouds underpins forest inventory, biomass estimation and ecosystem monitoring, but remains challenging in structurally complex stands, where vertical heterogeneity and point‐density degradation weaken the robustness of centre‐offset‐based instance grouping. We present TreeSegAgent, an extensible framework for forest point‐cloud analysis, whose core segmentation component is a multi‐anchor framework for tree segmentation (MA‐TreeSeg). MA‐TreeSeg stabilizes instance formation through two modules. First, a multi‐anchor (three‐vertical‐anchor) structural grouping module within an enhanced PointGroup‐style instance segmentation network, explicitly encoding tree vertical structure to improve grouping stability under sparse canopy conditions and to better recover low‐stature and understory trees. Second, we incorporate segment anything model (SAM)‐driven trunk constraint module. SAM is applied on two‐dimensional projections to identify trunk regions and generate trunk candidates, which are then employed as spatial hard constraints to regularize centre‐offset predictions and suppress clustering drift under canopy overlap. To support reproducible ecological workflow, TreeSegAgent further provides a task‐driven agent for automated, specification‐driven orchestration of common point‐cloud operations (e.g. instance segmentation, DEM generation and height‐based filtering) across datasets. Across multiple forest point‐cloud benchmarks, our method yields more spatially coherent individual‐tree instances and improved robustness to density variation, offering an extensible solution for large‐scale forest point‐cloud analysis.
n13a59ef7daa3: Photopigments, formed by an opsin protein bound to a light‐sensitive chromophore, underlie vertebrate vision. Long‐wavelength–sensitive (LWS) opsins mediate red‐light detection, and most teleosts retain a single functional LWS1. A shorter‐shifted green‐sensitive paralog (LWS2) is found only in a few lineages. By mining teleost genomes and sequencing retinal transcriptomes, we identify elopomorphs as an additional lineage retaining LWS2 (alongside characins and osteoglossomorphs). Surprisingly, we reveal a previously overlooked, shorter‐shifted paralog, LWS3, restricted to gobies (Percomorpha) and arising from an ancestral duplication either in the teleost or in the percomorph ancestor. Structural modelling of twelve LWS opsins reveals convergent evolution at four key amino acid sites (214, 259, 261, 269) in the retinal‐binding pocket, indicating convergent substitutions in human MWS (an old‐world primate‐specific duplicate of the vertebrate LWS1), teleost LWS2, and goby LWS3 relative to red‐sensitive counterparts, consistent with repeated spectral shifts towards greener wavelengths. In several lineages, including characins, mormyrids, gobies, and primates, these shorter‐shifted LWS opsins have at least partially replaced the canonical green‐sensitive RH2‐based visual pigment. Retinal transcriptomes revealed variable lws3 expression across adult gobies, either complementing lws1 in most species, or dominating the visual opsin expression profile as in the sicydiines. In situ hybridisation in the whitebarred goby (Amblygobius phalaena; Valenciennes, 1837) showed that lws1 and lws3 are expressed in separate double‐cone members, analogous to rh2 expression in other fish species. Together, these results show that repeated convergence towards shorter LWS sensitivity in vertebrate evolution involves coordinated changes at the molecular, regulatory, and functional levels, providing a striking example of multilevel sensory adaptation.
n7c0c32db6080: Reproductive dynamics strongly influence genetic diversity and population structure, with important implications for ecological interactions and evolutionary trajectories. However, our understanding of plant reproductive dynamics remains limited due to the scarcity of long-term studies. Here, we propose a conceptual and methodological framework for tracking plant reproductive dynamics over long timescales using pollen, plant spore, and seed records preserved in sedimentary archives. The analysis of counts, morphology, and DNA from fossil propagules enables reconstruction of reproductive patterns over centennial to million-year timescales. When integrated with other palaeoproxies, these records provide insights into environmental drivers and eco-evolutionary consequences of reproductive dynamics. The proposed framework opens new avenues for optimising conservation strategies, safeguarding key ecological functions, and improving predictions of future biotic responses.
n7bc72ac7ac26: Drawing on two decades of research in East Greenland, this study shows that little auks, key seabird indicators of Arctic ecosystem health, can adapt to rapid environmental change through behavioural flexibility. However, increasing storms and mercury pollution are pushing resilience to its limits, providing an early warning of broader Arctic disruption. Abstract Long‐term ecological studies testing global change impacts are rare yet essential in the Arctic, a region warming nearly four times faster than the global average. These rapid environmental changes reshape ecosystem functioning across the pan‐Arctic and affect the livelihoods of local communities. Seabirds are widely recognised indicators of environmental change. Identifying species‐specific critical constraints is therefore essential for detecting early warning signals of population decline and ecosystem reorganisation. Little auks (Alle alle), the most abundant Arctic seabirds, are key ecosystem engineers shaping coastal environments through for example food‐web interactions and guano deposition. We present a 20‐year study (2005–2024) of an East Greenland little auk population, combining long‐term demographic monitoring with behavioural, physiological and ecotoxicological data. We quantified fitness‐related traits (adult body condition, overwinter survival and chick growth) alongside potential constraints, including parental foraging effort, trophic ecology, winter distribution, and mercury contamination in adults, eggs and chicks. Over the study period, climate‐driven ocean warming, sea‐ice decline, altered zooplankton communities, and increasing mercury exposure reshaped environmental conditions. Faced with these changes, little auks exhibited marked behavioural and dietary plasticity, allowing them to maintain relatively stable fitness metrics in most years. However, sustained monitoring revealed key constraints that undermine this apparent resilience: (a) Elevated mercury burdens may reduce aerobic diving capacity and thermal tolerance in adults and were associated with reduced reproductive performance. (b) Chick growth was strongly impaired during years with increased summer storm activity, which disrupted adult foraging trips and provisioning rates. Winter storms are also likely to negatively affect adult overwinter survival. Together, these findings show that little auks can partially buffer rapid Arctic change through behavioural flexibility, but multiple interacting climatic and contaminant stressors impose increasing, possibly cumulative constraints on performance. Identifying such critical constraints is crucial for understanding the limits of resilience in wild populations and for improving predictions of ecosystem responses to ongoing climate change.
n426fae913025: The development of durable and multifunctional nanomaterials for water treatment continues to represent a significant challenge in the field of environmental nanotechnology. In this study, ZnO/Se nanocomposites were prepared via a completely green synthetic route, utilizing Raphanus sativus –leaf extract for the biogenic production of ZnO nanoparticles and Citrus limon –peel extract for the synthesis of Se nanoparticles. The effect of selenium incorporation on the structural and functional properties of ZnO was investigated by preparing several ZnO/Se nanocomposites with varying Se concentrations, which were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), UV-Vis spectroscopy, energy dispersive X-ray analysis (EDX), and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM). The photocatalytic activity of the prepared materials was evaluated based on the degradation of methyl orange under UV irradiation, and their antimicrobial efficacy was tested against clinically relevant microbial strains. Among the tested compositions, the nanocomposite containing 2 weight percent (wt%) Se showed superior performance: it achieved a superior performance of 83.4 ± 0.7% dye degradation in 120 min, compared to 62.4% for pure ZnO. This enhanced degradation efficiency was found to be statistically significant (p< 0.05) when compared against the pristine ZnO matrix control group, as validated by independent biological triplicates (n = 3). The same Se concentration also showed the most effective antimicrobial activity compared to the other tested formulations. The improved performance at low Se concentration can likely be explained by the strengthening of the interfacial contact between ZnO and Se, which promotes efficient charge separation and reduces electron–hole recombination. These results indicate that controlled Se incorporation can significantly modulate the structural and functional properties of biogenically produced ZnO. At the same time, they highlight the potential of ZnO/Se nanocomposites prepared via green synthesis as promising candidates for multifunctional water treatment applications.
nedebf46c0bd4: Understanding how climate shapes ecosystem productivity through energetic constraints and changes in the functional properties expressed by vegetation remains challenging. This is central to trait‐based biodiversity–ecosystem functioning research in mountain grasslands where warming and environmental gradients interact. Here, we distinguish direct climatic controls on productivity from indirect pathways operating through changes in canopy functional composition, physiological state, and within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity across the European Alps. Using Sentinel‐2 time series (2017–2024), we quantified canopy functional structure from spectral proxies of pigment investment and water status, within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity using the functional richness (FRic) metric, and vegetation productivity using near‐infrared reflectance of vegetation (NIRv). We combined panel‐data models with piecewise structural equation modeling to partition climate associations into direct and trait‐mediated components operating through canopy functional properties and used varying‐coefficient models to evaluate how these pathways vary along environmental gradients. We identified two pathways linking climate to productivity. Warmer growing seasons increased productivity directly but were associated with a lower chlorophyll‐to‐carotenoid pigment balance, consistent with greater relative carotenoid investment, generating an opposing indirect pathway. Greater winter snow accumulation reduced productivity primarily through a direct pathway, while its canopy‐mediated pathways were uncertain. Climatic water deficit reduced canopy water status and within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity, but its direct and total associations with productivity were not distinguishable from zero. Environmental context modulated climate–vegetation relationships. Baseline temperature and moisture availability strongly shaped climate effects on canopy traits and productivity, whereas canopy‐property–productivity relationships varied little across space. Positive productivity responses to warming were stronger in wetter and more seasonally variable climatic contexts, but weakened where baseline winter snow accumulation was greater. Together, our findings show that short‐term productivity responses in mountain grasslands reflect a balance between direct energetic constraints and indirect pathways through integrated canopy functional properties, and that this balance varies along macroclimatic gradients. RÉSUMÉ Comprendre comment le climat façonne la productivité des écosystèmes à travers des contraintes énergétiques directes et des voies indirectes médiées par la biodiversité demeure un défi majeur en écologie du changement global, en particulier dans les prairies de montagne où le réchauffement rapide interagit avec de forts gradients environnementaux. Nous démêlons ici les effets climatiques directs sur la productivité des écosystèmes de leurs effets indirects opérant via la structure fonctionnelle de la canopée, à l'échelle de l'ensemble des Alpes européennes. À partir de séries temporelles Sentinel‐2 (2017–2024), nous avons quantifié la structure fonctionnelle de la canopée à partir de proxys spectraux liés aux pigments et à l'état hydrique, ainsi que la richesse fonctionnelle, et estimé la productivité à l'aide de la réflectance proche‐infrarouge de la végétation (NIRv). Nous avons combiné inférence causale et modèles d'équations structurelles pour partitionner les effets climatiques totaux en composantes directes et médiées par les traits, puis utilisé des modèles à coefficients variables pour analyser la modulation de ces voies le long des gradients environnementaux. Nos résultats montrent que deux voies concomitantes relient le climat à la productivité.…
n8bd63f66cc68: Trait‐based approaches help reveal how ecosystems respond to global change, but trait selection and diversity metrics can lead to different conclusions. In a semi‐arid grassland, we show that methodological choices influence inferences about functional diversity and ecosystem stability under drought. Traits aligned with environmental mechanisms captured community responses differently than commonly used traits, highlighting the value of hypothesis‐driven trait selection. Abstract Trait‐based approaches are powerful tools for understanding ecosystem resistance and resilience under global change. Yet, relationships between global change drivers, functional trait diversity and ecosystem stability remain unclear. Some inconsistencies arise from differences in trait selection and diversity indices, which reflect distinct hypotheses and can lead to divergent interpretations. This complicates determining whether observed patterns stem from methodological choices or true ecological variation. We evaluated how methodological decisions influence ecological inference by comparing functional diversity metrics and community‐weighted means calculated from different trait subsets. Using a four‐year rainfall manipulation experiment in a semi‐arid grassland near Boulder, Colorado, USA, we quantified community responses to extreme drought, irrigation and ambient conditions. We measured nine leaf, root and whole‐plant traits and grouped them into six sets based on trait‐based literature: (1) all traits, (2) commonly used traits (e.g. specific leaf area, root dry matter content), (3) mechanistic drought traits, (4) economic spectrum traits, (5) above‐ground traits and (6) below‐ground traits. For each set, we assessed drought and irrigation effects on community composition using community‐weighted means and four functional diversity indices: richness, evenness, divergence and dispersion. We also examined how trait and metric selection influenced temporal biomass stability across treatments. Treatment effects varied across metrics: functional divergence was generally robust to trait selection, while evenness, richness and dispersion were more trait‐dependent. Relationships between functional diversity and biomass stability were both metric‐ and trait‐dependent: functional dispersion tended to decrease stability under drought and irrigation for above‐ground and commonly used traits. Functional evenness increased stability under irrigation for select sets, and functional divergence and richness showed weak or inconsistent relationships with stability across treatments and trait sets. Synthesis. Our results show that methodological choices in trait selection and metrics influence conclusions about functional diversity. Trait suites aligned with environmental drivers (e.g. mechanistic drought traits) captured community responses differently than commonly used traits, highlighting the value of hypothesis‐driven selection. We recommend prioritizing traits linked to the focal ecological mechanism and testing robustness across alternative trait subsets and diversity metrics. This approach improves mechanistic interpretation, clarifies when and where diversity stabilizes ecosystem function and increases comparability across systems and studies.
nb9b9fde9e4a6: Environmental RNA (eRNA) has been increasingly used to move beyond ‘who is there’ toward ‘who is active’ and ‘what is happening’ in ecosystems. Yet, most workflows have been optimised for laboratory sequencing, and decision‐grade field use has remained sporadic. In this article, field‐ready eRNA panels are defined as curated sets of transcripts paired with process controls and a transparent scoring rule, and a build–test pathway is described from marker discovery to deployment. Candidate markers are prioritised with field constraints in mind (abundance, specificity, persistence, and confounding seasonality), and RNA class choice (mRNA, rRNA, small, and other non‐coding RNAs) is treated as a design lever for robustness. Pre‐analytics are discussed as panel engineering, with emphasis placed on capture, rapid stabilisation, and inhibitor management to preserve multi‐marker relationships. Field readout options are then compared, including isothermal amplification, CRISPR‐assisted detection, portable qPCR, and portable nanopore sequencing for on‐site verification and panel refresh. Finally, minimum controls and staged validation levels are proposed to support defensible ecological claims. Deliberate attention is directed toward shared terminology and testable standards so that discussion within and between ecology, diagnostics, and conservation practice is stimulated and priorities for future investigations are sharpened.
n61f9a883586b: Seminal fluid proteins (SFPs) play crucial roles in reproduction by shaping female post‐mating physiology and behaviour, male sperm competition and sexual conflict between the sexes. However, we know little about how abiotic ecological factors regulate SFP expression and transfer. Here, we use quantitative proteomics in adult flies from a wild Drosophila melanogaster population to test how exposure to natural temperature variation (20°C, 24°C and 28°C) across two time scales (48 h and 13d), and under either no‐ or high‐sperm competition risk, interact to shape SFP production and transfer. Short‐term exposure to different temperatures resulted in lower SFP production and transfer at 24°C under no sperm competition risk, but no differences under high sperm competition risk. In contrast, both the production and transfer of SFPs were consistently reduced across sperm competition treatments after long‐term (13d) exposure to low (20°C) and high (28°C) temperatures, including for key proteins in the sex peptide and ovulin networks that mediate female post‐copulatory responses, sperm competition and sexual conflict. Our results show that natural temperature fluctuations can have a strong effect on SFP production and transfer, and thus on post‐copulatory sexual selection dynamics.
n54ec58115f09: Understanding how demography and natural selection interact during colonization of novel environments is a central question in evolutionary biology. The Baltic Sea region combines one of the world's strongest salinity gradients with a well‐characterized postglacial history of less than ~12,000 years. The Proper Baltic Sea population showed drift‐dominated divergence consistent with a founder effect, while two discrete genomic islands of differentiation with selective sweep signatures were identified between North and Belt Sea populations, pointing to recent positive selection. A non‐synonymous mutation in SCNN1D showed striking allele frequency divergence along the salinity gradient, confirmed across ~400 individuals. nf1144a29e6e8: Effective wildlife conservation and management depends on a thorough understanding of both neutral and adaptive intraspecific genomic variation. Population structure is often well understood in many ecologically or economically important species, but the extensive population genomic resources required to characterize putatively adaptive variation and punctuated genomic regions is typically only recently available for some species, if available at all. No other regions of major differentiation were observed in the analysed samples in the Chilcotin or Quesnel River systems. These results provide additional evidence for the importance of both homeologous regions holding lrrc9 and lrrc9‐like in different geographic regions and underscore the uniqueness of upper Fraser River sockeye in this potentially adaptive island of divergence.
n99d65dfa7c6b: As climate change drives rapid environmental shifts, crops face significant challenges due to their limited adaptive genetic diversity, threatening food security. Crop wild relatives and potentially feral populations can serve as valuable reservoirs of adaptive diversity for breeding. Exploring and conserving this diversity is therefore essential, as it may encompass a wide range of adaptations. In this study, we investigate the genetic basis of local climate adaptation and the risk of maladaptation under future conditions in spontaneous populations—naturally occurring in the wild—of Brassica rapa (field mustard). A total of 62 populations were sampled, revealing strong differentiation between feral (France, Slovenia) and wild (Algeria, Sicily) populations. A genome–environment association analysis identified genomic regions associated with climatic variables, with broader patterns suggesting a polygenic architecture. Feral populations broadened the climatic range explored, but their reduced genetic diversity limited our ability to capture the full spectrum of adaptive variation in wild populations, indicating that the genetic architecture of climate adaptation is only partly shared between the two groups. We also used genomic offset (GO) analyses to assess mismatches between current and predicted‐optimal genetic composition under 2050 climate projections. A common garden experiment indicated that GO captures some component of fitness variation, with feral populations providing additional predictive information beyond the environmental space occupied by wild populations. These findings highlight the complex genetic architecture of climate adaptation in B. rapa, as well as the potential and limitations of genomic tools for guiding conservation and crop improvement under climate change.
n6d02756183bd: There are multiple mechanisms that can underlie parallel adaptation to similar habitats at the genetic level, including de novo mutations, introgression, and shared standing variation. While evidence for each pathway is emerging, few studies have directly examined how demographic processes, range expansion and introgression interact to shape the fate of adaptive alleles. By combining gene–environment association analyses with demographic inference and historical gene flow reconstruction, we evaluated whether repeated adaptation arises from de novo convergent mutations or introgression. The candidate SNP set departed strongly from neutral expectations in DMC analyses; standing variation was the best‐fitting model, although its separation from migration was modest. We also found heterogeneous allele sharing and historical introgression involving range‐margin populations, coinciding with demographic expansion. These findings suggest that standing variation, demographic history, and heterogeneous introgression may jointly contribute to repeated genomic responses across ecological gradients. A limited subset of environmentally associated candidates also overlapped with floral morphology‐associated candidates, but the magnitude of overlap was strongly threshold‐ and denominator‐dependent. These overlaps identify hypotheses concerning ecological and floral trait differentiation, but do not establish pleiotropy or a shared causal architecture. This work highlights how parallel adaptation in plants may emerge from the interplay of neutral and adaptive evolutionary mechanisms in recently diverged lineages.
nca2bb352946b: The extraordinarily polymorphic Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is an iconic genomic region that has been associated with, for example, disease susceptibility, mate choice, and fitness. Both the MHC class I and II gene families have expanded considerably in songbirds (Passeriformes) compared to other bird orders, but our understanding of the functional relevance of the large number of gene copies in songbirds is hampered by lack of data on gene expression. We therefore took advantage of longitudinal data from our wild long‐term monitored population of great reed warblers Acrocephalus arundinaceus as well as a long‐term experiment to study patterns of MHC class I (MHC‐I) gene expression during individuals' lifetimes and across generations, and between tissues. As could be expected within a species, the expressed diversity increased linearly with genomic MHC‐I diversity. However, most MHC‐I alleles were expressed at low levels, with only a handful of alleles showing moderate to high expression in each individual. The MHC‐I expression patterns in blood were highly consistent (i) over an individual's lifetime, (ii) between parents and offspring, and (iii) among siblings, and (iv) were strongly correlated with expression in other tissues. The moderately to highly expressed MHC‐I genes likely play a key role in antigen presentation in adaptive immunity and thus comprise primary targets for studies of host‐pathogen coevolution.
n98a64fac4755: The metallic colour variation of beetles is a spectacular feature that has inspired diverse human cultures. However, little is known about the genetic basis of this trait or its ecological importance. In this study, we characterize the geographical distribution, optical mechanism, genetic basis and ecological and evolutionary importance of metallic colour variation in the Nebria ingens complex, an alpine ground beetle in the Sierra Nevada, California. We find that elytral colour varies continuously across two allopatric species (from black N. ingens to green N. riversi), with hybrid populations showing intermediate coloration, and we demonstrate that the metallic colour is generated from multilayer reflectors in the epicuticle of the elytra. This finding, together with a significant correlation between colour variation and water availability, suggests that metallic variation evolves as a local adaptation to environmental variation in the N. ingens complex.
n65476f2dd8cb: Invasion fronts are the advancing edges of non‐native species' ranges and represent dynamic, non‐equilibrium boundaries where colonization, biotic interactions and rapid evolutionary processes interact. Although biological invasions are increasingly well studied, the ecological and evolutionary mechanisms operating at invasion fronts remain conceptually fragmented despite their disproportionate influence on spread dynamics, exerted impact and management. Here, we synthesize how invasion‐front geometries arise from interactions among propagule pressure, landscape permeability, long‐distance dispersal and environmental heterogeneity, producing continuous (including satellite colonies), patchy/fragmented or coalescing fronts that shift with invasion stage and spatiotemporal scales. We integrate ecological and evolutionary evidence from macro‐organisms to show how gradients from core to front can result in declining population density, increased trait divergence, spatial sorting, serial founder effects, expansion load, and behavioural and physiological differentiation. We further draw parallels with climate‐driven range expansions, while emphasizing the stronger disequilibrium and novel biotic contexts characteristic of non‐native invasion fronts. Finally, we map these dynamics onto impact trajectories, demonstrating how trait‐mediated interactions, resource reallocation and system‐level reconfiguration can emerge sequentially along the invasion gradient. By unifying ecological and evolutionary processes across appropriate spatial and temporal scales, we establish invasion fronts as powerful natural laboratories and critical leverage points for predicting, monitoring and managing biological invasions.
n1ce94024a97e: Over the past decade, chemical ecology has become increasingly integrated into the development of biological control programs, particularly Conservation Biological Control (CBC). Conservation Biological Control exploits a set of habitat manipulation practices to maintain and enhance the reproduction, survival, and efficacy of arthropod natural enemies that prey upon or parasitize insect pests. Specifically, chemical cues that convey information between living organisms, named semiochemicals, can enhance the management of herbivore populations by mediating interactions among plants, herbivores, predators, parasitoids, and their surrounding habitats. Nevertheless, translating mechanistic knowledge of chemically mediated interactions into reliable control of pest insect populations remains a major challenge. A central constraint is the persistent gap between results obtained under simplified laboratory conditions and outcomes observed in dynamic agroecosystems, where background odors, meteorological conditions, crop phenology, and multispecies interactions can modify semiochemical production and transmission, receiver responses, and ultimately, biological control agent efficacy. Additional priorities include moving from the study of individual compounds to ecologically realistic blends of bioactive volatiles; identifying non-target and food-web effects; integrating semiochemical-based interventions with habitat management and selective crop-protection practices; and developing standardized field metrics that connect natural enemy recruitment with predation, parasitism, herbivore population control, and reduction in crop damage. Progress will therefore require multiscale experimentation, closer integration of analytical chemistry with behavioral and field ecology that balance efficacy, ecological safety, and operational feasibility. From this perspective, CBC involves more than enhancing the abundance or activity of arthropod natural enemies: it requires the deliberate management of information flow across multitrophic levels to establish a more predictive and mechanistically grounded framework for biological herbivore population control. Here, are reviewed the principal issues that chemical ecology should address to advance CBC, focusing on how semiochemical production, transmission, and perception vary across plant genotypes, herbivore communities, natural-enemy guilds, microbiomes, agricultural practices, and landscape contexts.
nf3d0cdea7b37: How much is watershed management and the protection and restoration of habitat restoration contributing to salmon and steelhead population recovery? This question has led to expansion of research and monitoring programs whose goal is to understand and quantify the contribution watershed management and habitat restoration is making to salmon populations (Diefenderfer et al. 2016). One component of this evaluation effort has been the establishment of a network of watersheds where habitat treatments are coupled with intensive, long-term monitoring to evaluate physical and biological responses to these treatments (Bennett et al. 2016). These sites have been labeled Intensively Monitored Watersheds (IMWs) (Bilby et al. 2005;Bennett et al. 2016). Data required to evaluate the ecological response to habitat actions are expensive to collect and must be gathered over many years to provide confidence in their conclusions (Roni et al. 2008). Because they are costly to implement, IMWs occur in a few select locations with the goal of enabling enough data collection over a sufficient period to develop an understanding of fish and habitat response that can be applied more broadly to restoration efforts.The IMW approach has been used for over six decades to evaluate aquatic ecosystem response to land use practices and habitat restoration. The Alsea Watershed Study, which was initiated in the 1950s, evaluated the response of Coho salmon and Cutthroat trout to alternative logging methods in three small watersheds on the Oregon coast. Results from this study provided much of the technical rationale for the establishment of forestry regulations intended to protect aquatic habitat in the Pacific Northwest. In the 1970s, an ambitious watershed-level project was initiated at Carnation Creek on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, that evaluated the response of hydrology, water quality and salmonid fish populations to logging of a previously unlogged watershed (Tschaplinski, this volume). The results of this study led to a revision of the forestry code for B.C. and influenced revisions to forestry practice rules in other areas of the Pacific Northwest. In the early 2000s multiple IMWs were established in the Pacific Northwest to evaluate the response of habitat and fish populations to freshwater and estuarine salmon habitat restoration efforts. Similar long-term studies have been undertaken in other parts of the world where salmon recovery is an important societal objective.The IMW approach as it has been applied is not without flaws and complications (Bisson et al., 2024). Logistical challenges to implementing study designs due to differences between treated and references watersheds, complexity of statistical study designs, permitting, funding, and implementing habitat treatments have all been identified over the years, but despite these difficulties IMWs have generated information useful for improving restoration strategies (Bilby et al. 2022). Furthermore, intensive. long-term monitoring at watershed scales remains one of the few tools available for empirically quantifying the contribution habitat restoration can make to salmon population recovery.What were the objectives of this special issue?The goal of this issue, "IMWs -A tool to help us understand how ecological processes of stream ecosystems and how these processes are affected by stream and watershed restoration", was to identify ecosystem changes resulting from stream and watershed habitat restoration using the IMW framework and assess salmon and steelhead response to these changes.…
nd9d3b6501162: IntroductionWe use a reverse engineering approach to develop a linear programming model for the behavioural ecology of early hominins (australopithecines).MethodsOur models are based on a recently developed family of empirical models that use climate to predict how animals allocate time to core activities and, from this, whether or not they can balance their activity budget at a specific location as a guide to whether they could survive there. We first use models developed for baboons and chimpanzees to predict whether australopithecines could have survived at sites where they are known to have been present, had they been ecological baboons or ecological chimpanzees. We show that none of the hominins behaved ecologically like either baboons or chimpanzees: the models for these genera fail to predict their known distribution. We then use the equations from the baboon and chimpanzee models to build a model that predicts the known distribution of the australopithecines more precisely.ResultsThe results suggest that they had evolved their own distinctive response to environmental parameters that seems to be related to exploiting a habitat (lacustrine and riverine flood plains) that no other living primate exploits. Our analysis suggests that, in exploiting open flood plain habitats, australopithecines likely foraged as a single group for protection against predators rather than living in fission-fusion communities like modern chimpanzees. The models indicate that climate change post 2.4 Ma resulted in declining group sizes leading to eventual extinction, associated with the appearance of early Homo with novel adaptations for coping with a warmer, drier climate.DiscussionOur analyses suggest that exploiting quantitative models can offer novel insights into the behavioural biology of extinct species, thereby providing rich insights into the forces that drove evolution within particular lineages.
